Every permanent surface water body in Botswana is fed by rain that fell somewhere else — in the Angolan highlands, in Zimbabwe, or in South Africa — which makes water a diplomatic as well as a hydrological subject.

Against this dry, flat baseline sit two of the most remarkable landforms in Africa. In the north-west, the Okavango River, having flowed some 1,600 kilometres from Angola, fails to reach the sea and instead spreads across a tectonic depression into an inland delta of between about 6,000 and 15,000 square kilometres, depending on the season and the year. In the north-east lie the Makgadikgadi Pans, salt flats totalling around 12,000 square kilometres that are the desiccated floor of a vast Pleistocene lake.

Botswana's political geography reinforces the physical. It borders South Africa to the south and south-east, Namibia to the west and north, Zimbabwe to the north-east, and Zambia at a single point on the Zambezi at Kazungula where the boundary is only about 150 metres long — among the shortest international borders in existence. The nearest seaport, Walvis Bay in Namibia, is more than 1,100 kilometres away by road.

The boundaries are artefacts of the late nineteenth-century partition of Africa rather than expressions of physical or ethnic divisions. The straight lines of the western and southern frontiers were drawn in European capitals across sand that looks identical on both sides, and the Bechuanaland Protectorate was declared in 1885 largely to secure the road north to Matabeleland against German and Boer expansion. Only in the north-east does the boundary follow physical features.

sections.heading: Deep Foundations: Cratons, Karoo Rocks and Kalahari Sand
sections.body:
Beneath the sand, Botswana's geology records more than three billion years of Earth history, and it is the reason a country with almost no exposed rock became one of the world's great mineral producers.

The oldest and most important element is the Kaapvaal Craton, a fragment of Archaean continental crust more than 2.7 billion years old that underlies eastern Botswana and much of South Africa. Cratons of this kind are thick, cold, rigid and chemically depleted, and their deep keels — extending 200 kilometres or more into the mantle — sit within the pressure and temperature window where diamond is stable. That is why diamonds are found on old cratons and essentially nowhere else. The Zimbabwe Craton lies to the north-east, and the two are welded along the Limpopo Mobile Belt, a zone of high-grade metamorphic rocks that records their collision roughly two billion years ago. Western and central Botswana are underlain by younger Proterozoic belts, including the Ghanzi-Chobe Belt and the Kheis and Damara systems, which host the copper-silver mineralisation of the Kalahari Copperbelt.

Diamonds reach the surface through kimberlite pipes, narrow carrot-shaped conduits of volatile-rich magma that ascend from depths of 150 kilometres or more at speeds sufficient to carry diamond upward before it converts to graphite. Botswana's principal pipes were emplaced in the Cretaceous, around 90 to 100 million years ago, and they are extraordinarily rich: the Orapa pipe covers about 118 hectares at surface and Jwaneng is generally regarded as the most valuable diamond mine in the world by revenue.

Overlying the ancient basement across much of the country are sedimentary and volcanic rocks of the Karoo Supergroup, laid down from the Late Carboniferous to the Early Jurassic in a vast intracontinental basin that spanned Gondwana. The Karoo sequence records glaciation, then swamp forests that became coal — Botswana's coal resources are very large, with estimates commonly quoted in the region of 200 billion tonnes, though only a fraction is economically recoverable — then desert sandstones, and finally the Stormberg basalts erupted around 183 million years ago as Gondwana began to break apart.

Capping everything is the Kalahari Group: unconsolidated to weakly cemented sands, gravels and calcretes deposited from the Cretaceous onward and still accumulating. The Kalahari sand surface extends across some 2.5 million square kilometres from northern South Africa to the Congo Basin, making it the largest continuous sand surface on Earth. It is a depositional blanket, not a mountain range, and it is what makes Botswana geologically difficult: exploration must be done through up to 100 metres of cover using geophysics and drilling rather than by looking at outcrops.

Finally, the country is not tectonically inert. The Okavango Graben in the north-west is a young extensional structure and the south-western tip of the East African Rift System, and it generates genuine seismicity: an earthquake of magnitude 6.5 struck near Moiyabana in central Botswana in April 2017, felt across southern Africa. On geological timescales the rift is slowly tearing the region apart, and it is the reason the Okavango Delta exists at all.

sections.heading: The Kalahari: A Sand Basin, Not a True Desert
sections.body:
The Kalahari is the defining landscape of Botswana, covering roughly seventy per cent of the country, and it is routinely misdescribed. The name derives from the Setswana Kgalagadi, usually glossed as "the great thirst" or "the waterless place", and the thirst is real. But by the standard climatological definition — annual rainfall below 250 millimetres — only the extreme south-west qualifies as desert. Most of the Kalahari receives 250 to 500 millimetres a year and supports continuous vegetation cover of grasses, shrubs and open woodland. It is properly a semi-arid savanna on deep sand, sometimes called a thirstland: a place with plenty of rain by desert standards and almost no surface water, because the sand swallows everything that falls.

That contradiction is the key to understanding it. Kalahari sand is highly permeable, so rainfall infiltrates immediately rather than running off. There are few streams, few gullies and almost no drainage network. Water that does not evaporate or transpire percolates downward, and in most of the basin the water table lies tens to hundreds of metres below the surface. The consequence for ecology is profound: vegetation depends entirely on soil moisture held in the sand profile, plants are deep-rooted, and many Kalahari animals — gemsbok, springbok, eland — are physiologically adapted to obtain most of their water from vegetation, tubers and melons rather than from drinking.

The surface is not uniform. Large tracts, particularly in the south-west and in the north near the Namibian border, carry ancient linear dunes, mostly now fixed and vegetated, aligned with wind directions that prevailed during drier glacial periods and preserved as long parallel ridges tens of kilometres in length. Elsewhere the sand is a flat sheet. Duricrusts — calcrete formed by carbonate precipitation and silcrete by silica — outcrop where the sand is thin, and calcrete provides most of the country's road-building aggregate.

Two features deserve particular mention. Pans are shallow closed depressions, from a few metres to many kilometres across, floored with clay rather than sand, which hold water for days or weeks after rain and act as critical wildlife concentration points; there are tens of thousands of them. Mekgacha, or fossil valleys, are dry drainage lines such as the Okwa, Deception and Passarge valleys in the Central Kalahari, cut when the region was far wetter and now carrying water only in exceptional years.

Human presence in the Kalahari is ancient. San peoples — including the Ju/'hoansi, Nharo and G/wi — have occupied the region for many thousands of years, and the archaeological and rock-art record at sites such as the Tsodilo Hills documents continuous occupation over a very long span. The older anthropological picture of San communities as isolated survivors of a pristine hunter-gatherer past has been substantially revised: the archaeological evidence shows long-standing trade with farming and herding neighbours, and most contemporary Kalahari communities have mixed livelihoods.

sections.heading: Relief and Drainage: A Country With Almost No Rivers
sections.body:
Botswana's drainage is best understood as three separate and largely disconnected systems, none of which behaves like a normal river network.

The first is the eastern system, which drains to the Indian Ocean via the Limpopo. The Limpopo forms the south-eastern boundary with South Africa, and Botswana contributes to it through a series of tributaries running off the eastern hardveld: the Notwane, which passes Gaborone, the Bonwapitse, Mahalapye, Lotsane, Motloutse and Shashe. All are ephemeral or strongly seasonal, flowing for days or weeks after summer storms and standing as chains of sandy pools for the rest of the year. The eastern strip, where these rivers cut into rock rather than sand, is the only part of the country with recognisable relief: low hills, koppies and broken ground on the fringe of the plateau, and, unsurprisingly, it is where most Batswana live.

The second is the northern system, which does not drain to any ocean at all. The Okavango, the Kwando-Linyanti-Chobe and the Nata all terminate in Botswana's interior, either evaporating in the Okavango Delta or discharging into the Makgadikgadi basin. The Chobe is a hydrological curiosity: at very high Zambezi floods the flow at Kazungula can reverse and push water back up the Chobe, and the Savuti Channel, linking the Linyanti swamps to the Mababe Depression, has switched between flowing and bone-dry several times in the last century for reasons that appear to be tectonic rather than climatic.

The third is the southern system, essentially fossil. The Molopo forms the border with South Africa in the south and the Nossob runs through the Kgalagadi; both are dry valleys that have not flowed along their full length in living memory, though they carry water locally after exceptional rain. The Auob and Nossob dry beds in the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park have flowed only a handful of times in the last century.

Between these systems lies the Kalahari's endorheic interior, where there is no organised drainage at all. Rainwater collects in pans, evaporates, or sinks.

The relief that does exist is modest and localised. The Tsodilo Hills in the north-west rise about 400 metres above the surrounding sand as quartzite inselbergs, the highest reaching roughly 1,400 metres; they are sacred to local San and Hambukushu communities, carry more than 4,500 recorded rock paintings, and were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. The Aha Hills nearby contain the dolomite Gcwihaba Caverns, a rare karst system with stalactites and large bat colonies. The Tswapong and Lepokole hills in the east, and the Otse and Kgale hills near Gaborone, complete a very short list.

The Mababe Depression, between the delta and the Chobe, is a flat clay basin that was once a lake bed connected to the Makgadikgadi system, and it fills intermittently when the Savuti Channel runs. Its abrupt edges, the raised Magwikhwe Sand Ridge along its western margin — an ancient shoreline some 100 kilometres long — and its sudden transitions between grassland and mopane make it one of the clearest visible records of how much wetter this landscape used to be.

sections.heading: The Okavango Delta: How an Inland Delta Forms
sections.body:
The Okavango Delta is the largest and most celebrated of the world's inland deltas, and it exists because of an accident of tectonics superimposed on an accident of climate.

The river itself rises as the Cubango and Cuito in the Bié Plateau of central Angola, where rainfall exceeds 1,000 millimetres a year, and travels roughly 1,600 kilometres south-east, forming part of the Angola-Namibia border and crossing Namibia's Zambezi Region before entering Botswana. It carries about 9 to 11 cubic kilometres of water a year — figures vary by year and by measurement point — along with a substantial sediment load of fine quartz sand.

On entering Botswana the river is confined for about 100 kilometres within the Panhandle, a strip roughly 10 to 15 kilometres wide bounded by two parallel faults. These faults are the significant part. The Okavango Graben is the south-westernmost expression of the East African Rift System, a nascent rift propagating into the interior of southern Africa. At the Gumare Fault the confinement ends and the river spills onto a very gently sloping alluvial fan, and at the downstream end the Kunyere and Thamalakane faults act as a barrier that stops the water leaving. The delta is, in effect, water ponded in a slowly subsiding half-graben.

The gradient across the fan is extraordinarily low — on the order of 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 5,000, a drop of roughly 60 metres over some 250 kilometres. Water therefore moves at a walking pace or slower, spreading through a labyrinth of channels, lagoons, floodplains and about 150,000 islands.

The hydrological budget is startling. Somewhere in the region of 96 to 98 per cent of the water entering the delta is lost to evaporation and plant transpiration; only about two per cent leaves as outflow, principally down the Thamalakane and Boteti rivers past Maun toward Makgadikgadi, and a small further fraction recharges groundwater. By any normal expectation, a basin losing that proportion of its water to evaporation should become a salt pan. The Okavango's water instead remains remarkably fresh.

The explanation, worked out over several decades of research, is a subtle island-scale process. Trees fringing the many small islands transpire enormous volumes of water, drawing groundwater upward beneath the island and concentrating dissolved salts in the island centres, where they precipitate as carbonate crusts and eventually as bare white salt-encrusted cores. Dense saline water then sinks beneath the island rather than diffusing back into the surrounding swamp. The delta effectively packages its own salt into thousands of small dumps, keeping the flowing water clean — a mechanism with few close parallels anywhere.

Sediment behaves similarly. The roughly 170,000 tonnes of sand the river delivers each year is deposited within the fan rather than carried through, and the channels consequently build up their own beds above the surrounding floodplain, held in place by dense papyrus root mats along their banks. When a channel eventually chokes and its levees fail, the flow avulses sideways into a new course and the old one dries within a few seasons. The delta is therefore not a fixed map but a slowly migrating pattern.

sections.heading: The Flood Pulse and the Living Delta
sections.body:
What makes the Okavango extraordinary ecologically is not simply that it is wet but that its wetness arrives out of phase with everything around it.

The rains fall in the Angolan highlands between roughly December and March. Because the river is long and the delta gradient is minuscule, the flood takes months to arrive: the pulse reaches the Panhandle around March and spreads slowly through the system, reaching its farthest extent near Maun and the lower Boteti between June and August. This means that peak flooding occurs in the middle of the southern African dry season, when the surrounding Kalahari is at its most parched. The delta expands from a permanent core of perhaps 6,000 square kilometres to as much as 15,000 square kilometres at high flood, and the difference between a low-flood and a high-flood year can be several thousand square kilometres.

The consequences for wildlife are immense. As the dry season deepens and Kalahari pans empty, animals converge on the delta and on the Chobe and Linyanti systems, producing some of the highest dry-season concentrations of large mammals in Africa. Elephants, buffalo, zebra, giraffe, lechwe, hippopotamus and crocodile occupy the water and its margins, and the predator guild is essentially complete — lion, leopard, cheetah, spotted hyena, and one of the most important remaining populations of African wild dog. Bird diversity exceeds 480 recorded species, including large breeding colonies of storks, herons and egrets, and the delta is a key site for slaty egret and wattled crane.

Vegetation is arranged in sharp zones by flooding depth and duration: permanent swamp dominated by papyrus and Miscanthus reed, seasonally flooded grassland that is the most productive grazing in the region, and dry islands bearing riverine forest of jackalberry, sausage tree, mangosteen and real fan palm. Termite mounds built by Macrotermes species are the seed of most islands: a mound raises ground a metre or so above the floodplain, trees colonise it, sediment accumulates, and over centuries an island grows.

The system is dynamic rather than fixed. Channels silt up and are abandoned; papyrus blockages divert flow; new distributaries open. The Nqoga, Jao, Boro, Santantadibe and Thaoge channels have all been major or minor at different times over the last two centuries, and the Thaoge in the west largely failed in the nineteenth century, drying areas that had been permanently flooded.

The delta was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in June 2014, becoming the thousandth site on the list. Roughly a third of it lies within the Moremi Game Reserve, proclaimed in 1963 by the Batawana people — the first protected area in southern Africa created by a local community on its own land.

sections.heading: Makgadikgadi: The Floor of a Vanished Lake
sections.body:
East of the Okavango, across a low sand threshold, lie the Makgadikgadi Pans — the flat, blinding, salt-crusted floor of one of the largest lakes ever to have existed in Africa.

The two principal pans are Ntwetwe in the west and Sua, also spelled Sowa, in the east, together with numerous smaller pans such as Nxai and Kudiakam. Their combined surface is usually given as about 12,000 square kilometres, and they lie within a much larger basin. For most of the year they are dry, cracked, salt-encrusted clay so flat and featureless that the horizon curves visibly and vehicles navigate by compass and GPS. In good rainy seasons, water from local rainfall and from the Nata River, which rises in Zimbabwe, floods parts of Sua Pan to a depth of a few tens of centimetres, and the transformation is dramatic: tens of thousands of greater and lesser flamingos arrive to breed, along with pelicans and waterfowl, and the surrounding grasslands support a zebra and wildebeest migration that is among the largest remaining in Africa.

The pans are the residue of Palaeo-Lake Makgadikgadi, a body of water whose maximum extent is debated but which is commonly estimated to have covered somewhere between 60,000 and 80,000 square kilometres at its highest stands, with shoreline features preserved as beach ridges and wave-cut terraces at elevations around 945 metres. At its greatest, it was fed not only by the Okavango but by the Zambezi and Kwando as well, before tectonic movement along the Okavango Graben and the capture of the Zambezi by its lower course diverted those rivers away. The lake fluctuated repeatedly through the Pleistocene, filling during humid phases and shrinking during arid ones, and its final desiccation occurred within the last several thousand years.

This palaeoenvironment attracted wide attention in 2019 when a study led by Vanessa Hayes published in Nature proposed the Makgadikgadi-Okavango wetland as the homeland of the earliest anatomically modern human maternal lineage, roughly 200,000 years ago, based on mitochondrial DNA from southern African populations. The claim received substantial criticism from geneticists and palaeoanthropologists, who argued that mitochondrial DNA alone cannot locate a population origin and that the fossil and archaeological record points to a more distributed African origin. It remains an interesting hypothesis rather than an established finding, and it is worth treating with caution.

Economically the pans matter for their chemistry. Brines beneath Sua Pan are pumped and processed at Sua Town for soda ash and salt, the country's principal non-diamond mineral operation outside coal and copper. Ecologically they are fragile: the crust is thin, vehicle tracks persist for decades, and vehicles regularly break through into the mud beneath after rain. The Makgadikgadi Pans National Park and Nxai Pan National Park protect parts of the system, and the Nata Sanctuary, run by surrounding communities, protects a key flamingo area.

sections.heading: Climate: Semi-Arid, Highly Variable and Warming Fast
sections.body:
Botswana's climate is subtropical semi-arid, dominated by its position beneath the descending limb of the Hadley circulation around 20 to 27 degrees south, where subsiding air suppresses cloud formation for most of the year.

The year divides sharply. The rainy season runs from about November to March or April, when the Intertropical Convergence Zone and associated tropical lows push south and rainfall arrives almost entirely as afternoon and evening convective thunderstorms — intense, localised, and highly variable. It is entirely normal for one village to receive 40 millimetres and another 20 kilometres away to receive nothing on the same day. The dry season, May to October, is essentially rainless.

The rainfall gradient runs from north-east to south-west. Kasane in the extreme north-east averages roughly 650 millimetres a year; Gaborone in the south-east around 530; Ghanzi in the west around 400; and Tsabong in the far south-west under 250. Inter-annual variability is high, with coefficients of variation of 25 to 40 per cent, meaning that the "average" year is uncommon. Much of this variability tracks the El Niño-Southern Oscillation: El Niño events are strongly associated with drought in southern Africa, and the severe droughts of 1982-84, 1991-92, 2015-16 and 2018-19 all coincided with El Niño conditions.

Temperatures are continental in character because of the altitude and the distance from the sea. Summer maxima routinely reach 35 to 40 degrees Celsius and can exceed 43 in the Kgalagadi. Winter is dry and sunny with warm days around 22 to 25 degrees, but nights are cold: the clear dry air radiates heat efficiently, and frost occurs annually across much of the country, with Kalahari minima occasionally falling to minus 5 degrees or lower. The daily range in winter can exceed 25 degrees.

The critical climatic fact, however, is the water balance. Potential evaporation is roughly 2,000 to 2,600 millimetres a year, four to ten times the rainfall. There is no month in which rainfall exceeds potential evaporation anywhere in the country. Every drop that falls is competing against an atmosphere that wants it back.

Botswana is warming faster than the global average, as continental interiors generally do. Observed warming over recent decades is in the region of 0.02 to 0.03 degrees Celsius per year at many stations, and climate models project further warming of roughly 2 to 4 degrees or more by the end of the century under higher-emissions scenarios. Projections for rainfall are much less certain — models disagree on the sign of the change — but there is reasonable agreement that rainfall will become more variable, with a shorter, more intense wet season and longer dry spells within it. For a country whose agriculture is almost entirely rain-fed and whose water security is marginal, that variability may matter more than the mean.

sections.heading: Water: Groundwater, Dams and Shared Rivers
sections.body:
Water is the binding constraint on almost everything in Botswana, and the country's water geography has three distinct components.

Groundwater is the foundation. It supplies the majority of the country's water by volume for rural, livestock and mining use — figures around 60 to 80 per cent are commonly cited depending on how the accounting is done — and for most of the Kalahari it is the only source. Aquifers occur in Karoo sandstones, in fractured basement rock, and in localised Kalahari sands. Much of this groundwater is old, with radiocarbon ages of thousands to tens of thousands of years, recharged during wetter Pleistocene conditions, and receiving very little modern recharge — under 5 millimetres a year over much of the Kalahari, and in places effectively none. Where that is true, pumping is mining a finite resource rather than harvesting a renewable one, and drawdown around heavily used wellfields is a recognised problem. Water quality is also an issue: deep Kalahari groundwater is frequently saline or high in fluoride and nitrate.

Surface water storage is concentrated in the east, where the ephemeral Limpopo tributaries can be dammed. The major reservoirs are Gaborone Dam on the Notwane, Letsibogo Dam on the Motloutse, Dikgatlhong Dam on the Shashe — the largest by capacity — plus Thune, Ntimbale, Shashe and Bokaa. These are highly vulnerable to drought: Gaborone Dam fell below five per cent of capacity in 2015 and was effectively dry, forcing severe restrictions on the capital. The engineering response has been the North-South Carrier, a pipeline of some 360 kilometres transferring water from the northern dams to Gaborone, now being expanded in a second phase.

The third component is transboundary, and it is where geography becomes diplomacy. Botswana shares every significant river it has. The Okavango is governed by the Permanent Okavango River Basin Water Commission, established in 1994 between Angola, Namibia and Botswana; Namibia has periodically proposed abstraction from the river for its Eastern National Water Carrier, and Angola's post-war development plans include irrigation in the headwaters. Either would reduce inflow to the delta. The Zambezi is managed through the Zambezi Watercourse Commission, and Botswana has explored abstraction at Kazungula. The Limpopo is shared with South Africa, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, and is already heavily committed upstream.

Demand is rising from mining, from a growing urban population, and from irrigation ambitions. Consumption per person is modest, and Botswana has been comparatively effective at rural water supply, with the great majority of the population having access to an improved source. But the long-term arithmetic is uncomfortable: a warming, more variable climate, non-renewable groundwater in the west, drought-prone surface storage in the east, and rivers whose upstream users have their own plans.

sections.heading: Vegetation: Savanna Woodland on Sand
sections.body:
Botswana lies almost entirely within the Zambezian phytogeographic region, and its vegetation is savanna in the strict sense — a continuous grass layer with a discontinuous woody layer — modulated by rainfall, soil depth, fire and grazing.

The broadest division is between the drier south-west and the wetter north-east. In the south and centre, Kalahari Acacia-Baikiaea woodland and shrub savanna dominate, with thorn trees of the genera Vachellia and Senegalia — camel thorn, black thorn, umbrella thorn — over a grass layer of Eragrostis, Stipagrostis and Schmidtia species. Camel thorn is the keystone tree of the southern Kalahari, rooting to great depth, fixing nitrogen, and providing the only shade for tens of kilometres.

North of roughly the twentieth parallel, mopane takes over. Colophospermum mopane forms near-monospecific woodland across enormous areas of northern Botswana, recognisable by its butterfly-shaped leaves that fold vertically in the heat to reduce transpiration. Mopane tolerates heavy clay and seasonal waterlogging that other trees cannot, and it grows either as tall woodland or, where soils are poor or elephant pressure is high, as dense scrub a couple of metres tall — the notorious mopane scrub that makes off-road travel miserable.

On the deep Kalahari sands of the Chobe area, Zambezi teak, Baikiaea plurijuga, forms tall dry forest, historically logged for railway sleepers and now much reduced. Silver terminalia sandveld covers extensive areas of central and northern sand. Riparian forest along the Okavango, Chobe and Linyanti supports jackalberry, sausage tree, knobthorn, leadwood and marula, and the real fan palm, Hyphaene petersiana, is a signature of the delta islands.

Specialised communities occupy the extremes. Papyrus and Miscanthus reedbeds fill the permanent swamps. Halophytic grasses and low succulent shrubs fringe the salt pans, giving way to bare salt at the centre. Grassland without trees is uncommon but occurs on the seasonally flooded plains and on the pan margins.

Two vegetation-change processes are significant and both are contested in detail. Bush encroachment — the thickening of woody shrubs at the expense of grass — has been widely documented on Botswana rangelands, particularly around boreholes and in heavily grazed communal areas. The mechanism most commonly proposed is that heavy grazing removes the grass competition and suppresses fire, allowing shrub seedlings to establish; rising atmospheric carbon dioxide, which favours woody plants over tropical grasses, is a plausible additional driver. The second is elephant impact in the north, where very high densities have converted woodland to shrubland along the Chobe riverfront. Whether this represents degradation or a natural cycle of woodland and grassland alternation is genuinely disputed among ecologists, and the answer has real policy consequences.

Fire is the third great shaping force and is often underestimated. Large areas of northern Botswana burn every year in the late dry season, mostly from human ignition, and the fire regime determines whether savanna tips toward grassland or toward closed woodland. Frequent hot late-season fires kill woody seedlings and maintain open grass; fire exclusion allows shrubs to escape the flame zone and thicken. Managing fire, rather than eliminating it, is now the accepted approach in the protected areas.

sections.heading: Wildlife and the Protected-Area Estate
sections.body:
Botswana devotes an unusually large share of its territory to conservation. National parks and game reserves cover roughly 17 to 18 per cent of the land, and when Wildlife Management Areas and controlled hunting areas are included the total under some form of wildlife land use approaches 38 to 40 per cent — among the highest proportions of any country.

The Central Kalahari Game Reserve, proclaimed in 1961, covers 52,800 square kilometres, making it the second-largest protected area of its kind in the world and larger than several European countries. It protects the fossil valleys and pan systems of the central Kalahari and its arid-adapted fauna: gemsbok, springbok, eland, red hartebeest, giraffe and the black-maned Kalahari lion. It has also been the site of a long and bitter dispute over the residence rights of G/wi and G//ana San communities relocated from the reserve in the 1990s and 2000s, on which the Botswana High Court ruled in 2006 that the removals were unlawful; implementation has remained contentious.

Chobe National Park, about 11,700 square kilometres in the north, contains the highest elephant densities anywhere. Botswana holds the world's largest elephant population, most recent aerial surveys putting it in the region of 130,000 animals, with the wider Kavango-Zambezi population around 220,000 to 230,000. Moremi Game Reserve covers roughly 5,000 square kilometres of the eastern delta. Makgadikgadi Pans and Nxai Pan national parks protect the pan systems and the zebra migration, and the Northern Tuli Game Reserve in the eastern corner is largely privately held.

Two transboundary initiatives are notable. The Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park, formalised in 2000 with South Africa, was Africa's first formally established peace park and covers about 38,000 square kilometres of dune country across the Auob and Nossob valleys. The Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, signed in 2011 by Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, covers roughly 520,000 square kilometres and is the largest such area in the world, its purpose being to restore migration corridors between fragmented populations.

The principal conservation conflict is fencing. Veterinary cordon fences, built from the 1950s onward to separate cattle from buffalo and control foot-and-mouth disease so that beef could be exported to European markets, run for thousands of kilometres across the country. They achieved their veterinary purpose but severed migration routes. The Kuke fence, erected in 1958 across the north of the Central Kalahari, is associated with catastrophic wildebeest mortality during the droughts of the 1960s and 1980s, when animals moving toward water in the delta died against the wire in very large numbers. Balancing beef exports against wildlife movement remains an unresolved tension in Botswana's land-use planning, and several fences have since been realigned or removed where the veterinary case weakened.

White and black rhino were reintroduced to the Okavango from the 2000s and the population grew to several hundred, but a sharp escalation in poaching from about 2018 forced emergency dehorning and translocation of animals out of the delta. Losses over the following few years ran into the hundreds. Protected-area extent, however impressive on a map, does not by itself secure a species.

sections.heading: People and Settlement: The Eastern Corridor
sections.body:
Botswana's human geography is startlingly concentrated. Roughly eighty per cent of the population lives in the eastern hardveld, a strip perhaps 100 kilometres wide running from Ramotswa in the south to Kasane in the north-east, following the line of better soils, higher rainfall, exposed bedrock with accessible groundwater, and — decisively — the railway built in 1897 as part of Cecil Rhodes's Cape-to-Cairo scheme.

The 2022 census recorded 2,346,179 people. Gaborone, the capital, holds around a quarter of a million within the city boundary and considerably more in its surrounding conurbation, which includes Tlokweng, Mogoditshane and Gabane. Gaborone is unusual in being an almost entirely planned twentieth-century capital: until independence in 1966 the Bechuanaland Protectorate was administered from Mafeking, inside South Africa, and a new capital was laid out from 1964 on a greenfield site chosen for its water supply on the Notwane. Francistown in the north-east is the second city; Molepolole, Serowe, Maun, Kanye, Mochudi, Mahalapye, Palapye, Selebi-Phikwe and Lobatse complete the main urban list.

The traditional Tswana settlement pattern is distinctive and helps explain the census figures. Historically, Tswana merafe lived in very large nucleated villages — Serowe, Molepolole and Kanye each numbered in the tens of thousands in the nineteenth century, extraordinary for pre-industrial southern Africa — with a threefold residence system: the village proper, the lands where crops were grown some kilometres away, and the cattle post further out on the sandveld. Households moved seasonally between them. This means many people classified as rural in fact live in dense settlements, and it also means a great deal of the country's land is used extensively rather than being empty.

Urbanisation has been rapid: roughly 70 to 73 per cent of the population is now classified as urban or peri-urban, up from around ten per cent at independence, driven by mining employment, government service and drought pushing people off the land.

Ethnically and linguistically, Setswana is the national language and English the official language of government. The eight principal Tswana merafe — Bangwato, Bakwena, Bangwaketse, Batawana, Bakgatla, Bamalete, Barolong and Batlokwa — dominate politically and demographically. Substantial non-Tswana populations include the Kalanga in the north-east, the Herero and Hambukushu in the north-west, the Bayeyi and Basubiya of the delta and Chobe, and San peoples across the Kalahari, whose combined numbers are in the tens of thousands and whose position remains the most difficult question in Botswana's domestic politics.

Land tenure reflects this history: approximately 70 per cent of land is tribal land administered by land boards under the Tribal Land Act of 1968, about a quarter is state land including the national parks, and a small remainder is freehold.

sections.heading: Economic Geography: Diamonds, Cattle and Wildlife
sections.body:
Botswana's economy is a textbook case of how geology can restructure a country's geography within a single generation.

At independence in September 1966 the Bechuanaland Protectorate was among the poorest countries in the world, with a few kilometres of tarred road, a per-capita income in the region of seventy US dollars, an economy based on cattle and on remittances from men working in South African mines, and a treasury dependent on British grants. In 1967 the Orapa kimberlite pipe was discovered, followed by Letlhakane and, in 1972, by Jwaneng in the Naledi River valley south-west of Gaborone. Production began at Orapa in 1971 and at Jwaneng in 1982.

The institutional response mattered as much as the discovery. Botswana negotiated a fifty-fifty joint venture with De Beers, creating Debswana, and took a substantial equity stake in the parent company. Revenues were channelled through fiscal rules that limited recurrent spending and directed mineral income into infrastructure, education and health, and into a stabilisation fund. Between the 1960s and the 1990s Botswana recorded one of the highest sustained growth rates in the world. Diamonds have at times supplied more than eighty per cent of export earnings and around a third of gross domestic product, though the share has declined as the economy diversified and as diamond markets weakened. Karowe mine, operated by Lucara, has produced several of the largest gem diamonds ever recovered, including the 1,109-carat Lesedi La Rona in 2015 and the 1,758-carat Sewelô in 2019. In 2013 De Beers moved its rough-diamond sorting and sales operations from London to Gaborone, a significant piece of downstream capture.

Other mineral geography is less happy. Copper-nickel mining at Selebi-Phikwe supported a town of tens of thousands from 1973 until the BCL mine closed abruptly in 2016. Coal is mined at Morupule to fuel power stations, and Botswana's coal resources are enormous but stranded by distance from any port. Soda ash and salt come from Sua Pan.

Cattle remain culturally and spatially central even where they are economically secondary. The national herd fluctuates around two million head, concentrated on communal grazing in the east and on fenced ranches allocated under the Tribal Grazing Land Policy of 1975. Beef exports through the Botswana Meat Commission abattoir at Lobatse, historically to European markets under preferential access, are the reason the veterinary cordon fences exist. Overgrazing around boreholes produces the characteristic piosphere — concentric zones of bare ground, then degraded shrubland, then intact rangeland — visible from the air across the Kalahari.

Tourism is the third pillar and the most geographically concentrated. Botswana pursues a deliberate high-value, low-volume policy, charging substantial park fees and limiting concessions, with the industry focused overwhelmingly on the Okavango, Chobe and Makgadikgadi. Maun functions as its logistical capital. The policy is contested — it maximises revenue per visitor while limiting employment breadth — but it has kept visitor densities low in fragile ecosystems.

sections.heading: Transport and the Landlocked Constraint
sections.body:
Being landlocked shapes Botswana's transport geography more than any other single factor. Every export leaves and every import arrives across somebody else's territory, adding cost, transit time and political dependence.

The historical spine is the railway. The line from Mafeking to Bulawayo, built in 1897 during the push northward from the Cape, was routed through the eastern edge of the Protectorate, and it determined the location of nearly every significant town in the country. Botswana Railways took over domestic operation in 1987. The network is essentially a single north-south line of about 900 kilometres with short branches to Morupule colliery and Selebi-Phikwe, and it carries coal, soda ash and containerised freight toward South African and Zimbabwean ports.

Roads came much later and much faster. At independence there were only a few kilometres of tarred road in the entire country; today the paved network exceeds 10,000 kilometres. The Trans-Kalahari Highway, completed in 1998, runs west from Gaborone through Kang and Ghanzi to the Namibian border at Mamuno and on to Walvis Bay, giving Botswana an alternative Atlantic outlet roughly 1,900 kilometres from the capital and reducing dependence on South African ports. The Trans-Kalahari corridor was a deliberate act of geopolitical diversification as much as an engineering project.

The northern frontier changed significantly in May 2021 with the opening of the Kazungula Bridge, a 923-metre curved road and rail bridge across the Zambezi replacing a pontoon ferry that had long been a notorious bottleneck, with lorry queues of several days. The bridge's curve is not decorative: it was engineered to land within the narrow Botswana-Zambia frontage and avoid the disputed quadripoint with Namibia and Zimbabwe, one of the more elegant instances of political geography dictating civil engineering.

Air transport is disproportionately important given the distances and the low population density. Sir Seretse Khama International Airport at Gaborone is the principal gateway, but Maun Airport handles very large numbers of light-aircraft movements serving delta camps, since many lodges are reachable only by air, particularly during high flood. Kasane serves the Chobe area.

The costs of landlocking are real and quantifiable. Freight from an Indian Ocean or Atlantic port adds significantly to the delivered cost of imported goods, and transit through neighbours exposes trade to their industrial disputes, border congestion and currency arrangements. Botswana's membership of the Southern African Customs Union, one of the world's oldest customs unions, mitigates this substantially and has historically supplied a large share of government revenue.

Internally, the transport problem is different: enormous distances, very low traffic volumes, and settlements hundreds of kilometres apart. Long stretches of highway are unfenced and carry a serious hazard of collision with cattle, donkeys and wildlife at night — a leading cause of road deaths.

sections.heading: Environmental Pressures and the Limits Ahead
sections.body:
The environmental questions facing Botswana all reduce, in the end, to water and land, and most of them get harder rather than easier as the century proceeds.

Rangeland degradation is the most widespread. The combination of communal grazing, borehole-driven livestock concentration, suppressed fire and rising carbon dioxide has produced measurable bush encroachment and soil loss over large areas. The scale is genuinely contested — remote sensing studies disagree on how much of the change is directional degradation versus reversible fluctuation driven by rainfall — but the piosphere pattern around water points is not in dispute. Recovery of trampled sandveld is slow because rainfall is low and erratic.

Water is the sharper constraint. Non-renewable groundwater in the west, drought-vulnerable surface storage in the east, and rising demand from mining, irrigation and a growing urban population combine badly. The Gaborone Dam crisis of 2015, when the reservoir effectively emptied, is a preview rather than an anomaly. Upstream development on the Okavango in Angola, whose highland catchment was largely undeveloped through decades of civil war and is now attracting agricultural investment, represents the single largest external risk to the delta.

Climate projections add to the pressure. Warming of two to four degrees or more by 2100 under higher-emissions pathways is widely projected for the southern African interior, and warming alone raises evaporative demand sharply even if rainfall does not change. Rainfall projections remain genuinely uncertain in sign, and it is more honest to say that the rainfall future is unknown than to assert drying; but greater variability, later onset of the rains and longer dry spells within the season are more consistently projected and are, for rain-fed agriculture, at least as damaging as a change in the mean.

Human-wildlife conflict has intensified as elephant numbers have grown and as settlement has expanded into former wildlife range. Crop raiding, livestock predation and human deaths from elephants and lions are politically salient issues, and the reintroduction of controlled trophy hunting in 2019, after a suspension since 2014, is best understood in that light. It is a contested policy on which reasonable people disagree: opponents cite conservation and reputational costs, supporters cite rural income and tolerance for wildlife on communal land.

The country's own responses have been comparatively serious. Botswana has invested in transboundary water institutions, in the transfrontier conservation areas that reconnect fragmented habitats, in large-scale solar potential — insolation across the Kalahari is among the world's best, exceeding 2,200 kilowatt-hours per square metre annually — and in economic diversification away from diamonds.

The deep structural facts remain unchanged: a flat, sandy, evaporation-dominated interior, a population of a few million in a country the size of France, rivers that belong to other countries, and no coastline. Botswana's geography has never been generous, and the country's twentieth-century record consists largely of managing that inheritance unusually well.

guides.title: Geography of Burkina Faso
guides.summary: The physical and human geography of Burkina Faso: its landlocked position in the West African Sahel, the bedrock and laterite plateau beneath it, the monsoon that delivers a single short rainy season, its rivers, soils, vegetation, cities, economy and hazards.

sections.heading: Where Burkina Faso Is and Why Its Position Governs Everything
sections.body: Burkina Faso is a landlocked country in the interior of West Africa, occupying about 274,200 square kilometres of low plateau between roughly 9 and 15 degrees north latitude and between about 5 and a half degrees west and 2 and a half degrees east longitude. The Greenwich meridian runs through it, a little east of the capital. It is slightly smaller than the American state of Colorado and slightly larger than the United Kingdom, and about 23 million people live there, giving a population density of roughly 80 per square kilometre, which is high for the Sahel and higher still when measured against the land that can actually be farmed. Three facts of position explain most of what follows. The first is latitude. Burkina Faso lies almost entirely within the Sahel and the Sudanian savanna, the transitional belts between the Sahara to the north and the humid forests along the Gulf of Guinea to the south. Rain arrives from the south in a single annual pulse, and the amount that falls declines steadily as one moves north, from around 1,100 millimetres a year in the far southwest to under 500 in the far north. Nearly every difference in soils, crops, livestock, settlement density and diet within the country tracks that gradient. The second is that the country has no coast. Its nearest seaports, at Abidjan, Tema, Lome and Cotonou, are between 900 and 1,200 kilometres away by road, in four different foreign countries. Every tonne of fuel, fertiliser, cement and imported grain crosses at least one international border, and every tonne of cotton and gold leaves the same way. This inflates the delivered cost of nearly everything and makes the political stability of neighbours a domestic economic variable. The third is that Burkina Faso sits on the West African craton, an ancient and geologically stable block of Precambrian rock. That basement is the source of the country's gold, which is now its dominant export; it is also the reason the landscape is so flat, so weathered, and so poorly endowed with the deep, productive aquifers found in sedimentary basins. The name itself is geography of a different kind. Until 4 August 1984 the country was Upper Volta, named by French colonial administrators for the three headwater rivers of the Volta system that rise within it. Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso, combining burkina, upright or honest, from Moore, with faso, homeland, from Dioula, and forming the demonym Burkinabe with a suffix from Fulfulde: one name built from three of the country's languages, deliberately. A fourth fact is worth stating because it is often assumed away: Burkina Faso has no mountains, no sea coast, no navigable river and no oil. Its endowment is land, rain that is adequate but unreliable, a very young and rapidly growing population, and gold in the rock beneath. Almost every question about the country's development reduces to how those four are combined.

sections.heading: Borders, Neighbours and the Landlocked Condition
sections.body: Burkina Faso has six neighbours and roughly 3,600 kilometres of land boundary, none of it coastal. Mali lies to the north and west along about 1,325 kilometres, the longest of the six. Niger is to the east and northeast along some 620 kilometres. Benin takes a short southeastern stretch of about 390 kilometres, Togo an even shorter 130, Ghana about 600 along the south, and Cote d'Ivoire roughly 545 along the southwest. Almost all of these lines were drawn by French and British administrators between the 1890s and the 1940s and follow no physical feature for most of their length. Several run as straight geometric segments across flat savanna, and the consequence is that ethnic and linguistic groups straddle them routinely: Gourmantche people live in both Burkina Faso and Niger, Mossi communities extend into Ghana and Cote d'Ivoire, and the Fulani herding systems of the north operate across the Malian and Nigerien borders as a matter of course. One boundary segment, the Agacher or Beli strip on the Malian frontier, produced two short wars, in 1974 and again over five days in December 1985, before the International Court of Justice divided the disputed area roughly in half in a 1986 judgment that both states accepted. The landlocked condition is the single most consequential structural fact of Burkina Faso's economic geography. Four corridors carry the country's trade. The historically dominant one runs southwest to Abidjan in Cote d'Ivoire, served both by road and by the metre-gauge railway built by the French between 1904 and 1954, which reaches Ouagadougou after about 1,260 kilometres and is the country's only working rail link to the sea. The others run south to Tema and Takoradi in Ghana, southeast to Lome in Togo, and southeast to Cotonou in Benin. When Cote d'Ivoire's civil conflict closed the Abidjan corridor in the 2000s, traffic diverted to Lome and Tema at considerable cost, an object lesson in why a landlocked state maintains redundant routes even when they are more expensive in normal times. Estimates of the transport penalty vary, but landlocked developing countries typically pay something between 1.4 and 2 times the freight costs of comparable coastal states, and inland transit adds days as well as money. For bulky, low-value goods such as cereals, fertiliser and cement, that penalty can exceed the value of the commodity itself, which is why Burkina Faso's exports have converged on things with a high value-to-weight ratio, above all gold, and why food that is cheap on the world market can still be expensive in a Sahelian village. Transit also depends on legal machinery as much as on tarmac. Burkina Faso's access to the sea rests on bilateral transit agreements, on the customs union of the West African Economic and Monetary Union, and on the shared CFA franc, which removes currency conversion from cross-border trade. When those arrangements are strained by political rupture, as they were by the regional disputes of the 2020s, the physical geography of being a thousand kilometres inland becomes immediately expensive.

sections.heading: The Bedrock: Craton, Greenstone Belts and the Sedimentary Southwest
sections.body: Most of Burkina Faso is underlain by the Precambrian crystalline basement of the West African craton, some of the oldest continental crust on the planet. The dominant assemblage is Birimian, a term for Palaeoproterozoic rocks formed roughly 2.25 to 2.05 billion years ago and welded together during the Eburnean orogeny, the mountain-building episode that stabilised this part of Africa. The Birimian consists of alternating belts of volcanic and sedimentary rock, metamorphosed to greenstone, separated by broad domains of granite and granodiorite. Those greenstone belts run roughly northeast to southwest across the country and are the reason Burkina Faso has gold at all. Gold in Birimian terrain occurs mainly in quartz veins and sheared, sulphide-bearing zones along the contacts between greenstone belts and granitoids, and in the deeply weathered oxide caps above them. The same rocks host the goldfields of Ghana, Mali, Cote d'Ivoire and Guinea; the belts do not stop at borders. Burkina Faso also holds manganese at Tambao in the far north, zinc at Perkoa, phosphate at Kodjari, limestone at Tin Hrassan, and modest occurrences of copper, nickel and bauxite, most of them constrained less by geology than by the cost of moving heavy, low-value rock to a distant port. The southwestern corner is different. There the ancient basement dips beneath a cover of much younger sedimentary rock belonging to the Taoudeni Basin, a vast intracratonic basin extending northwest into Mali and Mauritania. The cover consists largely of Neoproterozoic to Palaeozoic sandstones, in places several hundred metres thick, together with siltstones and some dolomite. These sandstones weather and erode quite differently from granite, and they produce the only genuinely dramatic scenery in the country: the Banfora escarpment, a cuesta rising a hundred metres and more above the plain, the wind and water-sculpted rock towers known as the Peaks of Sindou, the rounded domes at Fabedougou, and the Karfiguela waterfalls. They also hold the best aquifers in the country, because water moves readily through the pore spaces and bedding planes of sandstone in a way it cannot through unfractured granite. One further geological unit matters practically. Long tropical weathering under alternating wet and dry conditions has produced a deep mantle of saprolite, decomposed rock in place, over much of the basement, often twenty to fifty metres thick. Boreholes in the basement typically draw from the base of this weathered layer and from fracture networks beneath it, which is why yields are low and why siting a successful well is a genuinely skilled exercise rather than a matter of drilling anywhere. The craton's stability has one further consequence worth noting. Burkina Faso is essentially aseismic and has no volcanoes, no young faulting and no earthquake risk of any practical significance, because it sits far from any active plate boundary in the interior of a block that has not been deformed for hundreds of millions of years. Building codes there worry about wind, rain and termites, not tremors.

sections.heading: Relief, Landforms and the Laterite Crust
sections.body: Burkina Faso is flat. Roughly nine tenths of its surface is a gently undulating peneplain lying between 200 and 400 metres above sea level, the eroded stump of mountain ranges worn down over two billion years. The highest point, Tenakourou in the southwest near Orodara, reaches only 749 metres, and the lowest, where the Mouhoun river leaves the country, is about 125 metres. The total relief of the entire nation is therefore around 620 metres, less than the height of many single hills elsewhere. A traveller crossing the country sees an almost unbroken horizon interrupted by scattered inselbergs, isolated granite domes standing above the plain because they resisted the weathering that removed everything around them. Against this flatness the southwestern sandstone country stands out sharply. The Banfora escarpment, or falaise de Banfora, is a west-facing scarp running for well over a hundred kilometres, formed where the resistant Taoudeni sandstones have been undercut and retreat has left a step in the landscape. Streams falling over it produce the country's only true waterfalls. The plateau behind it, around Bobo-Dioulasso and Orodara, is the most elevated and the wettest part of Burkina Faso and is agriculturally its richest. The single most important landform for daily life, however, is not a hill but a crust. Across enormous areas the soil profile is capped by laterite, known in French West Africa as cuirasse and in the plural form of the local landscape as bowe. Laterite forms where prolonged tropical weathering leaches silica and bases out of the rock and concentrates iron and aluminium oxides, which then harden irreversibly on exposure to air into a rock-like sheet, sometimes vesicular and slaggy, sometimes composed of cemented iron pisoliths. A mature cuirasse can be one to several metres thick and is essentially impenetrable to roots, ploughs and infiltrating water. Laterite has three practical consequences. It removes very large areas from cultivation entirely, leaving flat, bare, gravelly plateaus that support only sparse grass and scattered shrubs and are used for grazing and for quarrying gravel. It sheds rainfall as sheet runoff instead of absorbing it, so that storms that fall on bowe arrive downslope suddenly and erosively rather than recharging groundwater. And it is an excellent building material: cut into blocks while still moist and allowed to harden, hand-quarried laterite provides the durable red-brown masonry seen in older buildings and in the distinctive vernacular architecture of the southwest. The word laterite itself comes from the Latin for brick, coined in 1807 by the Scottish surgeon Francis Buchanan-Hamilton after watching Indian masons cut exactly this material. Flatness has a hydrological cost that is easy to overlook. With gradients often below one metre per kilometre, water moves slowly and spreads widely rather than concentrating in incised channels, so floodwater ponds over large areas instead of draining away, and shallow depressions hold seasonal water for weeks. It also means that a small earth embankment a few metres high can impound a reservoir covering many hectares, which is exactly why the country is dotted with them.

sections.heading: Climate: The West African Monsoon and Three Rainfall Belts
sections.body: Burkina Faso has one rainy season a year, and its length and reliability decrease steadily northward. The mechanism is the West African monsoon. Through the northern winter the Sahara is cool and dominated by dry continental air; through the spring it heats intensely, a thermal low develops over the desert, and moist air is drawn inland from the Gulf of Guinea as a southwesterly flow. The boundary between this humid southwesterly monsoon layer and the dry northeasterly Saharan air aloft is called the intertropical discontinuity or intertropical convergence zone, and it migrates north across West Africa from about February, reaching its most northerly position, around 20 degrees north, in August, before retreating south again through September and October. A place receives rain when it lies far enough south of that boundary for the moist layer to be deep enough, typically more than about 1,500 to 2,000 metres, to support convection. Because the boundary sweeps north and then south again in a single annual cycle, southern Burkina Faso gets a long season from roughly May to October while the far north gets a short one from roughly late June to early September. Almost no rain falls anywhere in the country between November and March. The rain itself does not usually arrive as gentle frontal drizzle but as organised squall lines, mesoscale convective systems that form to the east, often over the highlands of Nigeria, Cameroon or Sudan, and travel westward at 40 to 60 kilometres per hour. A squall line announces itself as a wall of dust ahead of a black cloud, delivers violent wind, then twenty to sixty minutes of extremely intense rain, then a longer period of lighter rain, and passes. Rainfall intensities of 60 to 100 millimetres per hour are common. These systems are steered and organised by African easterly waves, undulations in the African easterly jet, a mid-level east-to-west wind current that forms because of the sharp temperature contrast between the Sahara and the Gulf of Guinea. The same waves, on reaching the Atlantic, become the seeds of many Atlantic hurricanes. Three climatic belts are conventionally recognised. The Sahelian zone, north of about 14 degrees, receives under 600 millimetres in roughly three months and supports pastoralism and short-cycle millet. The Sudano-Sahelian zone across the centre receives roughly 600 to 900 millimetres and holds most of the population. The Sudanian zone in the south and southwest receives 900 to 1,200 millimetres over five or six months and grows cotton, maize, yams, mangoes and sugar cane. Mean annual temperature is around 28 degrees Celsius almost everywhere; the difference between zones is water, not heat. The boundaries between these belts are not lines on the ground but statistical averages of a rainfall field that shifts from year to year, which is why maps drawn a few decades apart place them differently and why farmers experience the zone they live in as a moving target rather than a fixed condition.

sections.heading: The Harmattan, the Hot Season and the Rhythm of the Year
sections.body: The Burkinabe year is usually described in three seasons rather than four, and each has a distinct physical character that shapes work, health and movement. From roughly November to February the country lies under the harmattan, a dry northeasterly wind blowing out of the Sahara. It carries enormous quantities of fine mineral dust, much of it lifted from the Bodele Depression in Chad, the single most productive dust source on Earth. Visibility can fall below a kilometre for days at a time in what is called a dust haze rather than a storm, the sun becomes a pale disc, and relative humidity can drop to 10 or 15 per cent. Daytime temperatures are pleasant by local standards, often 30 to 33 degrees Celsius, but nights in the north can fall to 10 to 15 degrees, and occasionally lower, which is genuinely cold for people without heating and for young livestock. The dry air cracks skin and lips, dries out wooden objects, and dramatically raises the risk of bacterial meningitis: Burkina Faso lies squarely within the African meningitis belt described by Leon Lapeyssonnie in 1963, where epidemics of meningococcal disease occur almost exclusively in the harmattan months and collapse with the first rains. From March to May comes the hot season, the most physically punishing part of the year. The sun is approaching overhead, the ground is bare and dry, and there is neither cloud nor moisture to moderate heating. Daily maxima routinely reach 40 to 43 degrees Celsius and can exceed 45 in the north, while nights stay above 25 or 28, so there is no recovery period. Heat stress in this season is a leading cause of illness among the elderly and among people doing outdoor manual work, and the practical adaptation is universal: work early and late, rest through the middle of the day, and drink continually. From roughly May or June to September or October the rains fall and the country transforms. Bare ochre landscapes turn green within two weeks. Humidity rises sharply, so that although temperatures fall to the low thirties the apparent heat can remain high. This is the agricultural season, and essentially the entire year's food is grown in it, which is why the timing of the first useful rain is a matter of intense concern. A false start, a good rain that prompts planting followed by a two-week dry spell that kills the seedlings, forces replanting with seed that may not exist. The season ends abruptly, and the harvest, from October to December, is followed immediately by the harmattan again. The hungry season, called soudure in French, falls in the months just before harvest, roughly June to September, when the previous year's granary is exhausted and the new crop is still in the field. It coincides exactly with the heaviest agricultural labour and with the peak of malaria transmission, a convergence of low food, hard work and disease that is the single most predictable nutritional stress in the Sahelian year.

sections.heading: Rivers and Drainage: Volta, Comoe and Niger
sections.body: Burkina Faso drains into three separate basins, and the divides between them are so subtle on the flat plateau that they are hard to see on the ground. By far the largest share, roughly two thirds of the national territory, belongs to the Volta basin, and the country supplies a substantial fraction of the water that eventually reaches Lake Volta in Ghana. Three rivers give the old colonial name its meaning. The Mouhoun, formerly the Black Volta, rises in the wetter southwest near Orodara, loops north and then swings east and south to leave the country toward Ghana, and is the only watercourse in Burkina Faso that flows all year along most of its length. The Nakambe, formerly the White Volta, rises on the central plateau north of Ouagadougou and flows south into Ghana; it dries to disconnected pools for part of the year. The Nazinon, formerly the Red Volta, is a smaller and more strongly seasonal parallel stream. The rivers were officially renamed in 1986 to replace the colour terms imposed by colonial cartography. The southwest drains separately into the Comoe, which rises near Banfora and runs south through Cote d'Ivoire to the Gulf of Guinea. Because it flows through the wettest and most sandstone-dominated part of the country, the Comoe and its tributaries are the most reliable streams in Burkina Faso, and their valleys support the sugar cane and fruit irrigation around Banfora. The northern and northeastern fringe, a comparatively small area, drains toward the Niger by way of seasonal rivers including the Beli, the Gorouol, the Dargol and the Goudebo. These are true Sahelian watercourses, flowing violently for a few weeks and then vanishing into sand. The dominant hydrological fact is extreme seasonality. Discharge in the Nakambe can vary by three orders of magnitude between September and April. Rivers are not, for most of the country, a year-round water supply, a navigation route or a reliable irrigation source; they are a flood pulse. Natural standing water is correspondingly scarce. Lake Bam, north of Kongoussi, is the largest natural lake at a few thousand hectares and has shrunk markedly with siltation; Lake Dem lies nearby; Lake Tengrela near Banfora and the Mare aux Hippopotames near Bobo-Dioulasso, a Ramsar-listed wetland and biosphere reserve, are the best-known permanent water bodies in the south. Seasonal ponds called mares, such as the Mare d'Oursi in the far north, are critical for pastoralists and disappear entirely by the end of the dry season, which is precisely why herds move. Because the country lies upstream of Ghana on the Volta and upstream of Cote d'Ivoire on the Comoe, every dam and irrigation scheme Burkina Faso builds reduces flow to a downstream neighbour, which makes water an item of regional diplomacy. The Volta Basin Authority, established in 2007 by the six riparian states, exists to manage exactly this, though its practical influence over national dam-building decisions has been modest.

sections.heading: Storing Water: Dams, Boreholes and the Dry-Season Problem
sections.body: Because the rain arrives in a single burst and the rivers empty, almost all water management in Burkina Faso consists of catching water when it falls and holding it until it is needed. The country has built well over a thousand small and medium reservoirs, called barrages, most of them earth embankments a few metres high across shallow valleys. They irrigate dry-season market gardens, water livestock, recharge shallow wells and supply small towns. They also silt up, sometimes within a decade or two, because degraded catchments deliver heavy sediment loads, and they lose enormous volumes to evaporation, which in this climate can exceed two metres of depth per year from an open surface. A shallow reservoir in the Sahel may lose more water to the atmosphere than it delivers to crops. A few large structures matter nationally. The Bagre dam on the Nakambe, completed in 1992, provides hydropower and supports the country's largest irrigation scheme. The Kompienga dam in the southeast, completed in 1988, is chiefly a hydropower reservoir. The Ziga dam, also on the Nakambe about 50 kilometres east of the capital, was built specifically because Ouagadougou had outgrown its local reservoirs; it came into service in the mid-2000s and remains the city's principal water source. In the northwest, the Sourou valley scheme exploits an unusual piece of hydrography in which a tributary relationship can be reversed by a barrage, allowing Mouhoun floodwater to be backed up into the Sourou depression and used for irrigation. Groundwater supplies most rural drinking water, and its behaviour follows the geology. Beneath the crystalline basement that covers most of the country there is no continuous aquifer at all. Water occurs in the weathered saprolite layer and in fractures in the fresh rock below, and a successful borehole depends on intersecting a productive fracture. Yields are typically low, often in the range of one to five cubic metres per hour, and dry boreholes are common enough that siting is done with geophysical surveys and lineament mapping rather than guesswork. In the sedimentary southwest, by contrast, sandstone aquifers are continuous, productive and comparatively easy to develop, and large springs such as those feeding the Kou valley near Bobo-Dioulasso emerge where the water table meets the surface. Water quality problems are real. Naturally occurring arsenic has been documented in some basement boreholes, notably in the north around Yatenga and Ouahigouya, at concentrations above the World Health Organization guideline of 10 micrograms per litre, and nitrate contamination from pit latrines and livestock affects shallow hand-dug wells in dense settlements. Maintenance, not construction, is the persistent weakness. A hand pump serving a village of a thousand people fails eventually, and rural water programmes across the Sahel have repeatedly found that somewhere between a fifth and a third of installed pumps are out of service at any given moment, usually for want of a spare part costing a few thousand francs and a mechanic who can be reached. The binding constraint on rural water is organisational as much as hydrogeological.

sections.heading: Soils, Land Degradation and the Zai Technique
sections.body: The soils of Burkina Faso are old, thin and chemically poor. Most are classified as ferruginous tropical soils, lixisols and plinthosols in international terminology, developed on deeply weathered basement under a climate that leaches nutrients during the rains and bakes the surface for the rest of the year. Organic matter contents below one per cent are common. Available phosphorus is typically the first limiting nutrient, nitrogen the second, and cation exchange capacity is low, meaning the soil holds little of any fertiliser applied to it. Many surfaces are prone to crusting: the impact of intense raindrops on bare ground rearranges fine particles into a thin, dense seal within minutes, so that a field which has just received 50 millimetres of rain may have absorbed only a fraction of it while the rest ran off. Degraded, sealed, bare land of this kind is called zipele in Moore. Against this, Burkinabe farmers developed and then dramatically extended a set of water-harvesting techniques that have become internationally influential. Stone bunds, cordons pierreux, are lines of rock laid along the contour to slow runoff and trap sediment. Demi-lunes are half-moon-shaped earth basins dug on the contour. The best known is zai, an old Mossi practice of planting into small pits that concentrate both water and manure. From the early 1980s, following the severe droughts of the previous decade, farmers in Yatenga province including Yacouba Sawadogo, later widely known as the man who stopped the desert, deepened the traditional pits and combined them with manure and stone bunds. Researchers such as Chris Reij have estimated that on the order of 200,000 to 300,000 hectares of abandoned land on the Central Plateau were brought back into production this way. The technique is labour-intensive, requiring perhaps 300 hours of digging per hectare, which is its principal limit.
steps: Choose a degraded, crusted field on gentle slope, ideally with a stone bund already laid on the contour upslope to slow runoff.
Dig during the dry season, roughly November to April, when labour is available; digging in the rains wastes the season.
Excavate pits about 20 to 30 centimetres across and 10 to 20 centimetres deep, spaced roughly 70 to 90 centimetres apart, giving around 10,000 pits per hectare.
Place the excavated soil in a small crescent-shaped ridge on the downslope side of each pit so that runoff entering the pit is retained rather than passing through.

Put roughly 0.3 to 0.6 kilograms of manure or compost into each pit. This step matters most: the organic matter attracts termites, whose galleries break the crust beneath the pit and open channels for water to infiltrate deeply.
Leave the pits open through the remainder of the dry season so they catch wind-blown dust, leaf litter and the first rains.
Sow millet or sorghum directly into each pit after a rain of about 20 millimetres or more, placing the seed in the manure at the centre.

Weed carefully by hand rather than by hoeing across the field, which would destroy the pit structure, and re-excavate and re-manure the same pits in following dry seasons rather than digging new ones.

sections.heading: Vegetation Zones and the Farmed Parkland
sections.body: Burkina Faso has no natural forest in the sense understood in wetter countries. Its vegetation is savanna, meaning a continuous grass layer with a discontinuous cover of trees and shrubs, and it grades predictably along the rainfall gradient. In the Sahelian north, under 600 millimetres of rain, the cover is thorn steppe: sparse, small-leaved, spiny trees, chiefly acacias, now formally reclassified into the genera Vachellia and Senegalia, along with the desert date Balanites aegyptiaca and the toothbrush tree Salvadora persica, standing over annual grasses that complete their whole life cycle in eight to ten weeks. Ground cover is patchy, and vegetation often organises itself into striking banded patterns, called brousse tigree or tiger bush, in which thickets alternate with bare crusted strips that shed runoff onto them. The Sudano-Sahelian centre carries denser shrub savanna dominated by Combretum and Guiera species. The Sudanian south and southwest support open woodland with broad-leaved trees such as Isoberlinia, Daniellia and Burkea, taller grasses reaching two or three metres, and, along watercourses, genuine gallery forest of evergreen species that survives only because roots reach permanent water. Overlaid on all of this is the most characteristic landscape in the country, the farmed parkland. Across the densely populated Central Plateau, fields of millet and sorghum are dotted with mature trees that farmers deliberately protected when clearing. The trees are not accidental survivors; they are an economic system. The shea tree, Vitellaria paradoxa, called karite, yields nuts whose fat is the basis of a major export and of household cooking; harvesting and processing is overwhelmingly women's work and a significant source of independent income. The nere, Parkia biglobosa, produces pods fermented into soumbala, a protein-rich condiment central to the local diet. Baobab leaves are a staple vegetable and its fruit pulp a vitamin C source. Faidherbia albida is agronomically remarkable because it is reverse-phenological, dropping its leaves at the start of the rains so that it does not shade the crop and fertilising the soil beneath it with nitrogen-rich litter. Since the 1980s a practice known as farmer-managed natural regeneration has spread widely across the Sahel: rather than planting seedlings, farmers protect and prune the shoots that sprout from the extensive stumps and root systems still living underground in apparently bare fields. It is far cheaper and far more successful than conventional tree planting, and satellite analysis has documented substantial increases in tree cover across parts of Burkina Faso and neighbouring Niger as a result. Fuelwood is the pressure that acts on all of this. Wood and charcoal supply the great majority of household energy, and demand from Ouagadougou alone strips woodland for a hundred kilometres and more around the city, delivered by truck along the main roads. Because the trees that survive in parkland are protected by their owners and their usefulness, the wood cut for fuel comes disproportionately from communal bush, which is precisely the land with no one to defend it.

sections.heading: Wildlife and the W-Arly-Pendjari Complex
sections.body: Burkina Faso's large fauna is concentrated overwhelmingly in the southeast, in the transboundary protected area known as the W-Arly-Pendjari complex, or WAP. The complex spans Burkina Faso, Niger and Benin and covers a total area exceeding 30,000 square kilometres, of which the Burkinabe portion comprises the Arly reserve system and the national share of W National Park, named for a double bend in the Niger river. W was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site for the Nigerien portion in 1996 and extended to include the Burkinabe and Beninese components in 2017. It is the largest and most intact block of savanna ecosystem remaining in West Africa. The complex holds the region's most significant surviving elephant population, historically estimated in the low thousands across the whole WAP, along with African buffalo, hippopotamus, roan antelope, hartebeest, topi, kob, waterbuck, warthog and several duiker species. Its predators are of disproportionate conservation importance because the West African lion is genetically distinct from eastern and southern populations and is critically endangered, with total numbers across its entire range plausibly in the low hundreds; WAP holds the largest remaining subpopulation. Cheetah and African wild dog persist there in very small numbers or may already be functionally lost. Over 350 bird species have been recorded. Elsewhere in the country wildlife is far more limited. The Nazinga game ranch in the south, established in the 1970s as an experiment in community-linked wildlife management, holds several hundred elephants and is the most accessible place to see them. The Deux Bales forest along the Mouhoun holds a small elephant population. The Mare aux Hippopotames near Bobo-Dioulasso protects a resident hippo group in an oxbow wetland. Beyond these islands, most large mammals were eliminated from the settled plateau long ago by hunting and habitat conversion. The situation has deteriorated sharply.
