Since about 2018 armed groups have established themselves in the wooded, sparsely populated protected areas precisely because they offer cover and are far from state control. Ranger patrols have been attacked and in places withdrawn, tourism has ceased entirely, and management of the Burkinabe portions of WAP has become extremely difficult. Conservation organisations have reported an increase in poaching in areas that can no longer be monitored, though the honest position is that reliable population data for the last several years simply do not exist, because nobody can safely conduct the aerial and ground surveys that would produce them. Smaller fauna is more widely distributed and more resilient. Nile crocodiles persist in ponds across the country, most famously at Bazoule near Ouagadougou and at Sabou, where local traditions of protection have kept habituated populations alive within a few metres of villages. Patas and green monkeys, jackals, civets, mongooses, hares and a rich reptile and bird fauna occupy farmed and settled landscapes, and the seasonal wetlands of the Sahel are important stopovers for Palearctic migratory birds travelling between Europe and equatorial Africa.

sections.heading: People on the Land: Population, Ethnicity and Settlement
sections.body: Burkina Faso's population, roughly 23 million and growing at close to 2.5 to 3 per cent a year, is one of the youngest in the world, with a median age around 17 and something like 45 per cent of the population under 15. That growth rate implies a doubling time of about 25 years, and it is the background variable behind almost every pressure on land, water and public services. The population is very unevenly distributed. The Mossi, the largest ethnic group at roughly half the national total, occupy the Central Plateau around Ouagadougou, and this is the most densely settled part of the country, in places exceeding 100 persons per square kilometre on soils that are not especially good. Fallow periods on the plateau have collapsed from decades to a year or none at all. Other major groups include the Fulani or Peul, pastoralists spread across the north and centre and throughout West Africa; the Gourmantche in the east; the Bobo, Bwa, Senufo and Lobi in the west and southwest; the Gurunsi in the south; and the Bissa in the southeast. Around sixty languages are spoken. French was the sole official language from independence in 1960 until a constitutional revision adopted in December 2023, which elevated national languages, principally Moore, Dioula and Fulfulde, to official status and reclassified French as a working language; implementation is ongoing. One episode reshaped the settlement map decisively. The fertile valleys of the Volta rivers were, for most of the twentieth century, dangerous to inhabit because of onchocerciasis, river blindness, caused by a filarial worm transmitted by Simulium blackflies that breed in fast-flowing water. In heavily affected villages blindness rates reached 10 per cent or more of adults, and communities retreated from the rivers, leaving good land empty while the plateau grew crowded. The Onchocerciasis Control Programme, headquartered in Ouagadougou and operating from 1974 to 2002 across eleven countries, used aerial larviciding of breeding sites and later ivermectin distribution to break transmission. It is regarded as one of the most successful disease control campaigns ever conducted, and it opened tens of thousands of square kilometres of river valley to resettlement. Migration is the other structural feature. Seasonal and long-term movement to Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana has been a normal part of Burkinabe economic life since the colonial period, when it was compelled by forced labour recruitment. Several million people of Burkinabe origin live in Cote d'Ivoire, and their remittances are a substantial component of rural income. Religion is distributed with a rough geography of its own: Islam predominates, particularly in the north and among Fulani and Dioula communities, Christianity is strongest in the centre and southwest, and traditional religious practice remains widespread and frequently coexists with both. Burkina Faso was long noted for the ease of that coexistence, including within individual families, which is part of why the arrival of sectarian armed violence after 2015 was experienced as such a rupture.

sections.heading: Cities: Ouagadougou, Bobo-Dioulasso and the Urban Pattern
sections.body: Burkina Faso remains predominantly rural, with something around 30 to 35 per cent of its people in towns, but urbanisation is rapid and heavily concentrated in two centres. Ouagadougou, the capital, sits almost exactly in the middle of the country on the Central Plateau at about 300 metres elevation. Its population is somewhere near three million and has roughly doubled every fifteen to twenty years. Its site is unpromising: there is no perennial river, the underlying basement yields little groundwater, and the surrounding soils are ordinary. The city exists where it does because it was the seat of the Mogho Naba, the Mossi paramount ruler, long before the French arrived in 1896 and made it their administrative centre. Water supply has been a chronic constraint, met first by three small reservoirs within the city, the barrages numbered one to three, and since the mid-2000s chiefly by the Ziga dam some 50 kilometres east, from which water is piped in. Growth has been overwhelmingly horizontal, spreading across the flat plain into unplanned peripheral settlements known locally as non-lotis, unsurveyed areas that lack legal title and, usually, piped water, drainage and paved roads. Bobo-Dioulasso, the second city with perhaps a million people, lies about 350 kilometres southwest in the Sudanian zone, and its geography is much more favourable: more rain, deeper sandstone aquifers, large springs in the nearby Kou valley, and better soils. It was the colonial economic capital, the railhead on the line from Abidjan, and remains the country's agricultural processing and industrial centre, handling cotton, fruit and cereals. Its old quarters, particularly Kibidwe, preserve the mud-brick Sudano-Sahelian architecture of the region. Below these two, a network of regional towns, Koudougou, Ouahigouya, Banfora, Kaya, Fada N'Gourma, Dori, Tenkodogo and Dedougou among them, serves as administrative and market centres, mostly in the tens of thousands. Administratively the country has for most of the past two decades been divided into thirteen regions, subdivided into 45 provinces and around 350 communes; the transitional authorities have since undertaken a redistricting, so published counts vary depending on the date of the source. Building tradition deserves a note because it is genuinely climate-adapted. Thick walls of sun-dried earth brick or rammed earth have high thermal mass, absorbing heat through the day and releasing it at night, which moderates a daily temperature swing that can exceed 20 degrees Celsius. The fortified compound architecture of the Gurunsi at Tiebele, with its painted geometric wall decoration, and the Sudano-Sahelian mosque at Bani in the north, are the best-known expressions of the tradition. Cement block and sheet metal roofing have largely displaced it in towns, at a real cost in indoor comfort.

sections.heading: Economic Geography: Gold, Cotton, Livestock and Corridors
sections.body: Four things dominate what Burkina Faso produces, and each has a distinct geography. Gold is now the leading export by value, typically accounting for well over two thirds of export earnings. Industrial production expanded rapidly from around 2007, reaching roughly 50 to 60 tonnes a year at its peak in the late 2010s and early 2020s, from mines strung along the Birimian greenstone belts: Essakane in the northeast, Mana and Hounde in the west, Bissa and Sanbrado in the centre, Boungou in the east and Karma in the north, among others. Alongside them, artisanal and small-scale mining, orpaillage, is estimated to involve somewhere between several hundred thousand and one and a half million people at some point in the year, working shallow shafts and processing ore with mercury and cyanide under largely unregulated conditions. Its geography is mobile and improvisational, with camps of thousands appearing within weeks of a discovery. Several industrial mines have suspended operations because of insecurity. Cotton, long called white gold, is the main cash crop of the wetter west and southwest, centred on the Houet, Kenedougou, Tuy and Mouhoun areas and organised through producer unions and the parastatal ginning company. Burkina Faso has at times been Africa's largest cotton producer. It is exposed to world price swings, to the cost of imported inputs, and to soil exhaustion; genetically modified varieties were adopted in 2008 and then abandoned in 2016 after complaints about fibre length. Livestock is the economy of the north and of the Fulani systems throughout the country, comprising many millions of cattle and far more sheep and goats. Transhumance, the seasonal movement of herds north into the Sahel in the rains and south toward the wetter savanna in the dry season, is the rational response to a landscape where forage and water appear in different places at different times. Where corridors are blocked by expanding cultivation, the result is the farmer-herder conflict that has become one of the region's most serious sources of violence. Cereals, mainly sorghum, millet and increasingly maize, occupy most cultivated land and are grown primarily for household consumption. Sesame, cowpea, shea nuts, cashew and mangoes make up secondary exports; the Banfora area produces sugar cane under irrigation. Everything that leaves the country and nearly everything that enters it moves along the four road corridors and the single railway to the sea, which is why a border closure or a coup in a neighbouring state registers within days in Ouagadougou market prices. Energy is the quiet constraint behind all of it. Burkina Faso has no oil, no coal and only modest hydropower at Bagre, Kompienga and Niofila, so most electricity is generated from imported diesel and heavy fuel oil or imported outright from Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana. Access rates remain among the lowest in the world, particularly in rural areas. Solar resources are excellent, with typical irradiation around five and a half to six kilowatt-hours per square metre per day, and utility-scale plants such as Zagtouli near Ouagadougou have begun to exploit them.

sections.heading: Natural Hazards: Drought, Flood, Dust and Disease
sections.body: Drought is the defining hazard, and it is not an occasional visitor but a recurring feature of the climate. The great Sahelian droughts of 1968 to 1973 and 1983 to 1985 were among the most severe multi-year rainfall deficits recorded anywhere in the twentieth century, reducing regional rainfall by 20 to 30 per cent below the mid-century average for years at a time, killing livestock in enormous numbers and driving mass displacement. Rainfall partially recovered from the 1990s, but the recovery has been uneven, and the more consequential change for farmers may not be the annual total at all but its distribution: a shorter season, a later start, and longer dry spells within the rains can destroy a crop in a year with a perfectly normal rainfall total. Flooding is the mirror hazard, and it is worst in cities. On 1 September 2009 Ouagadougou received roughly 260 to 300 millimetres of rain in about twelve hours, more than a third of its annual total in one night. Around 150,000 people were displaced, the main hospital was inundated, and thousands of earth-built houses simply dissolved. The causes were structural as well as meteorological: unplanned settlement in low-lying ground and in natural drainage channels, blocked storm drains, and hard crusted or paved catchments that deliver runoff faster than any drain can carry it. Serious urban flooding has recurred repeatedly since. Dust is a chronic rather than acute hazard. Harmattan dust loads raise rates of respiratory illness and eye irritation, and the seasonal timing of bacterial meningitis epidemics in the meningitis belt is closely linked to the dry, dusty air, which is thought to damage the nasopharyngeal mucosa and permit invasive infection. Serogroup A meningococcal disease, historically the main epidemic strain, has been largely eliminated across the belt by the MenAfriVac conjugate vaccine introduced from 2010, with Burkina Faso among the first countries to conduct mass campaigns; other serogroups continue to cause outbreaks. Other recurrent hazards include desert locust incursions in the north during favourable breeding years, bush fires in the late dry season, malaria, which is intensely seasonal and peaks in and just after the rains, and cholera and other diarrhoeal disease in flood conditions and where sanitation is poor. Heat is increasingly recognised as a hazard in its own right; projections for the Sahel indicate warming faster than the global mean, and days above 40 degrees Celsius are becoming more numerous, with implications for outdoor labour that are only beginning to be quantified. Early warning has improved materially. Regional systems combining satellite rainfall estimates, vegetation indices, market price monitoring and household surveys now issue seasonal food security assessments months ahead, and the agrometeorological services of the Sahel, coordinated through the regional centre AGRHYMET, provide planting advice as the season develops. The remaining gap is rarely prediction; it is the capacity to act on a warning quickly enough and at sufficient scale.

sections.heading: Degradation, Displacement and the Limits of What Is Known
sections.body: Two large questions hang over Burkina Faso's geography, and honesty requires acknowledging how much about each is disputed. The first is desertification. The image of an advancing Sahara swallowing farmland, widely propagated after the 1970s droughts, has not survived close examination. Satellite records since the early 1980s show that vegetation greenness across much of the Sahel, including large parts of Burkina Faso, has increased rather than decreased, chiefly because rainfall partially recovered and because farmer-managed regeneration and water harvesting restored degraded land. But greening measured from orbit is not the same as agricultural productivity or ecological health: it may reflect an increase in short-lived annual grasses and shrubs rather than the recovery of woodland, and it can mask serious local degradation where population pressure has eliminated fallow, stripped fuelwood and compacted soil. The accurate statement is that the Sahara is not advancing as a front, and that land degradation is nonetheless real, patchy, and driven at least as much by land use as by climate. The second is the security crisis. Since roughly 2015 armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates have expanded from northern Mali into Burkina Faso's Sahel, Nord, Est and Boucle du Mouhoun regions. By the mid-2020s the state was widely assessed to lack effective control over a large proportion of national territory, plausibly around 40 per cent, though such figures are estimates rather than measurements and depend heavily on definitions. Internal displacement rose from negligible levels in 2018 to a peak officially reported at over two million people in early 2023, roughly one in ten of the population, before the government suspended publication of the figures, which means the current number is genuinely unknown. The geographic consequences are severe. Farmland has been abandoned across whole provinces, some towns have been besieged and supplied only by air, protected areas have lost their management, mines have suspended operations, and displaced rural populations have concentrated in and around towns whose water and sanitation infrastructure was never designed for them. Anyone consulting sources on Burkina Faso should note that reliable data has thinned markedly since about 2020. Census and survey work cannot be conducted in inaccessible areas, wildlife counts have stopped, and some official statistics are no longer released. Figures in this account for population, displacement, gold output and territorial control should be read as best available estimates with real uncertainty attached, and anything time-sensitive should be checked against a current source. A related caution applies to historical baselines. Much of what is confidently asserted about pre-colonial vegetation and land use in the Sahel rests on colonial-era observations by administrators who assumed that any landscape less wooded than a European forest had been degraded by its inhabitants. Later ecological work, notably in neighbouring Guinea, has shown that this reading was often exactly backwards and that some wooded patches were created rather than destroyed by farming communities.

guides.safetyNote: Large parts of Burkina Faso, particularly the Sahel, Nord, Est, Centre-Nord and Boucle du Mouhoun regions and the W-Arly-Pendjari protected areas, have been affected by armed conflict since about 2015, and most foreign governments advise against all travel to much of the country. Conditions change quickly; check a current official advisory before relying on any description of access, roads or protected areas given here.

guides.title: Geography of Burundi
guides.summary: A full account of the physical and human geography of Burundi: its position in the East African Rift, its highlands, lakes and rivers, its climate, soils and vegetation, and how one of the most densely settled countries in Africa lives with that landscape.

sections.heading: A Small Country at the Continent's Hinge
sections.body:
Burundi occupies roughly 27,834 square kilometres in the interior of east-central Africa, which makes it slightly smaller than Belgium, Haiti or the American state of Maryland. It is one of the smallest countries on the African mainland and, by most estimates, one of the most densely populated, carrying somewhere around fourteen million people on that modest area. Almost nothing about the country can be understood without first understanding its land, because the population lives overwhelmingly by cultivating it directly, and the shape of the ground determines almost everything else: where people can farm, where rain falls, where roads can run, and how goods reach the sea more than a thousand kilometres away.

The country sits at a genuine geographical hinge. Its western edge drops into the Western branch of the East African Rift, a continental fracture that here holds Lake Tanganyika, the second-deepest lake in the world. Its central spine, the Congo–Nile Divide, is a watershed of continental significance: rain falling a few hundred metres apart on that ridge ends up either in the Atlantic Ocean by way of the Congo basin, or in the Mediterranean by way of the Nile, a journey of some 6,600 kilometres. The southernmost sources of the Nile are Burundian streams. To stand on that ridge is to stand between two of the great river systems of the planet.

The country lies just south of the equator, between roughly 2°20' and 4°28' south latitude and 28°50' and 30°53' east longitude. This equatorial position would ordinarily imply oppressive heat, yet most Burundians live in a temperate climate, because most of the country sits between 1,400 and 2,000 metres above sea level. Altitude, not latitude, sets the thermostat. The result is a landscape of green hills with mean temperatures in the high teens Celsius, cool nights, and two rainy seasons, which is why nineteenth-century European visitors so often reached for the word "Switzerland" — a comparison that flatters the scenery and badly misrepresents the economics.

Burundi is landlocked, bordered by Rwanda to the north along roughly 315 kilometres, Tanzania to the east and southeast along roughly 589 kilometres, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the west along roughly 236 kilometres, with Lake Tanganyika forming much of that western boundary. The total land frontier is about 1,140 kilometres. Every import and export must cross at least one other country, and that single fact shapes the price of fuel, fertiliser and cement in every market in the country.

Two further features complete the orientation. The country is a landscape of hills rather than plains or alpine mountains: rounded, cultivated, closely spaced ridges separated by narrow marshy valleys, a texture so consistent that Burundians speak of their homeland simply as a country of hills. And it has two capitals, Bujumbura on the lake serving as the economic and port city and Gitega on the central plateau designated the political capital from 2019, an arrangement reflecting the tension between the low western trading edge and the populous interior. Geography here is not scenery. It is the binding constraint.

sections.heading: Position, Boundaries and Territorial Extent
sections.body:
Burundi's territory forms a rough rectangle tilted slightly, longer from north to south than from west to east, measuring on the order of 260 kilometres by 180 kilometres. Of the total 27,834 square kilometres usually cited, about 25,680 square kilometres are land and roughly 2,150 square kilometres are water, the water figure consisting almost entirely of Burundi's share of Lake Tanganyika together with a scatter of smaller northern lakes. Different sources give slightly different totals, generally between 27,816 and 27,834 square kilometres; the variation comes from how the lake boundary is drawn rather than from any territorial dispute.

The northern boundary with Rwanda runs largely along the Kanyaru and Akanyaru rivers and across the marshy Bugesera depression, a landscape of shallow lakes and papyrus swamp shared between the two states. Because Burundi and Rwanda were administered together as Ruanda-Urundi under German and then Belgian rule, the line between them was drawn as an internal administrative boundary and later became international on 1 July 1962, when both territories became independent as separate states. The two countries share a language family, a settlement pattern and a great deal of physical geography, which is why generalisations about one usually apply to the other.

The eastern boundary with Tanzania runs through the lower, hotter country of the Kumoso depression and the Malagarasi drainage, partly along rivers and partly along surveyed straight lines. The southeastern corner reaches down toward the Malagarasi wetlands, one of the larger freshwater wetland systems in the region. The western boundary is the most dramatic: from the Rusizi River in the north it follows the rift floor to Lake Tanganyika, and then runs down the middle of the lake for roughly 175 kilometres, with the Congolese shore visible as a wall of mountains across the water on a clear day.

Burundi is administratively divided into provinces, which were reorganised in 2023 from eighteen into a smaller number of larger units, together with communes and the collines or hills that are the basic unit of rural life and identity. The colline is worth pausing on, because it is not merely an administrative convenience: Burundian rural settlement is genuinely organised around individual hills, each with its own name, its own crest, its own slopes and its own community, rather than around nucleated villages. Asking a Burundian where they are from characteristically produces the name of a hill.

Distance from the sea is the defining locational fact. Bujumbura lies roughly 1,400 kilometres by road and rail from Dar es Salaam on the Indian Ocean, and around 2,000 kilometres from Mombasa in Kenya. Transport costs on that journey have historically represented a substantial fraction of the landed price of imported goods.

sections.heading: Geological Foundations and the East African Rift
sections.body:
The rocks beneath Burundi are ancient. Most of the country is underlain by Precambrian basement: metamorphosed sediments, schists, quartzites and gneisses, intruded by granites, belonging largely to what geologists call the Kibaran or Karagwe–Ankole belt, a mountain-building episode dated to roughly 1,400 to 1,000 million years ago. These are the deeply eroded roots of mountains that were already old before multicellular life became common. Overlying them in places are younger Neoproterozoic sequences, and in the rift and its margins there are much younger Cenozoic sediments and some volcanic material. The old crystalline basement matters practically, because it weathers to deep, leached, acidic soils and because it hosts the country's mineral endowment: nickel in ultramafic intrusions, gold in quartz veins, tin and tantalum-niobium minerals in granitic pegmatites, and rare-earth and phosphate occurrences.

The dominant structural feature is the Western or Albertine branch of the East African Rift System. The East African Rift is a divergent plate boundary in the early stages of continental break-up, where the Somali plate is pulling away from the Nubian plate at a rate on the order of five to seven millimetres a year, roughly the speed at which a fingernail grows. Extension thins and stretches the crust; blocks drop down along steep normal faults to form elongated troughs called grabens, and the shoulders of those troughs are pushed up. Where the Eastern branch through Ethiopia and Kenya is volcanically spectacular, the Western branch is deeper, wetter and less volcanic. Its rift floors have filled with water to form a chain of lakes: Albert, Edward, Kivu and, the deepest, Tanganyika.

Burundi sits astride the eastern shoulder of this western rift. The Congo–Nile Divide is essentially a rift shoulder, uplifted as the adjacent crust foundered. That uplift explains the country's most striking asymmetry: from the divide, the land falls very steeply westward over perhaps twenty to thirty kilometres to the rift floor at around 800 metres, but slopes gently and unevenly eastward over a hundred kilometres or more of plateau toward Tanzania. Rivers reflect this. The short, steep, west-flowing streams cut violently into the escarpment, while the long east-flowing rivers meander through broad marshy valleys.

Because it lies on an active plate boundary, Burundi is seismically active. Earthquakes are frequent, generally moderate, and occasionally destructive; the region around the northern end of Lake Tanganyika has produced events in the magnitude 5 to 7 range, including a magnitude 6.8 event beneath the lake on 5 December 2005 that damaged buildings in Bujumbura and, more severely, in Bukavu and Kalemie across the border. Building stock of unreinforced masonry and mud brick is poorly suited to shaking, and seismic risk is under-appreciated relative to the far more visible hazards of flood and landslide.

sections.heading: Relief, the Congo-Nile Divide and the Natural Regions
sections.body:
Burundian relief is best understood as a staircase descending eastward from a high ridge near the western edge. The ridge itself is the Congo–Nile Divide, known in French as the Crête Congo-Nil, a north–south backbone typically 2,000 to 2,500 metres high running roughly parallel to and about twenty to fifty kilometres inland from Lake Tanganyika. The country's highest point, Mount Heha, stands on this ridge south of Bujumbura at about 2,684 metres, though figures between 2,670 and 2,690 metres appear in different sources. The lowest point is the surface of Lake Tanganyika at roughly 772 metres. Total relief is therefore about 1,900 metres, packed into a country you can drive across in a day.

Geographers conventionally divide Burundi into a series of natural regions, and these names recur constantly in agricultural, climatic and administrative discussion. The Imbo is the rift-floor plain in the west, roughly 770 to 1,000 metres, hot and comparatively dry. The Mumirwa is the steep escarpment above it, a belt perhaps ten to twenty kilometres wide climbing from 1,000 to 1,800 metres, with slopes commonly steeper than thirty per cent and severe erosion. The Mugamba is the high country of the divide itself, 1,800 to 2,500 metres, cool, wet and originally forested. Behind it the Bututsi forms a high grassy plateau in the south.

East of the divide the land descends in broad steps. The Kirimiro or central plateau, around 1,500 to 1,800 metres, contains Gitega and much of the country's densest farmland. Further east and north the Buyenzi in the north-west and the Bweru, Buyogoma and Moso or Kumoso regions form successively lower plateaus and depressions, the Kumoso in the far east falling to around 1,100 to 1,400 metres and becoming markedly hotter and more seasonal. In the north the Bugesera is a low, lake-studded depression shared with Rwanda, and in the far south the Buragane descends toward the Malagarasi.

The characteristic Burundian landform, repeated thousands of times, is the convex-crested hill with a rounded or flattened top, long cultivated slopes, and a marshy valley bottom carrying a small stream. These valley marshes, called marais, are agriculturally crucial: because they retain moisture, they carry crops through the dry season when the hillsides cannot, and they have been progressively drained and cultivated. The drainage of marshes is one of the country's most consequential ongoing land-use changes, converting a water-buffering, biodiverse habitat into seasonal cropland, with hydrological consequences downstream that are rarely measured.

Slope is the single most important physical variable in Burundian land use. A very large share of cultivated land sits on gradients that soil conservation manuals would classify as unsuitable for annual cropping without terracing, and much of it is nonetheless cropped annually because there is no alternative land.

sections.heading: The Imbo Plain and the Rusizi Valley
sections.body:
The Imbo is Burundi's rift-floor lowland, a narrow alluvial strip running along the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika and up the Rusizi valley toward Lake Kivu. It is perhaps ten to twenty kilometres wide at its broadest and narrows in places to almost nothing where the escarpment comes down to the water. Elevation runs from the lake surface at about 772 metres to roughly a thousand metres at the foot of the Mumirwa slopes. Because it lies almost 1,000 metres lower than the plateau, the Imbo is a different world climatically: mean annual temperatures around 23 to 24 degrees Celsius, daytime maxima commonly above 30 degrees, and rainfall of roughly 800 to 1,000 millimetres a year, markedly less than the highlands receive.

The plain is built from sediment shed off the escarpment by short, steep rivers — the Ntahangwa, the Muha, the Mugere, the Kanyosha and others — which drop over a thousand metres in a few tens of kilometres and consequently carry enormous sediment loads during storms. The result is a series of coalescing alluvial fans. This is fertile ground, well suited to cotton, rice, oil palm, maize and sugar cane, and it holds the only substantial irrigation schemes in the country, drawing on the Rusizi. It is also, precisely because it is a fan surface fed by flashy mountain streams, exposed to violent flash flooding and debris flows.

The Rusizi River defines the northern Imbo. It leaves Lake Kivu at about 1,460 metres and falls to Lake Tanganyika at 772 metres over roughly 117 kilometres, a drop of nearly 700 metres that makes it one of the region's better hydropower rivers; the Rusizi I and Rusizi II stations on its course supply power to Burundi, Rwanda and eastern Congo, and further schemes have long been under discussion. Near its mouth the river slows and spreads into a delta of papyrus swamp, oxbows and gallery forest, protected as the Rusizi National Park, and famous locally for large Nile crocodiles and hippopotamuses.

Bujumbura, the country's largest city and its economic capital, sits at the head of the lake on this plain, at about 774 metres. Its position is superb for trade — the port is the natural outlet for the whole northern Tanganyika basin — and problematic for safety, since the city occupies the very fans that the escarpment rivers build. Storm floods descending the Ntahangwa and neighbouring channels have repeatedly inundated the northern and lakeside quarters, and rising lake levels in wet periods, notably in 2020 and 2021, drowned lakeside districts and displaced tens of thousands of people. The plain's fertility and accessibility draw settlement into exactly the places most exposed to water.

sections.heading: Lake Tanganyika
sections.body:
Lake Tanganyika is the dominant water body of the region and one of the most remarkable lakes on Earth. It is roughly 673 kilometres long and averages about 50 kilometres wide, covering some 32,900 square kilometres, and it reaches a maximum depth of about 1,470 metres, making it the second-deepest lake in the world after Baikal and the deepest in Africa. Because its floor lies more than 600 metres below sea level, it is also one of the deepest cryptodepressions on the planet. It contains something like 18,900 cubic kilometres of water, roughly a sixth of the world's accessible surface fresh water, more than all the North American Great Lakes except Superior combined. It is shared by Burundi, Tanzania, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The lake occupies a rift graben and is old — estimates of its age cluster around nine to twelve million years, with the northern basin possibly younger. That antiquity, combined with isolation, has produced extraordinary endemism. Roughly 250 cichlid fish species are described from the lake, the overwhelming majority found nowhere else, along with about 150 non-cichlid fish, endemic snails with unusually thick shells, endemic crabs, shrimps, ostracods and sponges. Biologists treat Tanganyika as a natural laboratory of evolution comparable to the Galápagos, and its cichlid radiation is a textbook case of adaptive radiation into feeding, breeding and depth niches.

Physically, the lake is permanently stratified, or meromictic. Because tropical surface waters stay warm year-round, the density difference between warm surface water and cold deep water is never erased by seasonal cooling, so the water column does not overturn. Below roughly 100 to 200 metres the water is anoxic and rich in hydrogen sulphide, and it has been isolated from the atmosphere for centuries. Living things, therefore, occupy only the thin oxygenated upper layer; the vast majority of the lake's volume is biologically dead. This has a practical corollary: nutrients sink out of the productive zone and are effectively lost, so the lake's fisheries depend on wind-driven upwelling, strongest in the dry season at the southern end, to return phosphorus and nitrogen to the surface.

The fishery matters enormously to Burundi. It has historically centred on two small pelagic clupeids known locally as ndagala, together with predatory Lates species related to the Nile perch, and has supplied a large share of animal protein in Bujumbura and the lakeshore communes. Catches have declined substantially since the mid-twentieth century. The causes are contested: fishing pressure and destructive gear are clearly implicated, but there is credible evidence that warming surface waters have strengthened stratification, weakened upwelling and reduced primary productivity, meaning that part of the decline is climatic rather than purely a management failure. Sediment delivered by eroding hillsides also smothers the rocky shoreline habitat on which many endemic species depend.

sections.heading: Rivers, Drainage and the Sources of the Nile
sections.body:
Burundi's drainage is split by the Congo–Nile Divide into two systems of wildly unequal area and equal fame. West of the ridge, a narrow strip of perhaps fifteen per cent of the national territory drains into Lake Tanganyika, and thence via the Lukuga River into the Congo and ultimately the Atlantic Ocean. East of the ridge, the great majority of the country drains north and east into the Nile system by way of the Kagera, or south-east into the Malagarasi, which flows to Lake Tanganyika and so also belongs to the Congo basin.

The Nile-side rivers are the celebrated ones. The Ruvyironza, also written Luvironza, rises on the eastern flank of the divide in the Bururi–Rutana highlands near Mount Kikizi at around 2,000 metres. It joins the Ruvubu, which is the largest river wholly within Burundi, flowing north-east through a broad valley; the Ruvubu in turn joins the Nyabarongo coming out of Rwanda to form the Kagera, which flows into Lake Victoria. Because Lake Victoria feeds the White Nile at Jinja, and the White Nile joins the Blue Nile at Khartoum, the Ruvyironza is by the standard measure of remotest headstream one of the candidates for the ultimate source of the Nile — a claim marked since 1937 by a small stone pyramid erected at Kasumo by the German geographer Burkhart Waldecker.

The claim deserves honest treatment. "Source of the Nile" is a definitional question rather than a factual one, and the answer depends on whether one measures the longest continuous watercourse, the remotest headstream by distance, or the largest contributor of water. Burundi's Ruvyironza and Rwanda's Rukarara, rising in the Nyungwe forest, are the two principal contenders for remotest headstream, and a 2006 expedition argued for the Rukarara. The difference between them is a matter of a few kilometres of small mountain stream, and neither claim is unreasonable. What is not in doubt is that the ultimate headwaters of the Nile lie in this highland region straddling the Burundi–Rwanda border, roughly 6,600 kilometres from the Mediterranean.

The east-flowing rivers share a distinctive form: gentle gradients, wide floodplains and extensive papyrus marshes, with the channel meandering through a valley far broader than the present river could have cut. In the dry season these valley bottoms are the country's agricultural insurance. The Ruvubu, Ruvyironza, Mubarazi, Kanyaru and Malagarasi tributaries all show this pattern.

The west-flowing rivers are the opposite: short, steep, torrential and heavily loaded with sediment. The Rusizi is the exception in size, carrying the outflow of Lake Kivu, but the Ntahangwa, Mugere, Dama, Nyengwe and Murembwe are typical — quiet trickles for much of the year, capable of becoming destructive debris-laden torrents within an hour of an intense storm on the escarpment above. Burundi's northern lakes, including Rweru, Cohoha, Rwihinda and Kanzigiri, lie in the Bugesera depression and belong to the Kagera and therefore Nile system.

sections.heading: Climate: Tropical Latitude, Temperate Altitude
sections.body:
Burundi's climate is best described as tropical highland, and the governing principle is the environmental lapse rate: air temperature falls with height at roughly 6.5 degrees Celsius per thousand metres in the free atmosphere, and typically five to six degrees per thousand metres over this kind of terrain. Because the country spans about 1,900 metres of relief, it spans roughly ten to twelve degrees of mean temperature. Bujumbura on the lake averages about 23 to 24 degrees Celsius annually; Gitega on the central plateau at around 1,700 metres averages roughly 19 to 20; the Mugamba highlands above 2,000 metres average around 16 to 17, with night temperatures that can approach freezing on clear dry-season nights and occasional ground frost on the highest ground.

Seasonality of temperature is slight, as it is everywhere near the equator. The annual range between the warmest and coolest month is typically only two to four degrees, far smaller than the daily range, which commonly reaches ten to fifteen degrees in the highlands. In practical terms, the day-night cycle is the real season.

Rainfall is the variable that structures the year, and it is controlled by the seasonal migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, the belt of converging trade winds and deep convection that follows the overhead sun with a lag of a few weeks. As the ITCZ passes over the country twice a year, Burundi receives two rainfall maxima, which merge in practice into a long wet season. The conventional calendar recognises a short rainy season from roughly October to December, a short dry or reduced-rain interval around January and early February, a long rainy season from February to May, and a decisive long dry season from June to August or early September, during which many areas receive almost no rain at all.

Annual totals vary strongly with relief. The Imbo plain and the eastern Kumoso depression receive on the order of 800 to 1,100 millimetres; the central plateau around 1,200 to 1,400; the Congo–Nile Divide and the Mugamba highlands 1,400 to 2,000 millimetres, locally more. The mechanism is orographic: moist air forced to rise over the ridge cools, condenses and precipitates, and descends drier on the far side. The escarpment also generates intense convective storms in the afternoon and evening, which is why erosion and flash flooding are concentrated there.

Interannual variability is substantial and is linked to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation and to the Indian Ocean Dipole. Warm-phase events have historically been associated with heavy rainfall and flooding in the region, and cold phases with drought in the eastern lowlands. Because most farming is rain-fed and most households have little stored surplus, a failed or badly timed season translates quickly into food insecurity, and the timing of onset matters as much as the total.

sections.heading: Soils, Fertility and the Erosion Problem
sections.body:
Burundi's soils are largely the product of deep weathering of old crystalline rock under warm, wet conditions over very long periods. The dominant types are Ferralsols and Acrisols, together with Nitisols on some volcanic-influenced and basic-rock areas, and Histosols or peat in the valley marshes. Deep chemical weathering has stripped these soils of most of their readily available bases — calcium, magnesium, potassium — leaving a residue rich in iron and aluminium oxides and in kaolinite clay. That gives them their characteristic red or reddish-brown colour and their generally good physical structure and drainage, but poor chemical fertility.

Three chemical problems recur. First, acidity: soil pH commonly falls between 4.0 and 5.5, and at pH values below about 5.2 aluminium becomes soluble in forms toxic to root growth, which stunts crops regardless of how much fertiliser is applied. Second, phosphorus fixation: iron and aluminium oxides bind phosphate tightly, so a large fraction of any phosphate fertiliser added becomes unavailable within weeks, and phosphorus deficiency is nearly universal. Third, low organic matter and low cation exchange capacity, meaning the soil holds little reserve of nutrients and little buffering capacity, so nutrients applied are easily leached by heavy rain. Liming with locally available travertine or dolomitic material, and building organic matter through manure, compost and green manures, generally give better returns than mineral fertiliser applied alone.

Erosion is the more visible and probably the more serious problem. The combination of steep slopes, intense convective rainfall, continuous annual cropping and a shrinking fallow period is close to a textbook recipe for soil loss. Measured rates in the Mumirwa escarpment and on steep cultivated slopes elsewhere have been reported in ranges from around 18 to well over 100 tonnes per hectare per year, against a soil formation rate on the order of one tonne per hectare per year. At those rates a topsoil layer that took millennia to form can be removed within a working lifetime. Gullying is widespread, landslides are common on the escarpment after prolonged rain, and the sediment ends up in rivers, in Lake Tanganyika, and in the turbines and reservoirs of hydropower schemes.

Countermeasures are well known and unevenly applied. Contour bunds and ditches, progressive terracing, grass strips of Setaria or vetiver, agroforestry with nitrogen-fixing trees such as Calliandra, Leucaena and Grevillea, mulching, and permanent cover crops all reduce loss substantially. Their limitation is not technical but economic: they demand labour and land in the short term from households that cannot spare either, and their returns come slowly. Where soil conservation has succeeded at scale in this region, it has usually involved sustained collective labour organisation and secure enough tenure that the person doing the work expects to benefit.

sections.heading: Vegetation, Forests and Protected Areas
sections.body:
The natural vegetation of Burundi would, in the absence of people, form a gradient controlled almost entirely by altitude and rainfall. The Congo–Nile Divide above about 1,600 metres would carry montane rainforest, dense evergreen woodland with a canopy of Entandrophragma, Symphonia, Newtonia, Podocarpus and Prunus africana, tree ferns in the gullies and epiphytes throughout. Between roughly 1,300 and 1,600 metres a drier montane and submontane woodland would grade into wooded savanna. The eastern lowlands and the Kumoso would carry miombo woodland dominated by Brachystegia and Julbernardia, the characteristic dry woodland of south-central Africa. The Imbo would be wooded savanna and thorn scrub with gallery forest along the streams, and the valley bottoms throughout would be papyrus marsh.

Very little of this survives intact. Estimates of remaining natural forest cover vary with definition, but figures in the range of six to eleven per cent of national territory are commonly cited, against a pre-colonial cover that was certainly far higher. The proximate causes are agricultural clearance and fuelwood extraction. Wood and charcoal supply the overwhelming majority of household energy — figures around ninety per cent of primary energy consumption are routinely reported — and with a large, growing, overwhelmingly rural population, the arithmetic of fuelwood demand against forest growth is unforgiving.

The most important surviving block is the Kibira National Park, roughly 400 square kilometres of montane rainforest strung along the Congo–Nile Divide in the north-west. Kibira is contiguous with Rwanda's Nyungwe Forest, and the combined block is among the largest remaining montane forests in East Africa and a centre of Albertine Rift endemism. It is also, and not incidentally, the principal water tower for the north of the country: forest cover on that ridge regulates infiltration and dry-season baseflow for the rivers that supply Bujumbura and feed the Rwegura hydropower reservoir. Deforestation there has direct and measurable consequences for electricity supply.

The Ruvubu National Park, at roughly 500 square kilometres the largest protected area, follows the Ruvubu River in the east and protects savanna, gallery forest and wetland with populations of buffalo, hippopotamus, antelope and, at least historically, a few leopards. The Rusizi National Park protects the delta and palm savanna near Bujumbura. Smaller reserves include Bururi Forest, a fragment of montane forest in the south, and the Lake Rwihinda natural reserve in the north, an important waterbird site sometimes called the lake of birds.

Protection on paper is stronger than protection in practice. Parks are ringed by dense farming populations with immediate need for land, wood and grazing, and enforcement capacity is thin. The most successful conservation approaches in this region have generally been those that give adjacent communities a tangible interest in the forest's survival, whether through beekeeping, tourism revenue, controlled extraction of non-timber products, or reliable water supply.

sections.heading: Wildlife and the Albertine Rift Biodiversity Hotspot
sections.body:
Burundi sits within the Albertine Rift, a region running from the Rwenzori Mountains south to the northern end of Lake Tanganyika that is recognised as one of Africa's principal centres of endemism and one of the world's biodiversity hotspots. The reasons are geographical: the rift's mountains have functioned as refugia during Pleistocene climate cycles, when cooler, drier phases contracted African forests into isolated pockets where populations diverged. Steep altitudinal gradients pack many habitat zones into short distances, and the resulting mosaic supports species found nowhere else. More than a thousand vertebrate species are recorded from the Albertine Rift as a whole, with dozens of endemic birds, amphibians and mammals.

Burundi's share of that fauna is concentrated in Kibira and, to a lesser degree, in Bururi Forest. Primates are the most visible: chimpanzees persist in small numbers in Kibira, along with olive baboons, several guenon species including the blue monkey and the l'Hoest's monkey, black-and-white colobus, and nocturnal galagos. Bird diversity is high, with something over six hundred species recorded nationally, including Albertine Rift endemics such as the Rwenzori turaco and various forest warblers and sunbirds, and a rich waterbird assemblage on the northern lakes and the Rusizi delta.

The large-mammal fauna has been severely reduced. Elephants, which once occurred in the eastern woodlands and the Rusizi, are effectively gone as a resident population. Lions have disappeared. Buffalo persist mainly in Ruvubu. Hippopotamus and Nile crocodile remain in the Rusizi delta and along the lakeshore and larger rivers, and both are genuinely dangerous to people, causing fatalities most years; the hippopotamus in particular is responsible for more human deaths in Africa than most predators, and its habit of grazing on land at night brings it into contact with farms near water. Sitatunga survive in some papyrus swamps.

The aquatic fauna of Lake Tanganyika is the country's most globally significant biological asset. The cichlid radiation there, with roughly 250 endemic species, together with endemic molluscs, crustaceans and even a freshwater jellyfish, represents an evolutionary record with few parallels. Its vulnerability comes from three directions: sedimentation from eroding catchments smothering the rocky littoral habitats on which many species depend, over-harvest of pelagic stocks, and warming-driven changes in stratification that reduce productivity.

Honest assessment requires acknowledging how thin the data are. Systematic wildlife surveys in Burundi have been intermittent, interrupted by the civil conflict that ran through much of the 1990s and early 2000s, and population estimates for most species should be treated as informed approximations rather than measurements. Some species listed in older accounts may already be locally extinct without anyone having recorded the last individual, and conversely a few may persist in fragments nobody has surveyed. What is not in doubt is the direction of change for large terrestrial species and for forest habitat, which has been downward for a century.

sections.heading: Population Distribution, Density and Settlement
sections.body:
Burundi's population is the central fact of its human geography. Estimates around the middle of the 2020s place it near fourteen million, on 27,834 square kilometres, giving an overall density on the order of 470 to 500 people per square kilometre. Since roughly a quarter of the surface is water, protected forest, steep escarpment or marsh, the effective density on cultivated land is considerably higher — figures in excess of 600 people per square kilometre of arable land are plausible. This places Burundi among the most densely settled countries in Africa and comparable to densely populated parts of Asia, but without the industrial or urban employment that usually accompanies such densities.

Growth has been rapid. Total fertility has fallen from very high levels but remains high by global standards, in the range of four to five children per woman in recent surveys, and the age structure is extremely young, with something close to half the population under eighteen. The demographic momentum implied by that age structure means the population will continue to grow substantially for decades even if fertility falls quickly, and every projection implies further intensification of pressure on land.

The settlement pattern is unusual and important. Historically Burundians did not live in nucleated villages but in dispersed homesteads called rugo, each family compound sitting on its own plot within its hill's territory, surrounded by its banana grove and fields. The consequence is that the countryside looks continuously inhabited rather than dotted with villages: driving through rural Burundi, one is rarely out of sight of houses. This dispersal has real effects on service delivery, since providing water, electricity, clinics and schools to scattered homesteads is far more expensive per household than serving a village. Post-conflict resettlement policy has at times promoted grouped villages, with mixed reception.

Urbanisation is very low. Something in the region of fourteen per cent of the population lives in towns, one of the lowest urban shares anywhere. Bujumbura, on Lake Tanganyika, is by a wide margin the largest city, with a population usually put somewhere above a million in its metropolitan area, and remains the economic and port capital. Gitega, in the central plateau, was designated the political capital under a law passed in December 2018 and implemented from early 2019, restoring the seat of the pre-colonial monarchy to a central position; the transfer of institutions has proceeded gradually. Other towns — Ngozi, Rumonge, Muyinga, Ruyigi, Kayanza, Bururi, Makamba — are modest regional centres.

Population is not evenly spread. Densities are highest on the fertile, well-watered northern plateau around Ngozi and Kayanza and on the central plateau, and lower in the hot eastern Kumoso, parts of the Imbo, and the high, cold Bututsi grasslands.

sections.heading: Agriculture, Land Use and the Farming Calendar
sections.body:
Agriculture occupies the overwhelming majority of Burundians — commonly around eighty to ninety per cent of the labour force — and it is overwhelmingly smallholder, rain-fed and manual. The characteristic holding is well under a hectare, and average farm size has been shrinking steadily because customary inheritance divides land among sons at each generation. Fragmentation has reached the point where many households farm several plots each measured in fractions of a hectare, scattered across different slope positions, which is inefficient for labour but is itself a rational risk-spreading strategy, since a hillside plot and a marsh plot fail under different conditions.

The staple system is built around bananas, beans, cassava, sweet potato, maize, sorghum, taro and peas, with the specific mix varying by altitude. Bananas are extraordinarily important and occupy a large share of cultivated land: they are perennial, they hold soil, they produce year-round rather than seasonally, and a substantial part of the crop is brewed into banana beer, which functions as both a foodstuff and a store of value. Beans are the principal protein source and are grown almost everywhere, often intercropped with maize or bananas. Cassava provides drought insurance because it can be left in the ground and harvested when needed, though cassava mosaic and brown streak viruses have caused severe losses in the region.

The two cash crops of consequence are coffee and tea, and their distribution is dictated by altitude. Arabica coffee, largely of the Bourbon type, thrives on the plateau between roughly 1,400 and 1,800 metres and has long been the country's leading export earner, grown by hundreds of thousands of smallholders with a few hundred trees each and processed at washing stations. Tea prefers the wetter, cooler ground above 1,800 metres on the Congo–Nile Divide, where it is grown on estates and by outgrowers. Cotton, rice, oil palm and sugar cane occupy the hot Imbo lowlands.

The farming calendar follows the rains closely. Season A is planted around September and October with the short rains and harvested in January and February. Season B is planted in February and March with the long rains and harvested in June and July. Season C, from roughly July to September, is the dry-season crop grown in the drained valley marshes, and it is what carries many households through the lean months. The lean season itself, when the previous harvest has been eaten and the next is not ready, typically falls in the months before the Season A harvest.

Livestock are constrained by land. Cattle carry great cultural weight, historically central to social relations, but numbers per household are small and zero-grazing or tethered stall-feeding is increasingly the norm because there is no communal pasture left. Goats, sheep, poultry and rabbits are more common. The scarcity of livestock has a direct agronomic consequence: manure is the main practical source of soil organic matter, and there is not enough of it.

sections.heading: Minerals, Energy and Water Resources
sections.body:
Burundi's mineral endowment is genuine but largely undeveloped, and the reasons are geographical as much as geological. The best-known resource is nickel. The Musongati deposit in the east, part of a belt of layered ultramafic intrusions that also includes Waga and Nyabikere, is regularly described as among the world's larger undeveloped nickel laterite resources, with published estimates typically in the range of 150 to 300 million tonnes at grades around 1.2 to 1.5 per cent nickel, together with associated cobalt, copper and platinum-group elements. It has not been brought into production, and the obstacles are instructive: laterite nickel requires enormous energy input for smelting or high-pressure acid leaching, and a landlocked country with limited generating capacity and 1,400 kilometres of surface transport to a port is a difficult place to build such a plant.

Other minerals are worked mainly at artisanal scale. Gold occurs in quartz veins and alluvial deposits, particularly in the north and north-west, and is exported in quantities that are hard to measure because much of the trade is informal. Cassiterite for tin, together with columbite-tantalite, the ore of tantalum used in electronic capacitors, and wolframite for tungsten, occur in pegmatites; these are the so-called 3T minerals whose regional trade has been the subject of extensive conflict-financing concern and due-diligence regulation. Rare-earth potential has been explored at Gakara in the west, and there are substantial phosphate, kaolin, limestone and vanadium occurrences, along with peat deposits in the highland valleys estimated in the hundreds of millions of tonnes.

Energy is dominated by biomass. Firewood and charcoal supply something like eighty-five to ninety-five per cent of primary energy, and the resulting cutting pressure is the principal driver of deforestation. Electricity access is among the lowest in the world; national figures around ten to fifteen per cent of households have been reported, with rural access far lower still. Installed generating capacity is small — on the order of a hundred megawatts or less, though rising — and is dominated by hydropower.

Hydropower is the country's most promising indigenous energy resource, and it is a direct consequence of relief. Rivers dropping 700 metres from the divide to the rift floor and from Lake Kivu to Lake Tanganyika offer good head. The Rusizi I and Rusizi II plants on the Rusizi are shared regionally; Rwegura on the Kitenge in the north is the largest domestic station; Mugere, Nyemanga and a number of small plants supply the rest, and further schemes including additional Rusizi stations have long been planned. Two problems recur: sediment from eroded catchments fills reservoirs and abrades turbines, and dry-season low flows reduce output precisely when demand is steady, which makes catchment forest protection an energy policy question rather than merely an environmental one.

sections.heading: Natural Hazards: Flood, Landslide, Drought and Earthquake
sections.body:
Burundi's hazard profile follows directly from its physical setting, and the hazards interact rather than occurring in isolation. Flooding is the most frequent and, in terms of people affected, the most consequential. Two distinct kinds occur. Flash floods and debris flows descend the Mumirwa escarpment when intense convective rainfall lands on steep, deforested, cultivated slopes; these arrive with little warning, carry boulders and mud, and have repeatedly destroyed settlements and stretches of the Bujumbura–Rwanda road. Slow-onset flooding occurs on the Imbo plain and around the northern lakes when prolonged rain raises water levels. The rise of Lake Tanganyika during the exceptionally wet period of 2019 to 2021, when levels approached the historic highs last seen in the 1960s, inundated lakeside districts of Bujumbura and the Rusizi plain and displaced tens of thousands of people, many of them for extended periods.

Landslides are the escarpment's signature hazard. The mechanism is straightforward: deep weathered regolith on slopes often exceeding thirty degrees, saturated by days of rain until pore water pressure reduces the effective friction holding the mass in place, then triggered by a final intense burst or by undercutting from road construction or gully erosion. Loss of deep-rooted tree cover removes both mechanical reinforcement and transpiration drying, and steadily raises susceptibility. Fatal landslides occur most years, and the concentration of population on marginal slopes means exposure is rising.

Drought affects the eastern and northern lowlands more than the highlands. The Kumoso depression, parts of Bugesera and the Imbo are the driest zones, and a delayed onset or an early cessation of the rains in these areas can wipe out a season. Because household grain reserves are thin and markets are shallow, a single failed season produces measurable increases in acute malnutrition. Drought and flood are not alternatives; the same El Niño-influenced year may bring destructive rain to one region and deficit to another.

Earthquake risk is real but under-managed. The Western Rift generates frequent moderate seismicity, and events of magnitude 6 and above have occurred in the northern Tanganyika region, including the magnitude 6.8 event of 5 December 2005. Ground shaking in a landscape of unreinforced masonry, adobe and heavy tile roofs, on steep slopes with saturated soils, carries a compound risk: the shaking itself, plus seismically triggered landslides. Seismic building provisions exist more on paper than in practice.

Secondary and biological hazards deserve mention. Hailstorms and violent windstorms damage crops and roofs, particularly in the highlands. Malaria is endemic in the lowlands and has extended to higher altitudes as warming has raised the thermal limit for the parasite's development in the mosquito, producing epidemics in highland populations with little acquired immunity. Cholera outbreaks follow flooding in Bujumbura's lakeside quarters with grim regularity.

sections.heading: Living With the Geography: Constraints, Change and Prospects
sections.body:
The honest summary of Burundi's geography is that it presents a country of real natural advantages operating under a set of binding constraints that no single policy can lift. The advantages are genuine: reliable bimodal rainfall over most of the territory, a temperate highland climate that suits both people and a wide range of crops, deep soils with good physical structure, substantial hydropower head, an unusually valuable lake, and a mineral endowment of real magnitude. The constraints are equally genuine: landlocked position with long and expensive routes to any port, very high and rising population density on erodible slopes, an energy system dependent on wood that is being cut faster than it grows, and a hazard exposure that concentrates precisely where the best land and the largest city are.

The central geographical dilemma is the relationship between population and slope. When people were fewer, steep land could be left in forest or long fallow while cultivation concentrated on gentler ground, and the system was stable. As density rose, cultivation climbed onto slopes that cannot sustain annual cropping without heavy investment in terracing, fallow disappeared, soil organic matter fell, yields declined, and declining yields required still more land — a feedback loop that soil scientists recognise across the tropical highlands. The exits from that loop are well understood and all difficult: intensification through soil amendment and agroforestry, off-farm employment to reduce the number of people who must live directly from land, and fertility decline. All three are slow.

Climate change adds a further layer of uncertainty that should be described carefully rather than confidently. Warming is established: regional temperatures have risen and are projected to continue rising, which shifts the altitudinal zones for crops, pests and malaria upward. Projections for rainfall are much less certain; most models suggest an increase in total precipitation and, more consistently, an increase in the intensity of heavy rainfall events over East Africa, with the timing of season onset becoming less predictable. For a country whose principal hazards are erosion, landslide and flood, a shift toward fewer but heavier rain events is a materially worse outcome than a change in the annual total, because it is intensity that detaches soil and destabilises slopes.

What would change the picture most is not obscure. Protecting the forest on the Congo–Nile Divide would stabilise water supply and hydropower output together. Terracing and agroforestry at scale would slow soil loss. Reducing household dependence on charcoal would relieve the largest pressure on remaining woodland. Better transport links to Dar es Salaam would lower the cost of everything imported. Each is a known intervention with demonstrated effect elsewhere in the region.

For a reader trying to hold the country in mind, the useful mental image is a tilted block: a high wet ridge on the west, dropping abruptly into a deep rift lake, and sloping gently away eastward through terraced hills and marshy valleys toward drier plateau. Almost every fact about Burundi — where the rain falls, where the coffee grows, where the landslides happen, where the people are — follows from that shape.

guides.title: Geography of Cabo Verde
guides.summary: A full geographical account of the Cabo Verde archipelago: its position off West Africa, the mantle plume and ocean swell that built it, the volcanic and erosional landforms of each island, its Sahelian climate and chronic water scarcity, and how drought, emigration, hazards and the sea have shaped where and how people live.

sections.heading: Where Cabo Verde Is, and Why the Position Governs Everything
sections.body:
Cabo Verde is an archipelago of ten main islands and eight or so islets in the central Atlantic Ocean, lying roughly 570 kilometres west of the Cap-Vert peninsula of Senegal, the westernmost point of continental Africa, from which the country takes its name. The islands span latitudes of about 14 degrees 48 minutes to 17 degrees 12 minutes north and longitudes of about 22 degrees 40 minutes to 25 degrees 22 minutes west. Total land area is approximately 4,033 square kilometres, smaller than many single counties, but the exclusive economic zone that surrounds it covers on the order of 734,000 square kilometres, so the state is overwhelmingly a marine one with a few rocks in it. 

That latitude is the single fact from which most of the country's geography follows. Cabo Verde sits at the ocean end of the Sahel, the semi-arid belt that runs across Africa south of the Sahara, and it lies squarely within the belt of northeast trade winds. Air arriving over the islands has crossed the Sahara or the dry eastern Atlantic and it is subsiding, stable and thirsty. The result is that an archipelago sitting in the middle of an ocean, at a tropical latitude, is arid: annual rainfall on the flat eastern islands is under 100 millimetres, less than parts of the Mojave Desert, and even the capital receives only around 200 to 250 millimetres in an average year. The name Cabo Verde, green cape, describes the Senegalese headland the islands were named after and not the islands themselves, which are for most of the year brown. 

The position matters in a second way, which is that it sits astride the sea lanes between Europe, Africa and the Americas. The islands were uninhabited when Portuguese navigators reached them between 1456 and 1462, which is unusual and important: unlike almost every other Atlantic island group with a mainland so close, there is no indigenous population and no pre-colonial layer to the human geography. Everything on the islands, every crop, every animal, every village and every person, arrived by ship after 1460. Ribeira Grande on Santiago, now called Cidade Velha and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was founded in 1462 and was the first permanent European town in the tropics. 

A third consequence of position is atmospheric. The waters just upwind of the islands are the nursery of the Atlantic hurricane season. Easterly waves rolling off the West African coast frequently begin organising into tropical cyclones in exactly this longitude band, and meteorologists call the resulting storms Cape Verde-type hurricanes; a large share of the Atlantic basin's most intense hurricanes begin their lives here. The islands themselves are usually just west or north of where the storms consolidate, which spares them most of the time but not always.

sections.heading: The Archipelago: Ten Islands in Two Groups
sections.body:
The islands are conventionally divided into two groups named for their relation to the prevailing northeast trade wind. The Barlavento, the windward group, lies to the north and comprises six main islands: Santo Antão, São Vicente, Santa Luzia, São Nicolau, Sal and Boa Vista, plus the small uninhabited islets of Branco and Raso lying between Santa Luzia and São Nicolau. The Sotavento, the leeward group, lies to the south and comprises four: Maio, Santiago, Fogo and Brava, plus the tiny Rombos islets off Brava. Nine of the ten main islands are inhabited; Santa Luzia, about 35 square kilometres of dry ground, has no permanent population and is a nature reserve. 

By area the ranking is: Santiago, roughly 991 square kilometres and the largest; Santo Antão at about 779; Boa Vista at about 620; Fogo at about 476; São Nicolau at about 343; Maio at about 269; São Vicente at about 227; Sal at about 216; Santa Luzia at about 35; and Brava, the smallest inhabited island, at about 64 square kilometres. By population the ranking is completely different, and that mismatch is one of the most instructive facts about the country. Santiago alone holds a little over half the national population of roughly half a million, and São Vicente, the eighth-largest island by area, holds the second-largest population because of the deepwater harbour at Mindelo. Sal and Boa Vista, large and nearly rainless, held very few people for centuries and have filled rapidly only since the tourism boom of the 2000s. 

The arrangement of the islands on the map is itself a geological clue. They do not form a straight line, as the Hawaiian chain does. They form a rough horseshoe or open crescent, concave toward the west, with the eastern islands of Sal, Boa Vista and Maio forming one limb, the southern islands of Santiago, Fogo and Brava another, and the northern islands of São Nicolau, Santa Luzia, São Vicente and Santo Antão a third. A simple hotspot passing under a moving plate should produce a line. A horseshoe implies something more complicated, and it turns out to reflect the fact that the African plate is barely moving over the underlying mantle upwelling. 

Administratively the country is divided into twenty-two municipalities, called concelhos, unevenly distributed because population is unevenly distributed: Santiago carries nine of them while several small islands constitute a single municipality each, and Brava, with fewer than six thousand residents, is a municipality in its own right. The capital is Praia, on the southern coast of Santiago. The country uses UTC minus one hour, an hour behind Greenwich, which places it in its own narrow time band shared with the Azores. Distances between islands are short by ocean standards but awkward in practice: Santo Antão and São Vicente are separated by a channel only about twelve kilometres wide, yet Santo Antão has no functioning airport and is reached by ferry, while Brava has an airstrip that high winds make largely unusable. Internal geography in Cabo Verde is measured in boat schedules more often than in kilometres.

sections.heading: Deep Foundations: The Cape Verde Rise and the Mantle Plume
sections.body:
Cabo Verde sits on some of the oldest ocean floor on Earth. The crust beneath the islands is Jurassic to Early Cretaceous, formed roughly 120 to 140 million years ago as the Atlantic opened, and by rights it should be cold, dense and deep. Old oceanic lithosphere subsides as it cools, and crust of that age normally lies more than five kilometres below sea level. Instead, the seafloor here is anomalously shallow across an enormous area. 

This anomaly is the Cape Verde Rise, a broad domal swell of the ocean floor roughly 1,200 kilometres across on which the islands sit like warts on a blister. The seafloor within the rise stands up to about two kilometres higher than surrounding crust of the same age, and by that measure it is the largest bathymetric swell in any ocean. The rise is accompanied by a positive geoid anomaly and by unusually high heat flow, and the combination is the standard signature of a mantle plume: a column of hot, buoyant material rising from deep in the mantle, spreading out beneath the lithosphere and lifting it from below like a hand under a rug. 

The exact structure of that plume is genuinely contested. Seismic tomography images a low-velocity anomaly beneath the region that some studies trace down toward the core-mantle boundary, connecting it to the African large low-shear-velocity province, while other work argues the anomaly is shallower and confined to the upper mantle. Estimates of how much of the swell is supported thermally, by hot buoyant asthenosphere, and how much is supported by chemical buoyancy from depleted residual mantle differ substantially between studies. What is not in doubt is that something anomalously hot and buoyant sits under this patch of old Atlantic seafloor and has done for tens of millions of years. 

The near-stationarity of the African plate over this hotspot explains the archipelago's odd shape. Hawaii produces a linear chain with a clean age progression because the Pacific plate races over its plume at around ten centimetres a year. The African plate has moved only slowly and has at times been almost fixed relative to the deep mantle, so volcanism has had to build repeatedly in nearly the same place, migrating only a little. The result is a cluster rather than a chain, with a broad and messy age relationship rather than a clean conveyor belt. 

One further distinction sets Cabo Verde apart geochemically. The islands are among the very few places on Earth where carbonatites, igneous rocks composed largely of carbonate minerals rather than silicates, erupt through oceanic crust. They occur on Brava, Santiago, Fogo, Maio and São Vicente. Carbonatites are overwhelmingly a continental phenomenon, and their presence here is one of the reasons the archipelago receives attention out of all proportion to its size.

sections.heading: Volcanic Construction and the Age Gradient Across the Islands
sections.body:
Every island in Cabo Verde is the summit of a volcano, or a cluster of them, built up from a seafloor three to four kilometres below the surface. The visible islands are therefore the top few per cent of enormous cones. Fogo, whose peak stands 2,829 metres above sea level, is in total a structure roughly six kilometres tall from base to summit, which makes it one of the larger mountains on the planet by that measure even though almost all of it is underwater. 

The islands are not the same age, and the pattern of ages runs broadly from east to west. The eastern islands, Sal, Boa Vista and Maio, carry the oldest exposed rocks, with radiometric dates on Sal reaching back around 25 million years and the earliest submarine phases older still. The western islands, Fogo, Brava, Santo Antão and Santiago, are younger, with most of their subaerial construction within the last few million years, and volcanism on Fogo and Brava is ongoing. This east-to-west younging is consistent with a slow westward drift of the plate relative to the melting anomaly, but the progression is far from clean; several islands have long, interrupted histories with multi-million-year gaps between eruptive phases, and dormant islands have reawakened. Any account that presents Cabo Verde as a tidy age-ordered chain is oversimplifying. 

Each island's life cycle follows a broadly similar sequence, and reading it off the landscape is the core skill of island geology. A seamount phase builds a submarine edifice of pillow lavas and fragmental debris. An emergent phase, violent because seawater flashing to steam shatters magma, produces tuffs and hyaloclastites, which appear today as pale stratified rock low on several islands. A shield-building phase of fluid basaltic lava constructs the bulk of the cone rapidly. Then comes a long, slow decline in which eruption rates drop, erosion outpaces construction, and the island is gradually cut down. Some islands add a late rejuvenated phase, isolated eruptions after millions of years of quiet, which is why a supposedly extinct island cannot be assumed safe. 

You can read the whole sequence across the archipelago at once. Sal, Boa Vista and Maio are in deep old age: their volcanoes are worn to low, flat, sandy plains with only stumps of resistant rock standing above them, and on Maio and Sal uplifted Cretaceous marine sediments and reef limestones are exposed, showing that these islands have been shoved upward as well as built upward. Santiago and São Nicolau are in vigorous middle age, heavily eroded but still mountainous. Santo Antão is young, high and savagely dissected. Fogo and Brava are still under construction, with Fogo erupting three times in the last hundred years and the submarine Cadamosto Seamount just southwest of Brava counted among the more active volcanic centres in the Atlantic.

sections.heading: Fogo, Chã das Caldeiras, and Life Inside an Active Volcano
sections.body:
Fogo is the archipelago's defining landform: a nearly circular island 476 square kilometres in area that is essentially one enormous stratovolcano rising to Pico do Fogo at 2,829 metres, the highest point in Cabo Verde. Its name simply means fire, and it has earned it; historical accounts describe activity from the earliest years of settlement in the sixteenth century, and there have been on the order of thirty eruptions since. 

The most striking feature is not the peak but the structure that holds it. The eastern flank of the island is missing.
