Administratively the country has long been divided into prefectures, historically fourteen ordinary prefectures plus two economic prefectures, Nana-Grebizi and Sangha-Mbaere, and the autonomous commune of Bangui; a 2020 reform redrew the map into twenty prefectures, adding units such as Lim-Pende, though older sixteen-prefecture lists still circulate widely, and sub-prefectures, more than seventy, form the working tier beneath. The prefecture names themselves are a gazetteer of the country's rivers, Ouham, Lobaye, Ouaka, Kotto, Mbomou, Vakaga, a reminder that in a roadless country the drainage network has always been the real address system. For a geographer the essential point is continuity: the empty east, the raided north, the riverine axis of administration, and the westward tilt of population and power all predate the republic, the colony, and even the sultanates, and every government since has inherited the same stubborn map.

sections.heading: Conflict Geography: Why the Map Fights Itself
sections.body: The Central African Republic's recurring wars are often narrated as ethnic or religious, but their deepest logic is geographic, and reading the conflict through the map explains patterns that slogans cannot. Begin with distance and density: a state apparatus concentrated in one southwestern city must project authority across 600,000 square kilometers on earth roads, so for most citizens the state has always been an occasional visitor, and armed entrepreneurs face weak competition. Add the resource map: alluvial diamonds and gold are diffuse, diggable with hand tools, and impossible to fence, the classic profile of lootable resources that finance rebellion rather than treasuries, and the eastern diamond fields around Bria and the gold zones near Bambari duly became the paymasters of successive armed groups, while road checkpoints, each a miniature customs post, monetized every axis. Add the pastoral gradient: the southward push of transhumant herds, lengthening as Sahelian pastures degrade and Chadian and Sudanese herders arm themselves, drives an annual cycle of grazing disputes, cattle raids, and reprisals along the whole middle belt, and armed groups on all sides have taxed, protected, and plundered the herds. Add the borders: six of them, mostly rivers and bush, across which fighters, weapons, cattle, and refugees move freely; Chadian and Sudanese politics have repeatedly arrived in the north with mounted raiders or rebel columns, the Lord's Resistance Army once drifted through the southeast, and the two Congos have absorbed waves of Central African refugees. The 2013 crisis followed this template precisely: the Seleka coalition assembled in the neglected, largely Muslim northeast, rode the dry-season roads south to take Bangui, and the anti-balaka backlash organized in the western farming belt; the war then decayed into a patchwork of territorial rackets in which each group held the mines, roads, and cattle corridors of its home region. The sectarian violence that horrified the world mapped onto older lines, the trading diaspora of Muslim northerners in southern towns suddenly recast as enemies, PK5 in Bangui besieged, mosques and quarters emptied, a religious gradient centuries in the making torn along its seam. Peacekeeping geography followed conflict geography: the UN mission, deployed since 2014 with over ten thousand personnel, garrisons the same towns the colonial administration garrisoned, and government authority returns, where it returns, down the same few roads. None of this makes conflict inevitable; it makes it structured. Interventions that ignore the structure, disarmament programs without road-building, elections without rural administration, mining bans without livelihoods, have repeatedly failed, while the few durable improvements, the Chinko reserve's stabilization of part of the east, corridor security on the Douala road, negotiated transhumance agreements, all worked with the grain of the map. The country's geography does not doom it, but it prices every policy, and the price of pretending the map away has been paid many times.

sections.heading: Environmental Pressures, Hazards, and the Limits of What We Know
sections.body: By the standards of a continent under strain, the Central African Republic's environment is remarkably intact, and its gravest environmental stories are about fauna and governance rather than wholesale habitat loss. Deforestation in the southwestern rainforest has run at low rates compared with West Africa or the Amazon, restrained by roadlessness; the real forest concerns are selective, the logging concessions' road networks that open the canopy to hunting, and the slow conversion around Bangui and the highway towns where charcoal and farmland demand bite. The savannas' crisis is emptiness of a different kind: the collapse of the great mammal herds under commercial poaching, so that immense landscapes retain their vegetation but have lost their elephants, rhinos, and much else, an ecological hollowing with knock-on effects, from tree regeneration to grass fire behavior, that ecologists can measure only crudely here. Artisanal mining is the most visible scar: diamond and gold digging turns streambeds inside out, muddies rivers, and in the gold zones introduces mercury used in amalgamation, a neurotoxin that persists downstream; there is no meaningful remediation anywhere in the sector. Climatic hazards follow the gradient. The north shares the Sahel's droughts and its long-term rainfall volatility, and bears them with the least buffer; the south's hazard is water in excess, above all the Ubangi's floods, which in October 2019 reached levels described as the worst in decades, inundating Bangui's riverside quarters and displacing on the order of a hundred thousand people nationwide, and which recur in some measure most years. Violent squall winds, lightning, and crop pests, locusts occasionally in the far north, armyworm in maize, round out the hazard list; the country is seismically quiet and has no volcanoes, cyclones, or coastlines to fear. Disease geography deserves honest mention: malaria is holoendemic and the largest killer of children, the north lies within the African meningitis belt with its dry-season epidemics, sleeping sickness persists in old foci along the southern rivers, and waterborne disease tracks every flood, burdens that interact with an health system among the world's most fragile. Over all of this hangs an epistemic problem that any careful account must state plainly: the country is one of the least measured places on earth. The last census is decades old; population, forest, herd, and wildlife figures are extrapolations with wide error bars; rainfall and river gauges that functioned in the 1970s have long been silent, so climate trend statements rest on satellite reconstructions; and insecurity keeps field scientists out of exactly the regions where the unknowns are largest. Remote sensing has revolutionized what can be said about tree cover, burning, and flooding, but ground truth remains scarce. The practical conclusion for a reader is a habit of mind: treat every Central African statistic, including those in this guide, as an estimate with stated-or-unstated uncertainty, distrust suspicious precision, and prefer the direction and structure of a pattern, which the geography makes robust, to any single number, which it rarely can.

guides.title: Geography of Cameroon
guides.summary: The physical, climatic, ecological, human, and economic geography of Cameroon, the Central African country often called Africa in miniature, from its volcanic mountains and rainforests to the Sahel.

sections.heading: Africa in Miniature: Why Cameroon's Geography Matters
sections.body: Cameroon is routinely called Africa in miniature, and the nickname is earned rather than promotional. Within a single country of about 475,442 square kilometers, slightly larger than Sweden and a little bigger than the American state of California, the traveler moving from south to north passes through nearly every major landscape type the African continent offers: mangrove-fringed Atlantic coast, dense equatorial rainforest, high volcanic mountains, cool grassy highlands, wooded savanna on a broad interior plateau, hot semi-arid plains, and finally the drying floodplains of the Lake Chad basin at the edge of the Sahel. The country also compresses Africa's human geography: more than 250 ethnic groups speaking roughly 280 languages, a colonial inheritance split between French and English, Christianity dominant in the south, Islam widespread in the north, and traditional religions woven through both. Understanding Cameroon's geography therefore means understanding a set of gradients, of rainfall, altitude, vegetation, population, and culture, that run roughly from the humid southwest to the arid northeast, and most of the country's economic life, political tension, and environmental risk can be read off those gradients. Geographically, Cameroon occupies the hinge of the continent, the place where West Africa meets Central Africa. It faces the Gulf of Guinea, specifically the Bight of Biafra, along a coast of about 400 kilometers, and shares land borders with six countries: Nigeria to the west and northwest along a boundary of nearly 2,000 kilometers, Chad to the northeast, the Central African Republic to the east, and the Republic of the Congo, Gabon, and Equatorial Guinea to the south. At its far northern tip the country narrows to a corridor between Nigeria and Chad that reaches the shores of Lake Chad, giving Cameroon a stake in one of Africa's most consequential environmental stories, the shrinking of that great shallow lake. The physical centerpiece of the country is the Cameroon Volcanic Line, a chain of volcanoes and highlands that includes Mount Cameroon, at 4,095 meters the highest peak in West and Central Africa and one of the continent's few active volcanoes. The volcanic soils of this line support some of the densest rural populations in the region, and its rain-drenched seaward slopes include one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth. Administratively the country is divided into ten regions, two of which, the Northwest and Southwest, are anglophone, a legacy of the partition of the former German colony of Kamerun between Britain and France after the First World War, and this linguistic geography has hardened since 2016 into a serious internal conflict. Roughly 28 million people live in Cameroon, concentrated in the two largest cities, the port metropolis of Douala and the capital Yaoundé, in the fertile western highlands, and along the far northern plains. This guide surveys the country's geology, relief, climate, rivers, ecology, population, and economy, and closes with the environmental hazards, from volcanic gas to advancing desert, that make Cameroon's geography a matter of daily consequence.

sections.heading: Location, Size, Shape, and Borders
sections.body: Cameroon lies just north of the equator, spanning latitudes from about 1.7 to 13 degrees north and longitudes from about 8.5 to 16.2 degrees east. Its territory of 475,442 square kilometers includes about 2,730 square kilometers of water. The country's shape is often compared to an elongated triangle or a tall boot: broad in the forested south, pinching to a narrow neck in the center-north, and flaring slightly again toward Lake Chad. That shape is not an accident of nature but of diplomacy. The eastern and southern boundaries follow lines negotiated between Germany, which declared a protectorate over the coast at Douala in July 1884, and its colonial neighbors France, Britain, Spain, and Belgium; many segments run along rivers such as the Ntem in the south and the Kadéï and Sangha drainages in the east, while others are surveyors' straight lines through sparsely peopled forest. The western border with Nigeria descends from Lake Chad through the Mandara Mountains, follows the highlands southwest, and reaches the sea at the Bakassi Peninsula, a swampy, oil-flanked protrusion into the Gulf of Guinea whose ownership Nigeria and Cameroon disputed for decades until the International Court of Justice ruled for Cameroon in 2002, with the final handover completed in 2008 under the Greentree Agreement. Offshore, Cameroon's short coastline gives it a modest exclusive economic zone hemmed in by the maritime claims of Nigeria and Equatorial Guinea, whose island of Bioko sits only about 40 kilometers from the Cameroonian shore, close enough to be visible from the slopes of Mount Cameroon on clear days. That proximity matters: the Douala-Bioko corridor concentrates shipping, fisheries, and offshore oil infrastructure, and the Gulf of Guinea has in recent years recorded some of the world's highest rates of maritime piracy and armed robbery at sea. Cameroon's position at the hinge of West and Central Africa shapes its role in regional politics and trade. It is the economic anchor of the Central African Economic and Monetary Community, CEMAC, whose landlocked members Chad and the Central African Republic depend on Cameroonian roads, rails, and the port of Douala for most of their imports and exports; a truck route from Douala to N'Djamena, Chad's capital, runs about 1,800 kilometers and carries the bulk of Chad's overseas commerce. The far northern corridor between Nigeria and Chad, barely 100 kilometers wide in places, funnels trans-Saharan trade and, since the 2010s, the violence of the Boko Haram insurgency spilling over from northeastern Nigeria, making border geography a security question as well as an economic one. Finally, the country's north-south elongation, about 1,200 kilometers from the Gulf of Guinea to Lake Chad, is the simple physical fact behind its celebrated diversity: it stretches Cameroon across the full climatic gradient from wet equatorial to semi-arid Sahelian, a range that most countries several times its size never approach.

sections.heading: Geological Foundations: Craton, Basement, and the Benue Trough
sections.body: The deep structure of Cameroon involves three geological elements: an ancient continental nucleus in the south, a broad belt of somewhat younger crystalline basement across the center and north, and a great rift-related trough in the west, all later punctured by the volcanism that built the country's mountains. The southern third of the country rests on the northern edge of the Congo Craton, a block of Archean crust more than 2.5 billion years old that underlies much of Central Africa; in Cameroon its exposed portion is called the Ntem Complex, a terrain of granites, gneisses, and greenstone belts containing iron formations that host the large Mbalam iron-ore deposits near the Congolese border. North of the craton margin lies territory deformed during the Pan-African orogeny, a continent-wide episode of collision and crustal reworking around 600 million years ago that welded older fragments into the supercontinent Gondwana; most of central and northern Cameroon is built of Pan-African granites, schists, and migmatites, which is why the plateaus of the interior expose weathered crystalline rock rather than young sediments. Slicing through this basement runs the Central Cameroon Shear Zone, a major ancient fault system that geologists correlate, across the Atlantic, with the Pernambuco lineament of northeastern Brazil, one of many matches that made the fit of Africa and South America an early argument for continental drift. The third element dates from the breakup of Gondwana itself. In the Early Cretaceous, roughly 130 million years ago, as the South Atlantic began to open, a failed arm of the rifting propagated northeast into Africa, creating the Benue Trough, a sediment-filled depression that runs from the Niger Delta region through eastern Nigeria and clips northern Cameroon, where its extensions form the Garoua basin along the Benue River. Failed rifts like the Benue subside and collect kilometers of sandstone, shale, and limestone, and Cameroon's modest onshore sedimentary basins, the coastal Douala and Rio del Rey basins and the interior Garoua and Logone-Birni basins, all descend from this Cretaceous stretching; the Rio del Rey and Douala basins later matured organic-rich sediments into the oil and gas that dominate the country's exports. Two practical consequences of this geological architecture deserve emphasis. First, the crystalline basement that floors most of the country weathers into thick tropical soils but yields groundwater only from fractures and the weathered mantle, so rural water supply depends on carefully sited boreholes rather than large aquifers, a chronic development constraint in the north. Second, the ancient shear zones did not die: they provided the crustal weakness along which, much later, magmas of the Cameroon Volcanic Line ascended, meaning the country's Precambrian scars set the stage for its modern volcanoes, its most fertile soils, and its most distinctive natural hazards.

sections.heading: The Cameroon Volcanic Line
sections.body: The Cameroon Volcanic Line is the country's geological signature: a 1,600-kilometer chain of volcanoes, volcanic plateaus, and crater lakes running southwest to northeast, from islands deep in the Gulf of Guinea onto the African mainland and into the interior highlands. The oceanic section comprises the islands of Annobón, São Tomé, Príncipe, and Bioko; the continental section begins with Mount Cameroon at the coast and continues inland through Mount Manengouba, the Bamboutos Mountains, Mount Oku at 3,011 meters, and the Ngaoundéré plateau toward the Adamawa. What makes the line scientifically famous is that it ignores the usual rules of plate tectonics. Volcanic chains normally form either at plate boundaries or as age-progressive tracks left by a plate drifting over a stationary mantle hotspot, with volcanoes getting steadily older in one direction, as in Hawaii. The Cameroon line shows no such age progression: eruptions of similar ages are scattered along its whole length, activity has continued for more than 65 million years, and the line crosses the boundary between oceanic and continental crust without changing character, a combination found almost nowhere else on Earth. Explanations remain genuinely contested. Some geophysicists invoke small-scale convection cells at the edge of the deep, hot mantle structure beneath southern Africa; others argue for decompression melting along reactivated Precambrian shear zones, the ancient faults of the basement acting as channels; still others propose several minor mantle plumes rather than one. No hypothesis has won consensus, and the line remains a standing test case for theories of intraplate volcanism. For the people who live along it, the line's importance is more concrete. Its basaltic rocks weather into deep, dark, mineral-rich soils that support intensive agriculture, which is why the western highlands and the slopes around Mount Cameroon carry rural population densities exceeding 100 and locally 200 persons per square kilometer, among the highest in Central Africa, in a country whose overall density is nearer 60. The highlands' altitude also moderates temperature, historically limiting malaria transmission and attracting settlement, trade towns such as Bafoussam and Bamenda, and colonial plantations. The volcanic line's hazards are the mirror of its gifts. Besides eruptions from Mount Cameroon, the chain's dormant centers are studded with more than thirty maars and crater lakes, water-filled volcanic explosion craters, some of which trap magmatic carbon dioxide in their depths; two of them, Lakes Monoun and Nyos, released catastrophic gas bursts in the 1980s. Smaller hazards include landslides on oversteepened, deeply weathered volcanic slopes, notably around the Bamboutos caldera and Limbé, where heavy rains periodically trigger fatal debris flows. The line even defines the country's freshwater geography: its uplands intercept moist Atlantic air, wringing out several meters of rain a year, and thereby serve as the water towers feeding the rivers on which the lowlands depend. In short, the Cameroon Volcanic Line is at once the country's most distinctive scientific puzzle, its agricultural heartland, and its most concentrated zone of natural risk.

sections.heading: Mount Cameroon: Living with an Active Volcano
sections.body: Mount Cameroon rises almost directly from the Atlantic shoreline to 4,095 meters, a massive basaltic shield and stratovolcano roughly 50 kilometers long and 35 wide, known locally as Fako or, in older usage, Mongo ma Ndemi, the Mountain of Greatness. It is the highest summit in West and Central Africa and by far the most active volcano on the Cameroon Volcanic Line, with at least seven eruptions recorded since 1900, most recently in 1999, 2000, and 2012. Its eruptions are typically Hawaiian to Strombolian in style: fissures open on the flanks, lava fountains build cinder cones, and fluid basaltic flows descend the slopes. The mountain's eruptive record reaches deep into history; a Carthaginian expedition led by Hanno the Navigator in perhaps the fifth century BC reported a fiery mountain on this coast that many scholars identify with Mount Cameroon, which would make it the earliest documented volcano in sub-Saharan Africa, though the identification is debated. The 1922 eruption sent lava all the way to the sea; the 1999 eruption cut the coastal road south of Buea and stopped only about 200 meters short of the shoreline, forcing evacuations but causing no direct deaths. The volcano's dangers are mostly to property and livelihoods, lava overrunning farms, plantations, and roads, and to aviation through ash, rather than the explosive pyroclastic flows of steeper, more silicic volcanoes. The mountain makes its own weather. Rising straight from a warm ocean into the path of the southwest monsoon, its seaward flank is one of the wettest places on Earth: the village of Debundscha at its western foot records roughly 10,000 millimeters of rain in an average year, and the lower slopes are wrapped in cloud forest almost year-round. Rainfall declines dramatically with altitude and on the leeward side, so the summit zone is a windswept alpine desert of cinder and tussock where overnight temperatures fall below freezing, and climbers ascend through five distinct vegetation belts, lowland rainforest, montane forest, montane grassland, subalpine heath, and bare lava, in a horizontal distance of barely 25 kilometers. This compression makes the mountain a celebrated natural laboratory for ecology, protected since 2009 in Mount Cameroon National Park, home to forest elephants, drills, and Preuss's monkeys, and the venue of an annual Race of Hope that sends runners to the summit and back, the record standing near four and a half hours. Around its base spreads one of Cameroon's most important agro-industrial landscapes: the volcanic soils support oil palm, rubber, banana, and tea plantations established in the German era and now run largely by the Cameroon Development Corporation, one of the country's largest employers. Buea, the colonial German capital perched at 900 meters on the mountain's flank, and the port and refinery town of Limbé anchor a population of several hundred thousand living within reach of the volcano's flows, a coexistence managed through monitoring by the Mount Cameroon Observatory at Buea rather than through any realistic hope of relocation.

sections.heading: Relief Regions: Coastal Plain, Southern Plateau, Highlands, and the Adamawa
sections.body: Cameroon's terrain organizes itself into five great steps. The first is the coastal plain, a belt 15 to 150 kilometers wide of sediments, mangroves, and estuaries along the Gulf of Guinea, hot, humid, and in the north of the belt extraordinarily wet. Its two great indentations are the Rio del Rey estuary near the Nigerian border, a maze of mangrove creeks draining the Bakassi Peninsula, and the Wouri estuary, where Douala, the country's largest city and port, sits about 30 kilometers from the open sea. South of Douala the plain narrows past the resort beaches of Kribi, near which the Lobé River performs the rare trick of cascading directly into the ocean. The second step is the South Cameroon Plateau, the country's largest single landscape: an undulating surface of 600 to 900 meters elevation, developed on the ancient crystalline basement and covered by dense equatorial rainforest, that occupies most of the territory south of the Sanaga River. Its monotony is relieved by inselbergs, isolated granite domes rising abruptly from the forest, and it slopes gently eastward toward the Congo basin, sending its rivers in three directions, to the Atlantic, to the Congo, and northward. The third step is the western highlands, the continental spine of the Cameroon Volcanic Line: a chain of volcanic massifs and high lava plateaus, the Grassfields, running from Mount Cameroon northeast through Mount Manengouba, the Bamboutos range, and the Bamenda and Oku highlands, with general elevations of 1,000 to 2,500 meters and peaks beyond 3,000. Cool, fertile, and densely settled by the Bamiléké, Bamoun, and Grassfields peoples, this is Cameroon's demographic and agricultural core outside the cities. The fourth step is the Adamawa Plateau, a broad east-west swell of savanna-covered basement and basalt averaging about 1,100 meters, which forms the country's waist and its principal drainage divide; rivers flowing north off the Adamawa feed the Niger and Lake Chad systems, while those flowing south feed the Sanaga and the Congo. The plateau's southern edge drops in dramatic escarpments toward the forested plateau below, and its surface, pocked with old cinder cones and crater lakes, supports the great cattle economy of the Fulani herders. The fifth step descends from the Adamawa's northern rim through the Benue depression, a lowland of 300 to 500 meters around Garoua where the Benue River gathers its Cameroonian headwaters, and onward to the far northern plains, which slope from about 400 meters down to roughly 280 meters at Lake Chad. Between the Benue lowland and the Chad plains rise the Mandara Mountains, a rugged granite massif along the Nigerian border reaching about 1,494 meters at Oupay, famous for its volcanic plug landscapes around Rhumsiki, where sheer basalt towers rise from terraced fields. Each step in this staircase has its own climate, ecology, and human economy, and the boundaries between them, escarpments, river crossings, and mountain passes, have channeled trade and conflict for centuries.

sections.heading: Climate: From Equatorial Downpour to Sahelian Drought
sections.body: Cameroon's climates are governed by the annual migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, the belt of rising air where the moist southwesterly monsoon off the Atlantic meets the hot, dusty northeasterly harmattan off the Sahara. As the convergence zone swings north in the boreal summer and south in winter, it drags the rains with it, and the length of the wet season falls off almost linearly with latitude. The far south, below about 4 degrees north, has a true equatorial regime with four seasons: two rainy periods, roughly March to June and September to November, separated by two drier interludes, delivering 1,500 to 2,000 millimeters a year at Yaoundé. The coastal belt exaggerates this into one of the wettest climates on Earth wherever the monsoon slams into high ground: Douala receives about 4,000 millimeters annually, and Debundscha, on the windward foot of Mount Cameroon, roughly 10,000 millimeters, with July and August so wet that a single month can exceed the annual total of Paris five times over. Moving north onto the Adamawa Plateau, the two wet seasons merge into one, May to October, with totals near 1,500 millimeters, moderated temperatures because of altitude, and a long, dusty dry season under the harmattan. North of the Adamawa the totals drop quickly: Garoua in the Benue valley sees about 1,000 millimeters concentrated in five months, and the far north around Maroua and toward Lake Chad receives 400 to 800 millimeters in a three-to-four-month wet season, a Sahelian regime in which year-to-year variability of 30 percent or more is normal and a late or failed monsoon means failed harvests. Temperature patterns invert the rainfall map. The cloudy, rain-cooled south rarely exceeds 32 degrees Celsius, and the highlands are genuinely cool, with Bamenda and Buea averaging below 20 degrees and the Adamawa experiencing chilly harmattan nights; the far north is the hot pole, with March and April maxima routinely above 40 degrees at Maroua and Kousséri before the rains break. Humidity in the coastal south hovers near saturation for much of the year, a fact with consequences from mold and malaria to the corrosion of infrastructure, while the harmattan season in the north brings desiccating air, dust haze that can ground aviation, and the seasonal spike of meningitis that follows the dry, dusty belt across the whole Sahel. Climate change is measurably tilting these patterns. Mean temperatures have risen close to a degree since the 1960s, the northern rains have become more erratic with a documented tendency toward intense downpours separated by longer dry spells, and flooding in the Logone floodplain and around Maroua has become a recurring emergency, as in the disastrous inundations of 2012, 2022, and 2024 that displaced hundreds of thousands. The practical geography is stark: the same country must manage drainage and landslides in a city that gets four meters of rain and irrigation and drought relief in provinces that pray for forty centimeters, and national planning that treats Cameroon as one climate fails everywhere at once.

sections.heading: Rivers and Drainage: One Water Tower, Four Basins
sections.body: Cameroon is unusual among African countries in feeding four separate great drainage systems, a consequence of the Adamawa Plateau and western highlands acting as a water tower at the hinge of the continent. The largest share of the territory drains to the Atlantic. The master stream is the Sanaga, about 918 kilometers long, which gathers the Djérem and Lom from the Adamawa and the eastern plateaus, crosses the southern plateau, and tumbles over the Edéa falls to the coast; its basin of roughly 133,000 square kilometers makes it the country's hydraulic backbone, and its falls and reservoirs, Song Loulou and Edéa on the river, regulated since 2016 by the large Lom Pangar storage dam upstream, generate the majority of Cameroon's electricity, which is more than 70 percent hydroelectric. Smaller coastal rivers include the Wouri, whose estuary hosts Douala; the Mungo and Dibamba feeding the same mangrove complex; the Nyong, a slow blackwater river of the forested plateau; and the Ntem on the Gabonese border. The second system belongs to the Niger. The Benue, the Niger's greatest tributary, rises on the northern flank of the Adamawa, passes Garoua, where it becomes seasonally navigable for barge traffic in the August-September high water, and exits into Nigeria, eventually delivering Cameroonian water to the Atlantic through the Niger Delta; its Cameroonian tributaries, the Faro and Mayo Kébi, drain the whole Benue depression. The third system drains to Lake Chad, an interior basin with no outlet to the sea. The Logone rises on the Adamawa as the Vina, flows north to join the Chari at the twin cities of Kousséri and N'Djamena, and enters the lake; its annual flood spreads across the Grand Yaéré floodplain of the far north, a seasonal wetland critical for fish, flood-recession sorghum, and Sahelian pastoralism, and the Waza-Logone floodplain's partial restoration after damaging upstream works in the 1980s is a textbook case in African water management. The fourth system sends the southeastern plateau's water to the Congo: the Kadéï and Boumba join the Sangha, a major right-bank Congo tributary, tying eastern Cameroon ecologically and economically to the Congo basin. Navigation on most Cameroonian rivers is blocked by rapids at the plateau edges, which is why railways and roads, not barges, carry the interior's goods; the great exception historically was the lower Sanaga and the estuaries, and today the Benue's seasonal window. Hydropower potential, estimated among Africa's largest after the Democratic Republic of the Congo, remains only fractionally developed; new stations at Memve'ele on the Ntem and Nachtigal on the Sanaga, the latter adding 420 megawatts from 2024, are gradually converting the water tower's altitude into electricity. The rivers also mark vulnerability: hydro dependence makes the grid hostage to drought, and the north's life depends on flood pulses that upstream dams, climate variability, and Lake Chad's decline all threaten.

sections.heading: Lakes, Crater Lakes, and the Nyos Disaster
sections.body: Cameroon's lakes divide into two families with very different personalities: the great shallow floodplain lake it shares in the far north, and the deep, quiet crater lakes of the volcanic line. Lake Chad, at the country's northern tip, is the remnant of a vast paleolake that in wet millennia covered hundreds of thousands of square kilometers; in the 1960s it still spread over roughly 25,000 square kilometers, but drought and rising water withdrawals shrank it by the 1980s to a tenth of that, and today its southern pool, fed mainly by the Chari-Logone system, fluctuates seasonally between roughly 1,500 and a few thousand square kilometers. Cameroon's share is small but consequential: the lake's recession stranded fishing villages kilometers from water, converted open water to swamp and dune, and helped push fishermen, farmers, and herders into competition that the Boko Haram insurgency has since exploited. Grandiose schemes to refill the lake by transferring water from the Congo basin, the Transaqua proposal, have circulated for decades without financing, and the honest scientific position is that the lake's future depends chiefly on rainfall in the Chari headwaters and on restraint in upstream irrigation. The crater lakes are the opposite: small, deep, and dangerous not by drying but by exploding. Dozens of maars, volcanic explosion craters, along the Cameroon Volcanic Line hold lakes whose still, stratified waters can accumulate dissolved carbon dioxide seeping from magma below. In a permanently stratified tropical lake the dense, gas-charged bottom water never turns over, so CO2 concentrations can build for decades toward saturation until some trigger, a landslide, storm, or internal wave, starts an overturn; rising gas-rich water then effervesces like an opened bottle, and the released gas erupts as a cold, invisible, suffocating cloud denser than air. This is a limnic eruption. On 15 August 1984, Lake Monoun released such a burst, killing 37 people; on 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos, a 208-meter-deep maar in the Northwest highlands, released an estimated cubic kilometer or more of CO2 that flowed down valleys for over 20 kilometers and asphyxiated about 1,746 people and more than 3,500 head of livestock in the villages of Nyos, Cha, and Subum, the deadliest gas disaster of natural origin in recorded history. The scientific response became a model of hazard engineering: since 2001 French-Cameroonian teams have installed self-powered degassing columns, pipes that lift bottom water and let its gas fizz off continuously at the surface, three of which now keep Nyos far below saturation, with a similar column at Monoun, and monitoring continues because the lake's natural dam, a weak pyroclastic barrier, could fail and send both flood and gas downstream. Other notable lakes include Barombi Mbo near Kumba, Cameroon's largest crater lake and home to a famous flock of endemic cichlid fishes; the twin male and female lakes of Manengouba's caldera; Lake Oku high in the Kilum-Ijim forest; and the artificial reservoirs of Lagdo on the Benue, Mbakaou on the Djérem, and Lom Pangar on the Lom, which now rank among the country's largest water bodies.

sections.heading: Vegetation Zones and Forest Ecology
sections.body: Cameroon's vegetation reads like a transect of tropical Africa, arranged in latitudinal bands that track the rainfall gradient and modified locally by altitude and human hands. Along the coast, brackish estuaries carry one of Africa's larger mangrove complexes, perhaps 2,000 square kilometers of Rhizophora and Avicennia forest in the Rio del Rey and Wouri systems, nurseries for fish and shrimp and buffers against coastal erosion, but shrinking under wood-cutting for fish-smoking and urban expansion around Douala. Behind the mangroves and up to roughly 700 meters lies lowland evergreen rainforest, part of the Lower Guinean forest block, which covers most of the southern plateau: a closed-canopy forest 30 to 50 meters tall, rich in legume trees, mahoganies, and the commercially prized azobé, sapelli, and ayous, with more than 8,000 recorded plant species nationally and exceptional numbers of endemics in the coastal hills. Botanists rank the forests between Mount Cameroon and the Cross River among Africa's oldest and most diverse, likely Pleistocene refugia where forest persisted through glacial dry spells; Korup National Park protects a celebrated fragment. Southeastern Cameroon grades into semi-deciduous forest and then, in the far east, into the immense Congo basin forest shared with the Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic, where Cameroon's share of the Sangha Trinational landscape, Lobéké National Park, adjoins protected areas across the borders. Above about 800 meters on the volcanic line, lowland forest yields to submontane and montane forest, cool, mossy, epiphyte-laden woodlands that occupy a tiny national area but hold a wildly disproportionate share of endemic birds, amphibians, and plants; above the tree line around 2,200 to 2,800 meters come montane grasslands and afro-subalpine heath, the Bamenda Highlands and Mount Oku forming one of Africa's most threatened endemism hotspots, largely converted to farms and pasture outside community-managed remnants like the Kilum-Ijim forest. North of the forest zone the vegetation steps down through the classic West African sequence: Guinean savanna, tall grass with fire- tolerant trees and gallery forests along rivers, across the Adamawa; Sudanian savanna of shorter grass, Isoberlinia woodland, and farmed parkland dotted with sheanut and néré trees through the Benue basin; and Sahelian thornbush of Acacia, Balanites, and seasonal grasses toward Lake Chad, with the Yaéré floodplain's seasonally inundated grasslands as a distinctive wetland community. Two human signatures overprint everything. First, fire: the savannas burn annually, mostly set by herders and farmers, and the forest-savanna boundary across central Cameroon is substantially a fire-maintained line that has moved with human pressure for millennia. Second, the farm mosaic: cocoa agroforests under thinned forest canopy in the south, the intensive bocage of hedged fields in the Bamiléké highlands, and the parkland systems of the north are ancient, productive landscapes in their own right, and any account that divides the country simply into forest and farmland misses the managed continuum in between.

sections.heading: Wildlife and Protected Areas
sections.body: Cameroon's fauna matches its habitats in range and rarity. The southern forests hold forest elephants, western lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, forest buffalo, bongo, sitatunga, giant pangolins, and leopards, along with a primate roster, mandrills, drills, red colobus, and the endemic Preuss's monkey, that ranks among the world's richest; the Dja Faunal Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage site of about 5,260 square kilometers ringed by the Dja River's loop, and the parks of the southeast, Lobéké, Boumba Bek, and Nki, are the strongholds. The country's single most significant evolutionary treasure lives on the Nigeria border: the Cross River gorilla, the rarest great ape subspecies, with only about 300 individuals surviving in scattered highland forests, a handful of them in Cameroon's Takamanda National Park, and the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee of the same border forests is itself the most endangered chimpanzee subspecies. Montane specialties include Mount Cameroon's francolin, the Bamenda Highlands' Bannerman's turaco, and an extraordinary amphibian fauna featuring the goliath frog, the world's largest frog at up to 3.3 kilograms, found only in the fast rivers of coastal Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, and the hairy frog, whose males grow vascular filaments. The northern savannas carry the classic large mammals: savanna elephants, lions, giraffes, elands, roan antelope, kob, and hippos concentrated in Waza National Park in the Yaéré floodplain, Bénoué, Faro, and Bouba Ndjida parks in the Benue basin, the last of which suffered a notorious massacre in early 2012 when Sudanese horseback poachers killed several hundred elephants for ivory in weeks. That episode illustrates the general pressure: poaching for ivory and bushmeat, herder-wildlife conflict as transhumance routes cross parks, and insecurity from Boko Haram in the Waza region have emptied parts of the northern parks, while in the south commercial bushmeat hunting along logging roads is the main drain on wildlife. Cameroon's protected estate covers roughly 11 percent of the land in some 30 national parks and reserves, supplemented by community forests, sport-hunting zones that in principle fund management, and, importantly, wildlife sanctuaries for rescued apes such as Limbé and Mefou. Marine and coastal protection lags, though the Douala-Edéa reserve spanning the Sanaga mouth and the Ebo forest, a proposed park holding gorillas, chimpanzees that crack nuts with stone tools, and forest elephants, are focal conservation battles; Ebo's fate, contested between logging concessions and the Banen communities' land claims and conservation advocates, is the emblematic test of whether Cameroon's biological wealth survives its economic development. For a field observer the practical geography is simple: the south rewards patience in dense forest where animals are heard more than seen; the north offers open-country viewing in the dry season, November to April, when wildlife concentrates at water; and the highlands hold the endemics, best sought with local community guides around Mount Cameroon, Mount Oku, and the Bamenda escarpment.

sections.heading: Population Geography, Peoples, and Languages
sections.body: Cameroon's roughly 28 million people are spread across the territory with striking unevenness, and the pattern is old. Three zones concentrate settlement. The western highlands, blessed with volcanic soils, reliable rain, and altitude above the worst malaria belts, carry rural densities that locally exceed 200 persons per square kilometer, the historic homeland of the Bamiléké and the Grassfields kingdoms whose fon-ruled chiefdoms, Bafut, Nso, Bali, and dozens more, remain living institutions. The far north, the old Sahelian corridor of empires and trade, is the second cluster, where the Fulani, established through the nineteenth-century jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate's eastern emirates around Maroua and Garoua, live alongside the so-called Kirdi peoples, Mafa, Kapsiki, Mofu, and others, whose ancestors took refuge from slave raiding in the Mandara Mountains and built the terraced mountain agriculture still visible today, and the Shuwa Arabs and Kotoko of the Logone floodplain. The third cluster is urban and coastal: Douala's agglomeration approaches 4 million people and handles most of the country's trade, while Yaoundé, the inland capital on its seven forested hills at 750 meters, is of comparable size; secondary cities, Bafoussam, Bamenda, Garoua, Maroua, Ngaoundéré, Bertoua, and the port of Kribi, each anchor their regions. Between the clusters lie two great voids: the sparsely peopled rainforest of the south and east, where population clings to roadsides and rivers and Baka and Bagyeli hunter-gatherer communities inhabit the deep forest, and the middle belt of the Adamawa, historic raiding frontier, now cattle country. The linguistic map is among the world's densest: about 280 living languages from three of Africa's four phyla, Niger-Congo Bantu and Grassfields languages in the south and west, Chadic languages such as Mafa and Masana in the north, Nilo-Saharan Kanuri near Lake Chad, plus Shuwa Arabic, with Fulfulde as the northern lingua franca, Cameroonian Pidgin English dominant in the west and the cities, and a hybrid urban youth speech, Camfranglais, growing in Douala and Yaoundé. Over it all sit the two official languages, French and English, whose territorial split, eight francophone regions against the two anglophone ones holding about a fifth of the population, is the country's deepest political fault line; since 2016-2017 an armed separatist conflict in the Northwest and Southwest has killed thousands and displaced, at its height, close to a million people, redistributing population toward francophone cities and Nigeria. Religion follows latitude loosely, Christianity strongest in the south and the highlands, Islam in the north and among the Bamoun, with traditional practice interlaced everywhere. Demographically Cameroon is young, median age near 18, growing around 2.6 percent a year, and urbanizing past the 60 percent mark, so the population map is being redrawn toward the cities within a single generation.

sections.heading: Historical Geography: How the Map Was Made
sections.body: The modern map of Cameroon is the product of five layers of history, each of which left visible geographic marks. The deepest layer is the Bantu question: linguistic and archaeological evidence places the homeland of the Bantu languages, which today cover a third of Africa, in the borderland of southeastern Nigeria and western Cameroon, from which farming and iron-working communities began dispersing south and east three to five thousand years ago; in a real sense the human geography of half the continent begins in these hills. The second layer is the northern state tradition: the Sao culture of the Chad plains, the Kanem-Bornu empire that ruled the Lake Chad shores for centuries, the Kotoko city-states, and finally the Fulani jihad of Modibo Adama, who from 1809 carved out the emirate of Adamawa, named after him like the plateau itself, subordinating the mountain peoples and fixing the Muslim-emirate geography that the north retains. The third layer is coastal trade: from the late fifteenth century Portuguese sailors named the Wouri estuary Rio dos Camarões, river of prawns, for its swarming shrimp, the word that became Cameroon; Douala's ruling families grew rich brokering ivory, slaves, and later palm oil between interior and Atlantic economies, and in July 1884 the Douala kings signed a protectorate treaty with Germany, whose consul Gustav Nachtigal hoisted the flag days ahead of a British mission. German Kamerun, expanded inland by expedition and treaty and briefly enlarged in 1911 by the Neukamerun cession from French Equatorial Africa, built the plantations around Mount Cameroon, the Buea capital, and the first railways. The fourth layer is partition: after Germany's defeat in the First World War, the League of Nations divided Kamerun in 1919-1922 into a large French mandate and two slender British strips along the Nigerian border, administered from Nigeria. The two territories developed separately for forty years, in language, law, schooling, and administration, and when independence came, French Cameroun in January 1960 and the British trust territory through a 1961 plebiscite, the northern British strip voted to join Nigeria while the southern strip federated with the new republic, creating the anglophone Northwest and Southwest regions and the bilingual state whose internal tensions define Cameroonian politics today. The fifth layer is post-independence centralization: the federation was abolished in 1972 in favor of a unitary state, the capital consolidated at Yaoundé, and regional boundaries redrawn into today's ten regions. Reading the map with these layers in mind explains its oddities: why the border with Nigeria cuts through culturally continuous highlands, why plantation agribusiness clusters on former German estates at the coast, why the rail network runs from Douala inland to Yaoundé and Ngaoundéré and no farther, and why a line of language, invisible on relief maps, is the country's most consequential geographic feature.

sections.heading: Economic Geography: Farms, Forests, Oil, and Minerals
sections.body: Cameroon possesses the most diversified economy in Central Africa, and its sectors map tightly onto its physical zones. Agriculture employs roughly 40 percent of the workforce. The humid south grows the export tree crops: cocoa, of which Cameroon is consistently among the world's top five producers with 250,000 to 300,000 tonnes a year, grown by smallholders in the Centre, South, and Southwest; robusta coffee in the lowlands and arabica on the volcanic highlands; bananas, rubber, and oil palm on the coastal plantations; and timber from the eastern forests, where logging concessions cover much of the southeast and sawn wood, veneer, and logs rank among the top exports despite chronic concerns about illegal cutting. The highlands are the country's market garden, supplying maize, beans, potatoes, and vegetables to the cities, while the north lives on sorghum, millet, groundnuts, rice in the irrigated Logone schemes, onions, and above all cotton, the cash crop of more than 200,000 Sahelian farming families organized around the parastatal Sodecoton, and on the cattle, several million head, that the Fulani herd across the Adamawa and northern plains. Hydrocarbons pay the state's bills: oil from the offshore Rio del Rey basin, produced since 1977 and refined or exported from Limbé, plus newer gas developments including the Kribi gas-fired power plant and, since 2018, the Hilli Episeyo floating liquefied natural gas vessel off Kribi, one of the world's first, together supply roughly 40 percent of export earnings, though fields are mature and output has drifted down from its 1980s peak near 180,000 barrels per day to well under 100,000. The Chad-Cameroon pipeline, a 1,070-kilometer line completed in 2003 from Doba in Chad to a marine terminal off Kribi, earns transit fees and stands as the country's largest infrastructure asset. Mining remains more promise than production: world-class bauxite at Minim-Martap on the Adamawa, iron ore at Mbalam and Lobé, cobalt-nickel at Lomié, rutile, and gold in the east are all mapped, and the first iron-ore shipments from the smaller Bipindi-Grand Zambi belt began only in the mid-2020s, held back for decades by the cost of railways and deep-water ports. Industry concentrates in Douala, food, drink, cement, textiles, and aluminum, the last smelted at Edéa since 1957 using Sanaga hydropower from imported alumina, and the services and informal sectors dominate urban employment. The geography of this economy has a persistent shape: value flows from the interior, cotton, cattle, cocoa, timber, transit trade, down a few corridors to Douala and Kribi, and the coastal-inland imbalance in infrastructure, electricity, and income, along with the anglophone regions' sense of exclusion from oil revenues pumped off their own coast, converts economic geography directly into political grievance. Gross domestic product, near 50 billion United States dollars in the mid-2020s, makes Cameroon the largest economy in the CEMAC zone, yet roughly a quarter of its people remain below the national poverty line, most of them in the rural north, the driest end of every gradient this country contains.

sections.heading: Transport, Cities, and Regional Connectivity
sections.body: Movement across Cameroon is a struggle against distance, terrain, and rain, and the transport map explains much of the country's economic geography. The spine is the Douala-Yaoundé corridor, the 250-kilometer link between the port and the capital, now a paved highway with a partially completed motorway, and the busiest freight route in Central Africa. From Yaoundé the single-track Camrail railway, 884 kilometers in total from Douala, continues north to Ngaoundéré on the Adamawa, the line built in the 1970s as the Transcamerounais; at Ngaoundéré everything transfers to trucks for the two-day haul down the national road through Garoua and Maroua to Kousséri and N'Djamena, the lifeline that makes Cameroon the gatekeeper of Chad's trade, or east toward the Central African Republic border at Garoua-Boulaï, Bangui's main supply route. The 2016 Eséka rail disaster, when an overloaded passenger train derailed killing at least 79 people, exposed the network's age; modernization and long-discussed extensions, to Kribi, to the Chadian border, to the iron and bauxite deposits, remain mostly on paper. Ports tell a similar story of concentration and strain: Douala, a river port on the Wouri requiring constant dredging and limited to vessels of about 8 to 9 meters draft, handles the great majority of traffic for Cameroon, Chad, and the Central African Republic, with chronic congestion; the deep-water port opened at Kribi in 2018, with drafts beyond 15 meters and a Chinese-built container terminal, is designed to take the overflow and to serve future mineral exports, and Limbé hosts the oil industry and a shipyard. Air links run through Douala and Yaoundé-Nsimalen international airports with regional fields at Garoua, Maroua, Ngaoundéré, Bafoussam, and Bamenda. The road network, about 120,000 kilometers of which well under a tenth is paved, is the real determinant of daily life: the rainy season closes laterite roads across the south and east for weeks, the Ring Road around the Bamenda highlands, scenic and strategically vital, has been under intermittent construction for two generations, and the anglophone conflict since 2017 has made travel in the Northwest and Southwest unpredictable, with frequent lockdowns. Urban geography follows the corridors. Douala, the commercial capital, sprawls across the Wouri with its port, industry, and the country's densest informal settlements on flood-prone lowlands; Yaoundé, cooler and administrative, climbs its hills 250 kilometers inland; and the secondary cities each command a region, Bafoussam the Bamiléké highlands, Bamenda the anglophone Northwest, Garoua and Maroua the north, Ngaoundéré the rail-truck break-of-bulk point, Bertoua the east, and Kribi and Limbé the coast's energy and leisure economies. Connectivity outward is stronger than sideways: it remains easier to ship goods from Douala to Europe or China than to move them by land to Libreville or Lagos, a Central African pattern the African Continental Free Trade Area is only beginning to address.

sections.heading: Environmental Change, Hazards, and Open Questions
sections.body: Cameroon's environmental story is a ledger of pressures moving at different speeds, and it should be read with honest uncertainty about the numbers. Forest loss is the slow-motion entry: Cameroon holds roughly 20 million hectares of forest, and satellite analyses indicate losses of tens of thousands of hectares of primary forest per year through the 2010s and 2020s, driven less by industrial clear-cutting than by smallholder expansion for cocoa and food crops, charcoal, roads, and selective logging that opens the canopy and the bushmeat frontier behind it; estimates differ by methodology, but the direction is unambiguous, and the ecological cost is concentrated where diversity is highest, in the coastal hills and the montane fragments. The fast entries are hydrological. In the north, the combination of erratic Sahelian rainfall, upstream withdrawals, and the long decline of Lake Chad has stressed the flood-pulse economy of the Yaéré, while paradoxically the same region now suffers repeated catastrophic floods, as in 2012, 2022, and 2024, when Logone dikes failed and hundreds of thousands were displaced; drought and flood are not opposites here but alternating faces of higher variance. Add the security emergencies that follow environmental stress, Boko Haram around Lake Chad since 2014, farmer- herder conflict spreading along the transhumance routes, and the separatist war in the anglophone regions, and Cameroon by the mid-2020s hosted well over a million internally displaced people and refugees, a human geography of displacement layered onto the physical one. The volcanic ledger never closes: Mount Cameroon will erupt again, the degassing columns at Nyos and Monoun must run indefinitely, the weak natural dam at Nyos still worries engineers, and several other crater lakes have never been fully surveyed for gas, a genuinely open scientific question. Coastal Douala faces sea-level rise and subsidence on its reclaimed swamps, with flooding already routine in neighborhoods like Makèpè; mangrove clearance removes the buffer just as the hazard grows. What should a reader retain from Cameroon's geography as a whole? First, the gradients: almost every national statistic, rainfall, income, religion, population density, is really a curve running from the humid southwest to the arid northeast, and policies fail when they ignore the slope. Second, the hinge position: Cameroon's ports, roads, and pipeline make it the indispensable corridor for its landlocked neighbors, so its stability is a regional public good. Third, the volcanic line as both gift and threat, the soils and rains that feed the densest populations sitting beside the continent's strangest volcanic and limnic hazards. Fourth, the unfinished map: mineral railways unbuilt, hydropower fractionally tapped, the census itself dated, with most population figures projections from 2005, so that basic quantities carry error bars a careful reader should respect. Cameroon in miniature mirrors Africa's whole predicament, extraordinary natural endowment, gradients of risk, and infrastructure that has not yet caught up with geography, and watching how this one country manages its water towers, its forests, and its two-language fault line is as good a lens as any on the continent's century.

guides.title: Geography of Chad
guides.summary: The physical and human geography of Chad: its basin structure, Saharan mountains, Lake Chad and the Chari river system, climate belts from desert to savanna, peoples and cities, resources, and the environmental pressures reshaping the country.

sections.heading: Chad in Outline: Position, Size, and Significance
sections.body: Chad is a vast, landlocked republic in north-central Africa, covering about 1,284,000 square kilometers, which makes it the fifth largest country on the continent and roughly twice the size of France or three times the size of California. It stretches nearly 1,800 kilometers from north to south, from the heart of the Sahara Desert to the moist savannas near the Central African Republic, and about 1,000 kilometers from east to west. Its neighbors are Libya to the north, Sudan to the east, the Central African Republic to the south, Cameroon and Nigeria to the southwest, and Niger to the west, giving it borders totaling roughly 6,400 kilometers, none of which touch the sea. The nearest coastline, at Douala in Cameroon, lies about 1,700 kilometers from the capital by road, and this extreme distance from any port is the single most important economic fact about the country: almost everything imported or exported must travel overland across at least one other state, multiplying costs and exposing trade to the politics of neighbors. Geographers often call Chad the meeting point of North Africa and sub-Saharan Africa, and the description is precise rather than poetic. The country spans the full transition from hyperarid desert receiving under 25 millimeters of rain a year to wooded savanna receiving more than 1,100 millimeters, and every belt of climate, vegetation, livelihood, and culture between those extremes crosses Chadian territory in rough east-west bands. Arabic and Islam dominate the center and north; the south is home to farming peoples, among whom Christianity and traditional religions are widespread; and the tensions and exchanges between these zones have shaped Chadian history from the trans-Saharan caravan kingdoms to the civil wars of the twentieth century. The name of the country comes from Lake Chad, the great shallow lake on its western border, whose own name derives from a local word, tsade, simply meaning lake or large expanse of water. That lake anchors the other defining structure of Chadian geography: the country occupies the larger part of the Chad Basin, an immense closed depression with no outlet to the ocean, into which rivers drain and evaporate rather than reaching any sea. Rain that falls on most of Chad will never touch salt water. Understanding the country therefore means holding two images at once: a shallow bowl centered near Lake Chad, rimmed by highlands on the north, east, and south, and a ladder of climate belts laid across that bowl from desert to savanna. The population, about 18 million people by the mid-2020s estimates, is distributed almost entirely according to those two structures, crowded into the wetter south and southwest and the lake margins, and sparse to nearly absent across the northern half. Chad matters to geography as a textbook case of an interior drainage basin, as home to the Sahara's highest mountains and the world's greatest dust source, and as a frontline of climate stress in the Sahel.

sections.heading: The Chad Basin: A Country Shaped Like a Bowl
sections.body: The fundamental structure of Chad is a sedimentary basin, one of the largest interior drainage basins on Earth, covering about 2.4 million square kilometers across parts of seven countries, of which Chad holds the greatest share. A drainage basin is called interior, or endorheic, when its rivers never reach the ocean; water flows toward the lowest part of the bowl, collects in lakes and wetlands, and leaves only by evaporation or by seeping into the ground. The Chad Basin formed over tens of millions of years as the African crust sagged between ancient uplifted massifs, and it has been filling with sediment washed from the surrounding highlands ever since, in places to thicknesses of several kilometers. The rim of the bowl is visible on any relief map of the country. To the north rise the volcanic Tibesti Mountains, the highest terrain in the entire Sahara; to the northeast lies the sandstone Ennedi Plateau; along the eastern border with Sudan runs the Ouaddaï highland massif around Abéché; and in the south the land rises gently toward the low plateaus and hills that separate Chad from the Congo River drainage, including the Guéra massif, whose granite peaks stand isolated above the plains near Mongo. Between these rims, the floor of the bowl descends in broad, almost imperceptible steps toward two low points: Lake Chad itself, at about 280 meters above sea level in the southwest, and the Bodélé Depression, a dry lake floor at roughly 155 to 180 meters, the lowest ground in the country, located in the north-central desert. The gradient is extraordinarily gentle; over hundreds of kilometers the land may fall only a few tens of meters, which explains why Chad's rivers meander, flood widely, split into distributaries, and form immense seasonal wetlands rather than cutting valleys. This flatness is also why the boundary of the basin matters so much to human life. Nearly all reliable surface water enters from the wetter southern rim, gathered by the Chari and Logone rivers, and flows northwest across the flats to die in Lake Chad. During the African Humid Period, a wet phase that peaked roughly 9,000 to 6,000 years ago when the monsoon reached far deeper into the continent, the bowl held a water body geologists call Lake Mega-Chad, which at its greatest extent covered as much as 350,000 to 400,000 square kilometers, an area larger than today's Caspian Sea, with a surface near 325 meters elevation. Ancient shorelines, fish bones in the desert, and the diatomite beds of the Bodélé are its remains, and prehistoric rock art in the northern mountains records the herds and hunters who lived on its margins. The basin also stores water underground: extensive aquifers in the sedimentary fill, some recharged in that humid past, supply wells across the country and represent a strategic reserve whose sustainable use is a live scientific and political question.

sections.heading: The Tibesti Mountains: The Roof of the Sahara
sections.body: In the far north of Chad, rising abruptly from the desert plains along the Libyan border, stands the Tibesti, a volcanic mountain massif about 480 kilometers long and 350 kilometers wide that contains the highest terrain anywhere in the Sahara. Its summit, Emi Koussi, is a colossal shield volcano crowned by a caldera some 12 to 15 kilometers across, reaching 3,445 meters above sea level at the crater rim, the highest point of both Chad and the entire desert. The massif is built of dark basaltic lavas and lighter volcanic rocks erupted over the last several million years atop an uplifted block of ancient basement rock, and its landscape is one of the most otherworldly on the continent: stacked lava flows, cinder fields, deep canyons, and enormous explosion craters. The most famous of these is the Trou au Natron, a pit roughly 8 kilometers wide and up to a kilometer deep whose floor gleams white with natron, a natural mixture of sodium carbonate salts deposited by mineral springs and evaporation. Several summits show fumaroles and hot springs, evidence that the volcanic system is dormant rather than dead, though no historical eruption has been recorded. Climatically the Tibesti is a modest island of relief in an ocean of hyperaridity. The surrounding desert may receive under 20 millimeters of rain in a year, while the high slopes intercept perhaps 100 to 150 millimeters, enough to feed seasonal torrents down deep wadis, the dry valleys of the desert that flow briefly after storms, and to sustain permanent water pockets called gueltas among the rocks. Around these waters survive relict plants and animals stranded since the Sahara's last humid phase, including Saharan cypress stands and, historically, desert-adapted Barbary sheep. Temperatures on the heights drop below freezing on winter nights even as the plains below bake, and light snow has occasionally dusted the summits. The human presence is ancient and thin. The Tibesti is the homeland of the Toubou people, camel and goat herders and oasis gardeners organized around clan territories, whose caravans historically linked the Fezzan in Libya with the Lake Chad lowlands, and whose knowledge of the passes made them formidable in every modern conflict fought over this ground. Date palm oases such as Bardaï and Zouar are the principal settlements. Rock engravings and paintings thousands of years old show cattle, giraffes, and hunters, testimony that these mountains overlooked grasslands within human memory of the species. The massif's remoteness is extreme: no paved road reaches it, distances to the capital exceed a thousand kilometers, and the region has repeatedly been a refuge for rebellion and a zone of landmines left by the Chad-Libya wars of the 1970s and 1980s, when Libya occupied the adjacent Aouzou Strip before the International Court of Justice confirmed Chadian sovereignty in 1994. For geography, Tibesti matters as the Sahara's chief water tower, its greatest volcanic province, and the northern rim of the Chad Basin bowl.

sections.heading: Ennedi, Borkou, and the Bodélé: The Desert Heart
sections.body: Northern and north-central Chad, administratively the historic Borkou-Ennedi-Tibesti region, is Saharan desert covering roughly the northern half of the national territory, and it contains three landscapes of world importance beyond the Tibesti itself. The first is the Ennedi Plateau in the northeast, a sandstone massif of about 60,000 square kilometers rising to around 1,450 meters, carved by wind and by the wetter climates of the past into a labyrinth of cliffs, towers, natural arches, and slot canyons; the Aloba Arch, with a span over 70 meters and a height of about 120 meters, ranks among the largest natural arches on Earth. Water lingers in the Ennedi's shaded gorges, most famously at the Guelta d'Archeï, a permanent rock pool where camel caravans have watered for millennia and where a tiny relict population of West African crocodiles survives hundreds of kilometers from any river, cut off since the desert dried. Thousands of rock art sites, spanning perhaps seven thousand years from wild fauna through cattle herding to camel caravans, earned the Ennedi inscription as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016. The second landscape is Borkou and the belt of oasis depressions at the desert's center, including the towns of Faya-Largeau, the largest settlement of the Chadian Sahara, famous for its date groves, and the string of lakes at Ounianga. The Lakes of Ounianga, a UNESCO site since 2012, are a scientific marvel: eighteen lakes totaling about 20 square kilometers persist in one of the driest places on the planet, sustained not by rain but by steady groundwater seepage from aquifers charged during the humid past; in the Ounianga Serir group, floating reed mats cover much of the fresh lakes and suppress evaporation, while Lake Yoa at Ounianga Kebir is deep, warm, and salty, its sediments preserving one of the finest continuous climate archives of the Sahara's transformation. The third landscape is the Bodélé Depression, the lowest floor of the Chad Basin at roughly 155 to 180 meters elevation, southwest of Faya. The Bodélé is the dried northeastern arm of ancient Lake Mega-Chad, floored with diatomite, the chalky remains of microscopic lake algae. Between the Tibesti and Ennedi massifs the trade winds accelerate through a natural wind tunnel, and in the winter months they scour the soft lakebed and loft an average of around 700,000 tonnes of dust on active days, making this single small depression the largest point source of mineral dust on Earth, responsible by common estimates for roughly half the dust exported from the entire Sahara. That dust darkens Sahelian skies as the harmattan haze, fertilizes Atlantic waters with iron, and, in one of geography's great long-distance connections, delivers tens of millions of tonnes of phosphorus-bearing sediment across the ocean each year, a nutrient subsidy measurable in the soils of the Amazon rainforest.

sections.heading: Lake Chad: A Shallow Giant and Its Shrinking
sections.body: Lake Chad, on the country's western border where Chad, Cameroon, Nigeria, and Niger meet, is the terminal lake of the basin and one of the most studied water bodies in Africa, because it is huge in area, astonishingly shallow, and dramatically variable. Its mean depth is only about 1.5 to 4 meters, with maxima around 10 to 11 meters, so modest changes in inflow translate into enormous swings of shoreline; the lake behaves less like a basin filling and emptying than like water spilled across a nearly level floor. In the early 1960s, a relatively wet period, its open water covered roughly 22,000 to 25,000 square kilometers, making it then the fourth largest lake in Africa. The great Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s cut the inflowing rivers, and by the 1990s the figure commonly cited for open water had fallen toward 1,500 to 2,500 square kilometers, a decline of more than ninety percent that made Lake Chad a global emblem of environmental change. The honest scientific picture is more nuanced than the slogan of a dying lake. Lake Chad has always pulsed; historical and geological records show it shrinking to marsh in the 1900s and expanding again, and since the 1990s the southern pool has partially stabilized and in wet years re-expanded, with much of the former lakebed now a mosaic of open water, dense papyrus and reed swamp, and seasonally flooded dunes whose crests form thousands of islands. Researchers therefore distinguish a Normal Lake Chad, one continuous water body, from a Small Lake Chad, the divided state prevailing since the 1970s in which a shallow sill, the Great Barrier, separates a perennially watered southern pool fed by the Chari River from a northern pool that floods only in good years. About ninety percent of the lake's inflow arrives from the Chari-Logone system in the south, with small contributions from Nigeria's Komadugu Yobe and local rain, and the water stays remarkably fresh for a closed lake, because dissolved salts leak away by seepage into surrounding aquifers and are sequestered in the dune islands rather than accumulating. The lake supports an economy of striking productivity and flexibility: fisheries that in good years yield on the order of 100,000 tonnes, farming of recession crops such as maize and cowpeas on the wet mud the retreating water exposes, and pasture for cattle on the aquatic grasses, with households commonly switching among all three as levels change. On the Chadian shore the main lakeside towns are Bol, center of the polder district where dune-flanked arms of the lake are diked and cultivated, and the fishing settlements of the islands. Around thirty to forty million people live in the wider basin depending on these waters. Proposals to stabilize the lake by transferring water from the Congo River system, the Transaqua scheme, have circulated for decades and remain studied but unbuilt, facing costs in the tens of billions of dollars and unresolved ecological and political questions.

sections.heading: Rivers and Wetlands: Chari, Logone, and the Seasonal Flood
sections.body: Chad's hydrology is concentrated in the far southwest, where its only two substantial perennial rivers, the Chari and the Logone, gather the runoff of the wet southern savannas and deliver it to Lake Chad. The Chari, about 1,200 kilometers long, rises in the highlands of the Central African Republic from headstreams such as the Bamingui and Gribingui, collects the Bahr Salamat and Bahr Aouk along the way, and flows northwest past the cities of Sarh and N'Djamena. The Logone, roughly 1,000 kilometers long, rises on the Adamawa Plateau of Cameroon and the highlands near Moundou, flows north along the Cameroon border, and joins the Chari at the capital itself; N'Djamena exists where it does because of this confluence, and the combined river enters the lake about a hundred kilometers downstream. Together the system delivers on the order of 20 to 40 cubic kilometers of water to the lake in a year, the total swinging by a factor of two or more between drought and wet years, with the flood peak passing N'Djamena in October and November after the southern rains. Because the land is so flat, the rivers do not stay in their channels. Each rainy season the Logone spills across its low banks into the Grand Yaéré floodplains shared with Cameroon, and the middle Chari floods the plains of Salamat in the southeast, fed also by the seasonal Bahr Azoum arriving from Sudan's Darfur highlands. These inundations, covering thousands of square kilometers for several months, are not disasters but the engine of the regional economy and ecology: they recharge groundwater, deposit fertile silt, raise a flush of perennial grasses that feeds hundreds of thousands of cattle in the dry season, support fisheries that migrate with the water, and enable flood-retreat farming of sorghum, notably the transplanted dry-season sorghum called berbéré grown on heavy clay plains as the water withdraws. The Salamat wetlands sustain Zakouma National Park's great wildlife concentrations, and the Logone floodplain sustains the Waza ecosystem across the border. Beyond this living system, the map of Chad is veined with fossil and seasonal drainage. The Batha is a typical wadi of the Sahel, flowing eastward only in the rains toward the closed depression of Lake Fitri, a miniature of Lake Chad ringed by its own fishing and herding economy. The enigmatic Bahr el Ghazal, a broad dry valley, leads northeast from Lake Chad toward the Bodélé Depression; when the lake stands exceptionally high it can carry overflow toward the desert, as it last did in ephemeral fashion during high stands of the nineteenth and mid-twentieth centuries, and in the Mega-Chad era it was a flowing connection. In the far north, wadis descend from Tibesti and Ennedi to die in the sands. Groundwater beneath these valleys, often shallow, supports wells, gardens, and the deep-rooted acacias that line the channels, so even a river of sand organizes life along its course.

sections.heading: Climate: The Rainfall Ladder and the Moving Monsoon
sections.body: Chad's climate is best understood as a single mechanism: the seasonal migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, the belt where the moist southwesterly monsoon flow from the Atlantic meets the hot, dry northeasterly wind off the Sahara known as the harmattan. In the northern winter the convergence lies south of the country and the harmattan sweeps the whole territory with dusty, rainless air; in the northern summer the convergence migrates north, carrying the monsoon and its thunderstorms deep into Chad before retreating. Because the moist layer thins toward its northern limit, the result is a remarkably regular ladder of rainfall totals laid across the country in east-west rungs. The far south, around Moundou and the border with the Central African Republic, receives roughly 900 to 1,200 millimeters a year in a wet season lasting from about May to October. The Sahelian center, including N'Djamena at about 500 to 600 millimeters, gets a shorter season centered on June to September. Abéché in the east records around 400 millimeters; the semidesert around Lake Fitri and Mao perhaps 200 to 300; Faya-Largeau in the Saharan center about 15 to 20 millimeters in an average year, and parts of the far north effectively nothing for years at a time. The gradient is astonishingly steep in human terms: a traveler driving the 1,000 kilometers from Moundou to Faya passes from cotton fields and shea trees to bare rock and sand, crossing in two days the same climatic span that separates coastal West Africa from the central Sahara. Temperatures follow the desert logic of high sun and dry air. The hottest weather comes in the late dry season, April and May, when afternoon readings of 40 to 45 degrees Celsius are routine in the center and north; the arrival of the rains cools the south into the low thirties; and the December-January harmattan season brings warm days and surprisingly cool nights, dropping near 10 degrees in the Sahel and below freezing on Saharan uplands. Rainfall variability, not the average, is the decisive fact of life. Year-to-year totals in the Sahelian belt commonly swing by 30 to 50 percent, and the region suffered a multidecadal drying from the late 1960s through the 1980s, the great Sahel drought, which shifted the effective rainfall belts south by roughly a hundred kilometers, devastated herds, and drove the shrinkage of Lake Chad. Rains have partially recovered since the 1990s, but with a changed character that observers and climate scientists describe consistently: more of the annual total falling in intense downpours, longer dry spells within the season, and greater variance, so that floods and droughts can strike the same district in successive years, as the catastrophic urban floods of N'Djamena in 2022 demonstrated.
