Climate models agree that Chad will continue to warm faster than the global average, but they genuinely disagree about the sign of future Sahel rainfall change, an honest scientific uncertainty at the center of the country's future.

sections.heading: Vegetation Belts and Soils: From Sand Sheet to Savanna
sections.body: The vegetation of Chad mirrors its rainfall ladder so faithfully that the country is a standard illustration of African bioclimatic zonation. The northern half is Saharan: sand sheets, dune fields called ergs, gravel plains called regs, and bare rock, with perennial plants confined to wadi beds and oases where roots can reach moisture; date palms, tamarisks, and scattered acacias mark the water. Vegetation cover over vast areas is below one percent. South of roughly the 200-millimeter rainfall line begins the Sahel proper, a belt of open grassland and thorn scrub two to three hundred kilometers deep, dominated by annual grasses such as cram-cram and by small thorny trees, Acacia species, desert date, and jujube, thickening southward from scattered shrubs to true wooded grassland. Two Sahelian trees deserve particular note for their economic geography: Acacia senegal, the source of gum arabic, of which Chad is consistently among the world's top two or three exporters, and the doum palm of the wadi margins, whose fiber and fruit enter local trade. South again, between about the 600- and 1,100-millimeter lines, lies the Sudanian savanna, the broad agricultural heartland: taller perennial grasses burned in annual fires, and an increasingly continuous tree canopy of shea butter trees, néré locust bean, kapok, tamarind, and broad-leaved Combretum and Isoberlinia woodland, grading in the wettest corners of the far south toward woodland with gallery forest, dense evergreen ribbons along watercourses. There is no rainforest in Chad; the country stops short of the humid zone, and its far southern tip is best described as wooded savanna heavily reshaped by farming. Across all belts, human use bends the natural pattern: around villages and towns stand managed parklands where farmers preserve and tend useful trees, especially shea and the remarkable Faidherbia albida acacia, which drops its leaves in the rains and leafs out in the dry season, fertilizing millet fields beneath it while providing dry-season browse. Soils follow the same geography with a logic worth spelling out. In the desert, soils are skeletal or absent, mere mineral surfaces. The Sahel is dominated by sandy soils formed on ancient dune systems stabilized by grass, easy to work with hand tools and quick to absorb rain, but poor in organic matter and nutrients, and prone to wind stripping when the vegetation that binds them is lost. The old lakebed plains around Lake Chad, Fitri, and the great floodplains carry heavy clays and vertisols, cracking black soils that are waterlogged in the rains and brick-hard when dry, difficult to plough but chemically rich, and it is on these that flood-retreat berbéré sorghum yields without fertilizer. The Sudanian south carries deeply weathered reddish tropical soils, moderately fertile, sometimes capped by ironstone crusts, supporting the sorghum, millet, groundnut, sesame, and cotton fields of the national breadbasket. Fire is a structural force: hundreds of thousands of square kilometers of savanna burn every dry season, set mostly by people for pasture renewal and clearing, maintaining the grassy, open character of the whole southern landscape.

sections.heading: Wildlife and Protected Areas: Zakouma and the Desert Refuges
sections.body: Chad retains wildlife of continental importance, concentrated where water concentrates, and its recent conservation history contains one of Africa's most cited recoveries. The flagship is Zakouma National Park, about 3,000 square kilometers of Sudanian savanna and seasonal floodplain in the Salamat region of the southeast, protected since 1963. Zakouma's elephants numbered around 4,000 in the early 2000s, then fell below 500 within a decade as horse-mounted poaching gangs, many crossing from the Darfur war zone, slaughtered herds for ivory. After the nonprofit African Parks assumed management in partnership with the government in 2010, with aircraft, radio networks, community programs, and rebuilt ranger forces, poaching was effectively halted; the herd stabilized and by the 2020s exceeded 600 and was breeding strongly again. The park also holds more than half of the world's remaining Kordofan giraffes, large populations of buffalo, roan antelope, Lelwel hartebeest, tiang, greater kudu, lions, leopards, and spectacular dry-season bird concentrations, including millions of red-billed queleas and great flocks of black crowned cranes. Northward, the protected-area system follows the climate ladder. The immense Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Faunal Reserve in the central Sahel, nearly 78,000 square kilometers, was the historic home of the scimitar-horned oryx, a desert antelope declared extinct in the wild in 2000 after drought and uncontrolled hunting. Beginning in 2016, a reintroduction program led by the government, the Sahara Conservation Fund, and the Environment Agency of Abu Dhabi released captive-bred oryx there; the free-living herd grew into the hundreds, calves have been born wild in numbers, and in 2023 the species was formally downlisted from extinct in the wild to endangered, a rare reversal in modern conservation. The same reserve supports dama and dorcas gazelles, and has been a release site for addax, the critically endangered white desert antelope whose last wild strongholds lie in the Termit region of neighboring Niger. In the far north, the Ennedi massif, managed with African Parks since 2018, shelters Barbary sheep, relict crocodiles at Guelta d'Archeï, and possibly the last northern individuals of several Saharan species; the Tibesti holds thin populations of aoudad and gazelle. The largest carnivores tell a harder story: the West and Central African lion population is endangered, cheetahs in the Sahel are nearly gone, and the last confirmed wild black rhinos in Chad were reintroduced to Zakouma from South Africa in 2018, with mixed early survival. Threats across the system are consistent and structural: armed poaching linked to regional conflicts, competition with expanding herds of domestic livestock for pasture and water, firewood cutting, and climate stress on desert waterholes. The recent Chadian lesson, drawn from Zakouma and the oryx, is that well-resourced, long-horizon management with genuine community stakes can rebuild wildlife even in poor, conflict-adjacent regions, and that abandoning such management loses decades of gains within a few years.

sections.heading: Peoples and Population: Where Chadians Live and Why
sections.body: Chad's population, estimated around 18 million in the mid-2020s and growing at more than three percent a year, one of the world's faster national growth rates, is distributed with extreme unevenness that follows water almost perfectly. Roughly half the national territory, the Saharan north, holds on the order of one percent of the people; the Sahelian center holds moderate densities along its wadis, around Lake Fitri, and near Lake Chad; and the Sudanian south and the capital region concentrate the great majority, with rural densities in the cotton belt and the Logone valleys among the highest in the country. The national average of about 14 people per square kilometer is therefore nearly meaningless; lived densities range from under 0.1 in Borkou to well over 100 in parts of the southwest. This geography of settlement is also a geography of peoples. Chad counts well over a hundred ethnic groups and some 120 to 130 languages, and geographers conventionally organize this diversity by livelihood zone. The Saharan north is Toubou country, the Teda and Daza camel pastoralists and oasis cultivators of Tibesti, Borkou, and Ennedi, with the Zaghawa, prominent in both Chad and Sudan, along the northeastern borderlands. The Sahelian center is the domain of Arabic-speaking pastoral groups, collectively the Chadian Arabs, including the cattle-keeping Baggara Arabs, who form one of the largest population categories in the country, alongside the Kanembu near Lake Chad, heirs of the medieval Kanem-Bornu empire that ruled the lake region for centuries, the Buduma of the lake islands, famous for reed boats and water-adapted cattle, and the peoples of the Ouaddaï highlands around Abéché, seat of the historic Wadai sultanate. The south is home to the country's largest single ethnic group, the Sara, perhaps a quarter to nearly a third of all Chadians, sedentary farmers of the Chari and Logone valleys, together with many smaller farming peoples. Religion follows the same gradient in broad strokes: Islam predominates in the north and center and among most pastoral groups, a small majority nationally; Christianity, both Catholic and Protestant, and traditional religions are strongest in the south. French and Modern Standard Arabic are the official languages, but the true lingua franca of markets and streets is Chadian Arabic, spoken as a vehicular tongue by a majority. Two structural population movements define the current era. First, urbanization: the urban share has climbed toward a quarter of the population, led by N'Djamena's explosive growth. Second, displacement: Chad hosts one of Africa's largest refugee populations relative to its means, more than a million refugees by 2024, dominated by Sudanese fleeing Darfur's wars into the arid east around Adré and Farchana, along with Central Africans in the south and Nigerians displaced by the Boko Haram insurgency around the lake, itself a conflict that has also displaced hundreds of thousands of Chadians internally. Median age is under seventeen, meaning the population geography of the next generation is already born.

sections.heading: Cities and the Urban Network: N'Djamena and the Regional Capitals
sections.body: Chad's urban system is dominated by a single primate city. N'Djamena, founded by the French in 1900 as Fort-Lamy and renamed in 1973, stands on the right bank of the Chari at its confluence with the Logone, directly opposite the Cameroonian town of Kousséri, to which a bridge crosses the river. The site logic is classical: the confluence gave water, fish, river transport toward the lake, and a defensible position at the hinge of the Sahelian and Sudanian belts, close enough to the south to be fed by it and central enough to administer the routes north and east. Greater N'Djamena has grown from a few hundred thousand people in the 1970s to well beyond 1.5 million, absorbing drought migrants, war displacements, and the ordinary pull of a capital that hosts nearly all national government, banking, and international connections, including the country's principal airport. The city's physical geography is a hazard in itself: it lies on a nearly flat floodplain of impermeable clays at about 295 meters elevation, and heavy rains or a high Chari regularly flood whole districts, as in 2012 and again catastrophically in 2022, when the river reached record levels and hundreds of thousands of residents were affected. Beyond the capital, the urban network is thin and regional. Moundou, on the Logone in the southwest with roughly 150,000 to 200,000 people, is the second city and the historic industrial center, seat of the cotton company, breweries, and the commerce of the oil zone. Sarh, on the middle Chari, anchors the southeast cotton country. Abéché, at around 100,000, is the metropolis of the east, ancient capital of the Wadai sultanate, staging point of trans-Saharan trade toward Libya and Sudan, and since 2003 the humanitarian hub for the Darfur refugee operations; its dry, dusty hinterland contrasts sharply with the riverine southern cities. Kélo, Pala, Doba, and Koumra fill out the southern tier of secondary towns; Mongo serves the central Guéra; Mao the Kanem sands; Bol the lakeside polders; Ati and Oum Hadjer the Batha; Am Timan the Salamat; and Faya-Largeau, with some tens of thousands of people, is the lonely capital of the Saharan north, a date-palm oasis a thousand kilometers from the sea of grass. Most of these towns share a common morphology: a colonial-era administrative core and grid, a great central market, expansive unplanned residential quarters of banco, sun-dried mud brick, and a growth rate that outruns every network, so that water supply, drainage, electricity, and paved streets reach only fractions of the population. Urban services statistics are among the region's lowest; national electricity access hovers around ten percent, overwhelmingly urban and generator-fed, and N'Djamena's grid is small and costly. Yet the cities are where Chad's economic future is visibly forming: the mobile-phone economy, the university system, construction booms funded by oil revenue and diaspora money, and the market integration of pastoral and farming hinterlands all radiate from these river and caravan towns.

sections.heading: Farming, Herding, and Fishing: The Livelihood Map
sections.body: Chad's economic geography at ground level is a livelihood map laid across the rainfall ladder, and some four-fifths of Chadians draw their living from it directly. In the Sudanian south, where rain suffices for reliable cropping, the staple grains are sorghum and pearl millet, supplemented by maize, rice in the floodplains, groundnuts, sesame, cowpeas, and cassava, grown in hand-hoed or ox-ploughed fields on household holdings of a few hectares. The historic cash crop is cotton, introduced under French rule and long the backbone of the money economy, grown by hundreds of thousands of smallholders in the Moundou-Sarh belt and ginned by the parastatal CotonTchad; output has fluctuated between glory years above 200,000 tonnes of seed cotton and slumps driven by prices, and by the state of the ginning company, but cotton remains the south's principal cash link. Shea nuts gathered by women, gum arabic tapped from Sahelian acacias, of which Chad exports on the order of 20,000 to 40,000 tonnes a year, second only to Sudan, sesame, and peppers from the Salamat add further trade crops. The heavy clay plains contribute the distinctive berbéré system: dry-season sorghum transplanted into receding floodwater, a technique that yields grain with no rain at all and anchors food security in Salamat and around Lake Fitri and Lake Chad. In the Sahelian center, cropping thins to fast-maturing millet on the sands and concentrates along wadis, while livestock takes over as the organizing wealth. Chad's national herd is enormous, plausibly among Africa's largest relative to population: commonly cited figures run to some 30 million cattle and comparable tens of millions of sheep and goats, plus roughly 6 to 7 million camels in the north. The dominant system is mobile pastoralism and transhumance, the regular seasonal movement of herds: north into the fresh Sahelian pastures during the rains, when temporary ponds and annual grasses erupt, and south toward the rivers, floodplain grasses, and crop stubble in the dry season. These movements, along customary corridors sometimes hundreds of kilometers long, knit the country together economically, cattle from the center walking to markets in N'Djamena and onward on the hoof to Nigeria, historically Chad's largest livestock customer, but they also generate the farmer-herder frictions over crop damage and water points that have sharpened as cultivated area expands and wet-season pastures shrink. Fishing is the third pillar: Lake Chad, the Chari-Logone, Lake Fitri, and the flood ponds yield tens of thousands of tonnes in an ordinary year, traded fresh, smoked, and dried as banda deep into Nigeria and Cameroon. The oases of the north complete the map with date culture, wadi gardens of the Kanem, and natron dug from lakeside pans, an old caravan staple still traded for livestock salt. The deep vulnerability of this whole livelihood geography is its rain dependence; almost nothing is irrigated by infrastructure, so a failed season translates within months into food crisis, and chronic malnutrition rates in the Sahelian belt are among the world's highest even in normal years.

sections.heading: Oil, Minerals, and Energy: The Subsoil Economy
sections.body: For its first four decades of independence Chad was routinely described as a country with no mineral economy worth the name; that changed abruptly in 2003, when the Doba Basin oilfields of the far south began producing and the country became a petroleum exporter almost overnight. The geological setting is a chain of Cretaceous rift basins, sediment-filled troughs beneath the savanna, of which Doba near the city of the same name holds the main producing fields, Komé, Bolobo, Miandoum and their satellites, with additional production later developed in the Bongor Basin southwest of the capital by Chinese operators, and reserves identified in the Lake Chad and Salamat basins. Because Chad is landlocked, the field development was inseparable from a transport megaproject: the 1,070-kilometer buried pipeline from Komé through Cameroon to a floating export terminal off Kribi on the Atlantic, completed in 2003 for about 3.7 billion dollars with World Bank participation under a much-publicized revenue-management scheme that was meant to earmark oil money for poverty reduction and was largely dismantled within five years as the government redirected funds, a governance episode now cited worldwide in debates over the resource curse. Production peaked early, around 170,000 barrels per day in 2004 and 2005, and has since declined toward roughly 60,000 to 130,000 barrels per day depending on year and count, but oil still supplies the large majority of export earnings and a major share of state revenue, tying the national budget to world price swings; the 2014 to 2016 price collapse produced a fiscal crisis and debt restructuring with the trader Glencore that shaped a decade of austerity. A modest refinery at Djermaya north of N'Djamena, built with Chinese investment in 2011, supplies domestic fuel from the Bongor crude. Beyond petroleum, the confirmed mineral economy remains small but geologically promising. Natron, soda ash crusts from the shores of Lake Chad and desert pans, has been dug and traded across the Sahara for centuries. Gold occurs in the basement rocks of the Ouaddaï, the Guéra, Mayo-Kebbi in the southwest, and the Tibesti; since the 2010s artisanal gold rushes, most dramatically at Kouri Bougoudi in the far northern Tibesti near the Libyan border, have drawn tens of thousands of informal miners, generated recurring violence, and remain largely outside state control. Mayo-Kebbi also hosts documented occurrences of marble, uranium, and bauxite; none has reached industrial mining, a gap explained less by geology than by distance, energy costs, and investment risk. Energy geography is a paradox: an oil exporter whose citizens have among the lowest electricity access rates on Earth, around ten percent nationally, with the grid confined to N'Djamena and a few towns and fed by expensive diesel generation. The obvious counterweight is solar; the Sahelian and Saharan zones receive some of the highest solar irradiance recorded anywhere, and the first utility-scale solar projects for the capital, along with donor-funded solarization of provincial towns and refugee camps, mark the beginning of what geography suggests should be the country's natural energy path.

sections.heading: Transport and the Tyranny of Distance
sections.body: Nothing constrains Chad like distance, and its transport geography can be summarized as a single problem: how to move goods and people across a country the size of Western Europe, with no railway, no seaport, few paved roads, and a capital 1,700 kilometers from the ocean. The paved network, on the order of only a few thousand kilometers, radiates from N'Djamena: south through Guélengdeng and Bongor toward Moundou, Doba, and Sarh, the vital cotton and oil axis; east toward Massaguet, Massakory and, after long unpaved stretches completed in stages during the 2010s, through Ati and Oum Hadjer to Abéché; and west across the bridge to Kousséri in Cameroon, the artery of external trade. Beyond these spines, movement happens on graded earth and sand tracks that the rainy season converts to mud for months; whole prefectures of the southeast are effectively cut off from July to October, and seasonal inaccessibility is a planning fact for markets, health services, and armies. The lifeline to the sea is the Douala corridor: trucks from N'Djamena cross at Kousséri or at the newer Nigerian routings and run through Cameroon via Ngaoundéré and Yaoundé to the port of Douala, a journey of one to three weeks with delays, at freight costs among the highest in the world per tonne-kilometer; studies of landlocked African trade regularly place Chad at or near the bottom of logistics rankings, and every imported liter of fuel or bag of cement carries that overland premium. Alternative corridors exist and matter politically: through Nigeria to Lagos or Port Harcourt, historically important for livestock exports and periodically disrupted by insecurity around the lake; northeast through Abéché and Adré into Sudan toward Port Sudan, severed by the Sudanese civil war after 2023 even as the same border became the entry for refugee flows; and the ancient trans-Saharan tracks north through Faya toward Libya, today carrying dates, livestock, migrants, and contraband rather than caravan salt. The Chari and Logone are seasonally navigable by shallow barges and pirogues between N'Djamena and the lake and up the Logone toward Bongor, a modest but locally important freight path during high water. Air transport bears an outsized burden for passengers and emergencies: N'Djamena's international airport connects to Paris, Addis Ababa, Istanbul and regional capitals, and a scatter of provincial strips at Abéché, Faya, Sarh, and Moundou sustain government and humanitarian aviation. Railway projects, notably a proposed line from Cameroon's railhead at Ngaoundéré to Moundou and N'Djamena, have been surveyed repeatedly and remain unbuilt. The consequences of this geography are pervasive: consumer prices in Chad run far above coastal averages, exports are effectively limited to high-value-per-weight goods, oil by pipeline, cattle on the hoof, gum arabic by truck, and every diplomatic crisis with a transit neighbor is instantly an economic crisis at home, a vulnerability the country shares with its landlocked Sahelian peers but suffers in unusually acute degree.

sections.heading: Environmental Pressures and the Country's Prospect
sections.body: The environmental question in Chad is not a single crisis but a compounding of pressures on a system with little slack, and it is best closed with an honest account of what is known, what is contested, and what failure and success would look like. The pressures are real and measurable. The Sahel warmed through recent decades faster than the global mean, and further warming of 2 to 4 degrees Celsius this century is projected in scenarios that differ mainly in degree; rainfall futures are genuinely uncertain, with some models projecting a wetter central Sahel and others continued volatility, but all projecting more intense extremes, which the floods of 2022, affecting well over a million Chadians, and the recurrent droughts both illustrate. Population growth above three percent doubles human needs roughly every twenty-two years, and the firewood and charcoal demand of that population is the principal driver of tree loss around every city, with N'Djamena's supply zone reaching a couple of hundred kilometers. Farmed area expands into pasture, herds grow and concentrate around boreholes, and the resulting overgrazed, trampled halos around water points are the genuine core of what is loosely called desertification: less an advancing wall of sand than a spreading loss of vegetation and soil structure in the zones people use hardest, patchy, human-scaled, and in principle reversible. The famous counterexample sits next door: farmer-managed natural regeneration, protecting the stumps and seedlings of native trees in fields, restored tree cover across millions of hectares in Niger, and the same techniques, with berbéré flood farming, zaï planting pits, half-moon water harvesting, and dune fixation, constitute the practical toolkit of the Great Green Wall initiative, of which Chad is a core member state; implementation to date is modest but demonstrably real at project scale. Lake Chad's future remains contested science: the lake has partially recovered from its 1980s minimum, groundwater seepage sustains its freshness, and careful hydrological work suggests the Small Lake state can persist and even support expanded flood-recession livelihoods, while the megaproject alternative, interbasin transfer from the Congo, would gamble tens of billions of dollars on a plumbing solution to what is substantially a climate and governance problem. Security and environment now interlock around the lake, where Boko Haram and its offshoots exploited the maze of islands, displacing fishing and farming communities and closing markets, an example of how conflict can do more damage to livelihoods than the environmental change itself. For a reader trying to judge the country's prospect, three markers are worth watching. First, the demographic arc: whether education and health investment bend the growth rate before it doubles again the demand on the same water. Second, the energy transition: whether Saharan-grade solar reaches towns and pumps before the woodlands are gone. Third, the management of mobility: whether transhumance corridors, land rights, and lake access are governed by negotiation or by force. Chad's geography is often described as a curse of distance and drought; it is more accurately a demanding endowment, holding groundwater, sun, floodplains, herds, and young people in quantities that competent stewardship could compound.

guides.title: Geography of the Comoros
guides.summary: A full geographical account of the Comoro archipelago at the head of the Mozambique Channel: its volcanic origin and active hazards, its climate and ocean setting, its water problem, its extraordinary endemic life, and the way a small area of young volcanic rock supports one of the densest rural populations in Africa.

sections.heading: Where the Comoros are, and why the position matters
sections.body:
The Comoro archipelago is a chain of four principal volcanic islands lying at the northern entrance of the Mozambique Channel, the broad seaway that separates mainland southeast Africa from Madagascar. In round terms the islands sit between about eleven and thirteen degrees south and between forty-three and forty-five degrees east, roughly 290 kilometres off the coast of Mozambique and around 300 kilometres from the northwestern tip of Madagascar. The chain runs northwest to southeast across about 300 kilometres of open ocean, and each island rises steeply from a seafloor three to three and a half kilometres deep, so that these are not shelf islands attached to any continent but isolated volcanic peaks standing alone in deep water.

There are four islands and each carries two names, a Comorian one and a colonial-era French one, and using both is not pedantry but a necessity for reading any source. From northwest to southeast they are Ngazidja, also called Grande Comore; Mwali, also called Mohéli; Nzwani, also called Anjouan; and Maore, also called Mayotte. The first three form the independent Union of the Comoros, with its capital at Moroni on Ngazidja. The fourth, Mayotte, is administered by France as an overseas department and has been since 2011, a status the Union of the Comoros does not accept and which the United Nations General Assembly has repeatedly declined to endorse. Any statement about the geography of the Comoros therefore has to specify whether it includes Mayotte, because doing so changes the land area by about a fifth and the population by more than a quarter.

Position explains a great deal about the islands. The Mozambique Channel is one of the world's major shipping corridors, carrying a substantial share of the tanker traffic that rounds southern Africa, and the archipelago sits astride its northern approach. That location made the islands a node in the western Indian Ocean trading world for at least a thousand years, tied to the Swahili coast, the Arabian peninsula, Persia, India and Madagascar, and the resulting culture is genuinely composite: a Bantu language closely related to Swahili, written historically in Arabic script, on islands with Malagasy and Arab and African and later French layers.

Position also explains the physical setting. The islands sit in the tropical southwest Indian Ocean, in the path of the seasonal monsoon reversal and near the northern margin of the region's cyclone belt. They lie in warm water within the belt of coral reef development. And they sit in a zone of the seafloor where the crust is being deformed and volcanoes are being built, which is why three of the four islands remain geologically restless and why one of them hosts one of the most active volcanoes in the Indian Ocean.

sections.heading: The numbers: area, height, population and density
sections.body:
The Union of the Comoros covers about 1,861 square kilometres of land, which makes it one of the smallest countries in Africa, smaller than many single national parks. Adding Mayotte brings the archipelago to roughly 2,236 square kilometres. Broken down by island, Ngazidja is comfortably the largest at about 1,148 square kilometres, Nzwani about 424, Maore about 374 including its offshore Petite-Terre, and Mwali the smallest at roughly 290.

The vertical dimension is far more dramatic than the horizontal one. Mount Karthala on Ngazidja reaches about 2,361 metres, the highest point in the archipelago, and because it rises from a seafloor around 3,000 metres deep, the volcano as a whole is a structure of well over five kilometres in relief, most of it underwater. La Grille, the older volcano at the northern end of the same island, reaches about 1,087 metres. Mount Ntringui on Nzwani reaches about 1,595 metres, an extraordinary height for an island of only a few hundred square kilometres, giving slopes that are steep almost everywhere. Mwali's high point, Mze Koukoulé, is around 790 metres, and Maore, the oldest and most worn down of the four, tops out at Mount Benara at about 660 metres. The pattern of decreasing height from northwest to southeast is the single most important clue to the archipelago's origin.

Population figures require care because censuses are infrequent and migration between the islands and to Mayotte is large. Recent estimates put the Union of the Comoros at somewhere in the region of 850,000 to 900,000 people, with roughly half on Ngazidja, most of the remainder on Nzwani, and only around 50,000 to 60,000 on Mwali. Mayotte, counted separately, has grown fast and recent French censuses place it above 300,000. Densities that follow from these numbers are among the highest in Africa. The Union averages roughly 450 to 480 people per square kilometre; Nzwani, with a small area, steep terrain and a large population, exceeds 700 per square kilometre in some accountings, and because much of its surface is too steep or too rocky to farm, effective density on usable land is a great deal higher still.

Two consequences follow immediately and shape almost everything else. First, the pressure on land is severe, which drives cultivation up steep slopes, into forest, and onto ground that erodes when cleared. Second, the ratio of coastline to land area is very high, so a large share of the population lives within a few hundred metres of the sea and is directly exposed to storm surge, coastal erosion and the loss of protective beaches. A small country with big mountains and a very long shoreline has a particular set of vulnerabilities, and the Comoros has all of them.

sections.heading: Volcanic origin and the contested hotspot
sections.body:
Every island in the archipelago is built of volcanic rock, principally basalt, erupted onto the floor of the Mozambique Channel and piled up until it broke the surface. The archipelago is therefore an oceanic volcanic chain rather than a fragment of a continent, and it has no ancient basement of granite or metamorphic rock of the kind found on the Seychelles or Madagascar.

The most striking pattern is an age progression. Maore, at the southeastern end, is the oldest, with volcanic rocks dated to roughly seven to eight million years and an eruptive history that appears to have ended long ago on the island itself. Nzwani is younger, with activity extending into the last few hundred thousand years. Mwali is younger again. Ngazidja, at the northwestern end, is the youngest of all, probably less than half a million years old at the surface, and is still building itself today. Alongside this age progression runs a morphological one: Maore is deeply eroded, low and rounded, ringed by a vast lagoon that marks where its original coastline used to be; Ngazidja is a raw, black, barely weathered lava field with almost no soil development on its youngest flows.

The obvious explanation for a chain of volcanic islands with ages increasing along its length is a hotspot: a fixed plume of hot mantle material beneath a moving tectonic plate, producing a conveyor belt of volcanoes of which only the youngest end remains active. This is the standard account of Hawaii and Réunion. The Comoros are often described this way in general reference works, and the age pattern is real. It is worth being honest, however, that the hotspot explanation for these particular islands is genuinely contested among specialists. The problem is that the direction and rate of plate motion in this part of the Indian Ocean do not fit the spacing and ages of the islands especially well, and the chain does not line up with other supposed products of the same plume.

The main alternative explanations invoke tectonics rather than a plume. The archipelago lies in a broad zone of diffuse deformation between the Somali plate and the Lwandle plate, in effect a poorly defined boundary that may represent the southeastward propagation of the East African Rift system into the ocean. Long north-south structures in the Mozambique Channel, notably the Davie Ridge, are seismically active. On this view the volcanoes are fed along lithospheric fractures rather than by a fixed plume, and the age pattern reflects the progressive opening of those fractures rather than plate motion over a stationary source. There is also a possibility that both mechanisms contribute. The debate is not settled, and it was reopened forcefully by events off Mayotte in 2018.

sections.heading: Karthala: the volcano that is Grande Comore
sections.body:
Grande Comore is essentially two volcanoes joined together, and the southern one, Karthala, dominates the island and the archipelago. It is a shield volcano, built of thousands of thin, fluid basaltic lava flows piled into a broad dome rather than a steep cone, and its summit carries a caldera measuring roughly three by four kilometres, among the largest active summit craters anywhere. Within it sits a deeper pit crater. The whole structure rises about 2,361 metres above the sea and around five and a half kilometres above the surrounding seafloor.

Karthala is genuinely active, not dormant. More than twenty eruptions have been recorded since the early nineteenth century, an average recurrence of roughly a decade, and the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries maintained that pace. The eruptions take two broad forms. Flank eruptions open fissures on the volcano's sides and produce fast-moving basaltic lava that can reach the coast in hours; the 1977 eruption sent a flow through the village of Singani on the western flank and destroyed it. Summit eruptions are typically explosive in a particular way, because groundwater and the crater lake that has periodically occupied the summit come into contact with rising magma, flashing to steam and blasting out large volumes of fine ash.

The eruptions of April and November 2005, followed by further activity in 2006 and 2007, showed exactly why ash matters more than lava on this island. The eruptions killed very few people directly. What they did was blanket much of Grande Comore in ash, and because the island's population depends overwhelmingly on rainwater collected from roofs into cisterns, the ash contaminated the water supply across a large part of the island at once. Estimates at the time put the number of people affected in the hundreds of thousands, with tens of thousands temporarily displaced, in a country whose entire population was under 700,000. A volcanic crisis in the Comoros is therefore, first and foremost, a water crisis, and that connection is not obvious from the volcanology alone.

Monitoring exists but is thin. The Karthala volcano observatory, established in the late 1980s, has operated for decades with limited instrumentation and intermittent funding, so warning times depend heavily on the character of a given episode. Because the summit is frequently hidden in cloud and the flanks are inhabited to a considerable altitude, an eruption can be well under way before it is widely recognised.

The northern volcano, La Grille, is older and considered dormant. It reaches about 1,087 metres and its surface is studded with scoria cones, small steep piles of cinder marking individual vents. Its greater age matters agriculturally: its lavas have weathered long enough to make real soil, so the north of the island supports cultivation that the raw flows of Karthala's flanks cannot.

sections.heading: Anjouan, Mohéli and the shapes that erosion leaves
sections.body:
Move southeast along the chain and the landscapes record what happens to a volcanic island as it ages, subsides and is worn down by rain. The sequence is one of the clearest natural experiments in island geomorphology anywhere, compressed into 300 kilometres.

Nzwani, or Anjouan, is a striking triangle, with three peninsulas radiating from a central massif crowned by Mount Ntringui at about 1,595 metres. Radial valleys cut deeply into the flanks, so the island is essentially a set of steep ridges separated by ravines, with very little flat ground outside a narrow coastal fringe and a few small plains. The volcanic rock has weathered long enough to produce deep red tropical soils, which are fertile but, once the forest holding them is removed, extremely erodible on gradients of this kind. A crater lake, Dzialandzé, sits in the highlands, a reminder that the island's volcanism, though long finished, was explosive in its final phases. The island's combination of high relief, deep soil, heavy rain and the highest rural population density in the country makes it the most environmentally stressed place in the archipelago by a wide margin, and the one where the connection between land use and water supply is most visible on the ground.

Mwali, or Mohéli, is a long, narrow island built along an east-west ridge that rises to about 790 metres, with a comparatively gentle southern coast fringed by a scatter of small offshore islets. It has the smallest population and, partly as a consequence, retains proportionally the most intact forest and the healthiest reefs in the Union. Its marine park, created in 2001 and later upgraded to national park status, was the country's first protected area and is built around community management of the reefs, the nesting beaches used by green turtles and the seagrass beds that support a small dugong population.

Maore, or Mayotte, is the end state. Its volcanoes stopped building millions of years ago and the island has subsided and eroded into a set of low, rounded hills reaching only about 660 metres. Its coastline is deeply indented and its rivers, unlike those of Ngazidja, are permanent. It is split into a larger Grande-Terre and a small Petite-Terre offshore, the latter containing Dziani Dzaha, a crater lake of extraordinary chemistry: strongly alkaline, saline, and coloured green by dense blooms of cyanobacteria. Researchers study it as a modern analogue for the oceans of the early Earth, when similar microbial communities dominated, which is a remarkable thing to find in a small maar crater on a small island.

Across the four islands, then, the sequence runs from bare young lava with no rivers, through deeply dissected middle-aged mountains with failing rivers, to a low worn island with permanent streams and a drowned coastline. Age is the variable, and almost every other physical difference follows from it.

sections.heading: The Mayotte lagoon and the submarine eruption of 2018
sections.body:
Mayotte's most remarkable geographical feature is not on the island at all but around it. As the volcanic edifice subsided and eroded over millions of years, the fringing coral reef that once hugged its shore kept growing upward to stay in the light, and the gap between reef and shrinking island widened into a lagoon. The result is one of the largest enclosed lagoons in the world, covering roughly 1,100 square kilometres, enclosed by a barrier reef about 160 kilometres long, with lagoon depths reaching several tens of metres and a series of passes cutting through the barrier. Along part of the southwestern side there is a double barrier reef, an outer and an inner barrier separated by deep water, a configuration that occurs in only a handful of places worldwide. The lagoon is the reason Mayotte has calm anchorages, extensive seagrass beds, mangroves and a reef fish fauna far richer than the narrow young fringing reefs of Grande Comore can support.

Then, in 2018, the region delivered one of the largest geological surprises of recent decades. On 10 May 2018 an intense earthquake swarm began beneath the sea east of Mayotte, unusual for an island long considered volcanically dead. Thousands of earthquakes followed, several above magnitude 5, felt strongly on an island with no memory of such things. On 11 November 2018 seismic stations around the world recorded a strange, very long-period signal lasting about twenty minutes, originating near Mayotte, which was detected as far away as Chile and Hawaii and which had no obvious explanation at the time. Meanwhile GPS stations showed the island itself moving: several centimetres eastward and downward each month, accumulating over the following year to roughly twenty centimetres of eastward displacement and on the order of ten to twenty centimetres of subsidence.

Oceanographic surveys beginning in May 2019 found the cause. About fifty kilometres east of the island, on a seafloor around 3,500 metres deep, an entirely new volcanic edifice had been built, standing roughly 800 metres high. It was later named Fani Maoré. The erupted volume, estimated at several cubic kilometres, makes it the largest submarine eruption ever directly documented, and the deflation of a very deep magma reservoir, apparently tens of kilometres down in the mantle, explains the island's subsidence and eastward drift.

The event has practical and scientific consequences. Practically, Mayotte's slow subsidence adds directly to relative sea-level rise on an island whose settlements crowd the coast, and the earthquake sequence has required a monitoring network that did not previously exist. Scientifically, the discovery that a large, deep magmatic system was active beneath the supposedly extinct end of the chain undermines the simplest hotspot model and strengthens the case that tectonic structures in the Mozambique Channel play a controlling role.

sections.heading: The water problem: an island with heavy rain and no rivers
sections.body:
Grande Comore receives a great deal of rain, in many places well over two metres a year and on the windward flanks of Karthala considerably more than that. It has no permanent rivers at all. Understanding why is the key to understanding daily life on the largest island in the country.

The reason is the rock. Young basaltic lava flows are riddled with voids: gas bubbles frozen into the rock, rubbly zones between flows, cracks formed as the lava cooled, and lava tubes left where molten rock drained out from under a solidified crust. Rain falling on such a surface does not run off; it disappears downward almost immediately. Only when lava has been weathered for a long time, its minerals broken down to clays that plug the pores, does an island of this type develop the low-permeability surface that streams require. Ngazidja's lavas have not had that time. The water goes straight into the ground and travels to the sea underground.

What it forms there is a freshwater lens. Fresh water is slightly less dense than seawater, so rainwater accumulating in a permeable island floats on top of the saltwater that saturates the rock below sea level, in a lens-shaped body thickest under the centre of the island and thinning toward the coast. The classic approximation, associated with the nineteenth-century work of Badon Ghyben and Herzberg, is that for every metre the water table stands above sea level, roughly forty metres of fresh water extend below it. The practical consequences are unforgiving. Coastal wells tap the thin edge of the lens and are commonly brackish. Pumping too hard draws the saltwater interface upward, a process called upconing, and a well can turn saline in weeks and take years to recover. Rising sea level pushes the interface inland.

So most households on Grande Comore rely instead on rainwater harvested from roofs into cisterns, supplemented by communal catchments. The system works in an average year and fails in three specific ways: during a long dry season, when cisterns empty; when volcanic ash contaminates every open catchment on the island at once, as in 2005; and when a cyclone damages roofs and tanks.

The other islands have surface water but their record is a cautionary tale. Anjouan once had a substantial network of perennial streams, with figures in the range of forty or more commonly quoted from the mid-twentieth century; today only a small fraction still flow year-round. The cause is the clearing of highland forest for cultivation. Forest soil under a canopy absorbs rain and releases it slowly; bare compacted ground sheds it in flash floods and stores nothing, so peak flows rise and dry-season base flows collapse. Mayotte, with permanent rivers and two reservoirs, is not immune either: a severe drought in 2023 drew its reservoirs down and forced water rationing across the island for months.

sections.heading: Climate: two monsoon seasons and a steep rainfall gradient
sections.body:
The Comoros have a tropical maritime climate governed by the seasonal reversal of the winds across the western Indian Ocean, and the local vocabulary for it is the most efficient summary available. The kashkazi runs from about November to April: hot, humid, with winds out of the northwest and the great majority of the year's rain. The kusi runs from about May to October: cooler, drier, with the southeast trade winds blowing steadily. The transition months are variable and often calm.

Temperatures are equable in the way that small islands in warm oceans always are, because the surrounding sea, at roughly 25 to 29 degrees Celsius through the year, buffers everything. At sea level average monthly temperatures run from about 23 to 28 degrees, with March typically the hottest month, when daytime highs reach the high twenties to around thirty, and July or August the coolest, when night-time lows near the coast fall to about nineteen or twenty. Humidity is high year round. Altitude changes this sharply: temperature falls roughly six degrees for every thousand metres of ascent, so the upper slopes of Karthala at 2,000 metres and above are genuinely cold at night, sometimes near freezing, and are frequently wrapped in cloud.

Rainfall is where the geography becomes dramatic, because the mountains create enormous gradients over very short distances. Moist air arriving off the ocean is forced to rise over the volcanic flanks, cools, and drops its moisture on the windward side; by the time it descends the far side it is dry. Moroni, on the western coast of Grande Comore, records something in the region of 2,700 millimetres a year. Parts of the windward slopes of Karthala are estimated to receive well over 5,000 millimetres. Yet other parts of the same island, in the rain shadow, receive a fraction of that. Mayotte, lower and flatter, is drier overall, generally in the range of 1,200 to 1,600 millimetres. Two places twenty kilometres apart can have entirely different agricultural possibilities.

Interannual variability is significant and is driven partly by large-scale climate modes. The El Niño-Southern Oscillation and the Indian Ocean Dipole both modulate rainfall and cyclone activity in this sector, so a dry season that fails or a wet season that arrives late is often traceable to conditions thousands of kilometres away in the Pacific or the eastern Indian Ocean. For a country whose agriculture is almost entirely rain-fed and whose drinking water on the largest island comes from roof catchment, this variability is not an abstraction; a single poor wet season translates directly into empty cisterns and failed crops, and forecasting skill for these modes, while real, remains limited at the seasonal lead times that would be most useful.

sections.heading: Cyclones and the storm hazard
sections.body:
The Comoros sit near the northern edge of the southwest Indian Ocean tropical cyclone basin, one of the world's more active cyclone regions, whose official season runs roughly from mid-November to the end of April. Most storms in this basin form well to the east, over the warm water between Diego Garcia and Madagascar, and track generally westward and then southward, which means Madagascar and the Mascarene islands take the brunt of them. The Comoros are struck less often. They are not struck rarely, and the storms that reach them find a population living almost entirely on exposed coasts in buildings of highly variable quality.

The reference event in living memory is Cyclone Kenneth in late April 2019. Kenneth formed in the northern Mozambique Channel, an unusual location, and passed directly across the northern Comoros while intensifying, before going on to make landfall in Mozambique as the strongest tropical cyclone on record to strike that country. Its effects in the Comoros were severe out of proportion to the wind speeds recorded there. Official figures put deaths in the country at around seven, but the wider impact was enormous: roughly 345,000 people affected, which is on the order of forty per cent of the national population, and something in the region of 11,000 homes destroyed. Crop losses were heavy in an economy where a large share of households farm. Damage estimates ran into the low hundreds of millions of US dollars against a national economy of little more than a billion.

The reason a moderate storm can do so much is a chain of local vulnerabilities. Roofs are commonly corrugated iron and are the first thing to go, and their loss also destroys the rainwater catchment that supplies drinking water. Steep deforested slopes on Anjouan turn heavy rain into landslides and debris flows. Coastal settlements sit metres above sea level with little natural buffer, because in many places the protective beach has been mined away for construction sand. Reefs damaged by bleaching dissipate less wave energy than healthy ones. And the small size of the country means a single storm can affect essentially all of it at once, so there is no unaffected region from which relief can be organised.

The direction of change is unfavourable, though the details are uncertain. The scientific consensus is reasonably firm that the proportion of tropical cyclones reaching the highest intensities is increasing in a warming climate and that rainfall rates within storms are rising, while whether the total number of storms in this basin will rise or fall is genuinely unresolved. Sea-level rise adds directly to storm surge, and for Mayotte the ongoing volcanic subsidence adds a local increment on top of the global signal. Preparedness measures that make the largest difference here are unglamorous: securing roofs, protecting cisterns, and stopping the removal of beach sand.

sections.heading: The ocean around the islands: currents, eddies and deep water
sections.body:
The sea around the Comoros is not a passive backdrop. It is one of the more energetic and peculiar circulations in the world ocean, and it determines the islands' fisheries, their coral connectivity and their weather.

The broad-scale picture starts far to the east. The South Equatorial Current flows westward across the Indian Ocean and strikes the east coast of Madagascar, where it splits. The northern branch, the Northeast Madagascar Current, runs along the coast, rounds the island's northern cape, and heads west directly toward the Comoros. Near the African mainland it divides again, part turning north as the East African Coastal Current and part entering the Mozambique Channel. The archipelago sits precisely at the junction, which is why water arriving at the islands has typically crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean and why larvae, drifting seeds and marine animals move readily between Madagascar, the Comoros and the East African coast.

What happens inside the Mozambique Channel is stranger. For a long time atlases showed a steady southward Mozambique Current down the length of the channel. Direct measurement, particularly from the 1990s onward using moorings and satellite altimetry, showed something quite different: instead of a continuous current, the channel is dominated by a train of very large rotating eddies, typically around 300 kilometres across, extending to great depth, drifting southward at a few kilometres a day and passing at a rate of roughly four to seven per year before eventually feeding into the Agulhas Current off South Africa. These eddies pass the Comoros and produce currents that reverse and strengthen unpredictably, which is a serious matter for small boats crossing between islands.

The eddies also matter biologically. The tropical open ocean here is generally nutrient-poor, and productivity is concentrated where physics brings deep, nutrient-rich water toward the surface. The edges of these eddies, the fronts between them, and the wakes downstream of the islands themselves all do this, producing patchy but locally rich feeding grounds that attract tuna, seabirds and cetaceans. The Comoros exclusive economic zone, of the order of 160,000 square kilometres, is many times the land area and is fished both by local artisanal fishers and, under access agreements, by distant-water tuna fleets.

One feature of the local bathymetry deserves emphasis because it shapes both fishing and science. The islands' flanks plunge steeply, so water 200 metres deep can lie only a kilometre or two from the beach and water 1,000 metres deep only a few kilometres out. A fisher in a small outrigger canoe or an outboard-powered skiff can be over genuinely deep water within minutes of leaving shore. That geometry is the reason Comorian handline fishers, working steep volcanic slopes at 150 to 400 metres for oilfish and other deep species, became the world's principal accidental collectors of one of the most famous animals in biology.

sections.heading: Reefs, seagrass, mangroves and the working coastline
sections.body:
Coral reefs fringe all four islands, but their form varies systematically with island age, which makes the archipelago a textbook illustration of the sequence Charles Darwin proposed in 1842: fringing reef, then barrier reef with lagoon, then atoll, as a volcanic island subsides while the reef keeps growing upward.

Grande Comore, the youngest island, has narrow, discontinuous fringing reefs, often only tens to a couple of hundred metres wide, because the reef has had little time to build and the steep young slopes offer limited shallow platform. Anjouan and Mohéli have better-developed fringing systems, and Mohéli in particular has extensive reef around its southern coast and its scatter of offshore islets. Mayotte, the oldest and most subsided, has the full barrier-reef-and-lagoon configuration, including a rare double barrier on part of its southwestern side. No island in the group has yet reached the final stage, an atoll with no land left in the middle, but the trend along the chain points unmistakably in that direction over the next several million years.

Associated habitats follow the same pattern. Seagrass meadows need shallow, sheltered, sediment-floored water, which the young islands largely lack and the lagoons of Mayotte and the sheltered bays of Mohéli provide. Those meadows support the archipelago's small and precarious dugong population, probably numbering only a few tens of animals, and they are a critical nursery habitat for reef fish. Mangroves are similarly limited on Grande Comore, where there are few sheltered muddy estuaries and no rivers to supply sediment, but form real stands on Mohéli and cover several hundred hectares on Mayotte.

The reefs have taken heavy damage. The mass bleaching event of 1998, driven by exceptional sea surface temperatures associated with a very strong El Niño, killed a large fraction of shallow-water corals across the western Indian Ocean, with mortality in many surveyed sites reported in the range of half to nine-tenths of coral cover; recovery has been partial and uneven, and further bleaching followed in later warm years, notably 2016. Damage from destructive fishing and sedimentation off deforested slopes compounds the thermal stress.

The single most locally consequential coastal problem, however, is sand. The Comoros has almost no accessible aggregate for construction other than beach sand and reef-derived material, and decades of extraction have stripped beaches from many stretches of coast. The consequences are direct: houses and roads undercut by the sea, loss of the natural buffer that dissipated storm waves, and destruction of turtle nesting habitat. The archipelago is regionally important for green turtles, with the beaches at Itsamia on Mohéli among the most significant nesting sites in the western Indian Ocean and the focus of a long-running community conservation programme. Humpback whales also use these waters, migrating north from Antarctic feeding grounds to calve and breed between roughly July and October, close enough inshore to be watched from land.

sections.heading: Endemic life on land: an island fauna under pressure
sections.body:
The Comoros form part of the Madagascar and Indian Ocean Islands biodiversity hotspot, and although the total land area is tiny the level of endemism is high, because oceanic islands that have never been connected to a continent accumulate species that arrived by chance and then evolved in isolation.

The birds are the best-documented group and include species found on a single mountain on a single island. The Karthala scops owl is restricted to the montane forest of Karthala on Grande Comore, essentially a strip of habitat around one volcano. The Mount Karthala white-eye lives only in the heath and stunted forest near the summit, above roughly 1,700 metres, which is to say in an area of a few square kilometres. The Anjouan scops owl was believed extinct for most of the twentieth century and was rediscovered in 1992 in remnant highland forest. A scops owl on Mohéli was described as a distinct species only in the late 1990s. Alongside these are endemic pigeons, a thrush, a drongo, flycatchers and sunbirds, giving the archipelago a list of endemic birds well into the twenties when subspecies are counted.

The most spectacular endemic mammal is Livingstone's fruit bat, one of the largest bats in the world, with a wingspan approaching a metre and a half and a dark, almost black pelage. It is confined to steep forested slopes on Anjouan and Mohéli, roosting communally in tall emergent trees, and its total population has been estimated at only around 1,200 to 1,300 individuals, which places it among the most threatened bats anywhere. Its dependence on mature forest on precisely the steep slopes that are being cleared for cultivation makes its decline a direct index of deforestation. A captive breeding population maintained in Europe exists as insurance.

There is also an instructive oddity: the mongoose lemur, a Madagascan primate, occurs on Anjouan and Mohéli, almost certainly introduced by people at some point in the past few centuries. As the species has declined in its native northwestern Madagascar, the introduced Comorian populations have become a meaningful share of the world total, which poses an awkward conservation question about the value of a non-native population of a threatened species.

The pressure on all of this comes from land clearance. Forest cover has contracted severely, particularly on Anjouan, and international assessments during the 2010s repeatedly listed the Comoros among the countries with the highest proportional rates of forest loss in the world, with annual figures cited in the high single digits of percentage; such figures depend heavily on definitions and baselines and should be read as indicating a severe trend rather than a precise rate. The mechanism is straightforward. A dense and growing rural population with little off-farm employment, no fertiliser to speak of, and declining yields on existing plots, moves uphill into forest. Introduced rats, cats and mynas do the rest.

sections.heading: The coelacanth and the steep submarine slopes
sections.body:
No account of Comorian geography is complete without the fish, because the animal and the place are inseparable: the coelacanth lives where it does because of the specific shape of these islands underwater.

Coelacanths are lobe-finned fishes, a group whose fins contain a bony internal skeleton attached to the body by a fleshy stalk rather than fanning directly off the trunk as in ordinary ray-finned fish. The lineage was known from fossils and was believed to have died out with the dinosaurs, around sixty-six million years ago, until a live specimen was trawled up off East London, South Africa, in December 1938. It was recognised as extraordinary by Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, curator of the small local museum, and described the following year by the ichthyologist J. L. B. Smith, who named it Latimeria chalumnae after her and the nearby Chalumna River. Smith then spent fourteen years searching for a second, and it turned up in December 1952 off Anjouan, where local fishers already knew the fish, called it gombessa, and regarded it as poor eating but useful, its rough scales serving as an abrasive.

For decades afterwards the Comoros were treated as the coelacanth's home, and although populations have since been found off Tanzania, Mozambique, Madagascar and South Africa, and a distinct second species was discovered in Indonesian waters in the late 1990s, the Comorian population remains the best studied. The reason the fish concentrates here is bathymetric. Coelacanths shelter by day in caves in volcanic rock at depths of roughly 150 to 250 metres, where the water is cool, around 15 to 20 degrees, and emerge at night to drift and feed. The steep, cave-riddled lava slopes plunging directly from the shoreline of Grande Comore provide exactly that habitat within a couple of kilometres of the beach, which almost no other coastline offers.

That same geometry is the threat. Comorian fishers working deep handlines for oilfish set their gear at precisely coelacanth depths, and incidental capture is essentially the only significant source of mortality. The animal is not eaten and has no commercial value; it simply dies. The Comorian population has been estimated at only a few hundred individuals, and the species' biology makes any loss serious: it grows very slowly, bears live young after a gestation that may exceed three years, and research published in 2021, based on counting growth rings in scales, suggested a lifespan approaching a century with sexual maturity delayed until roughly the age of fifty. Those figures are estimates from a small sample and should be treated as provisional, but the direction is clear.

One common claim is worth correcting. The coelacanth is often called the ancestor of land vertebrates. It is not. It is a surviving member of a related branch, and the closest living relatives of four-limbed land animals are the lungfishes. The coelacanth's value is as an unusually conservative survivor from a group that was otherwise lost.

sections.heading: Soils, farming and the perfume economy
sections.body:
Comorian agriculture is shaped by two facts that follow directly from geology: soil quality tracks island age, and water availability tracks porosity. On the raw lava flows of Karthala's flanks there is barely any soil at all, and cultivation proceeds in pockets of ash and weathered material between rocks, planted by hand with no possibility of ploughing. On the older northern volcano of Grande Comore, on Anjouan and on Mohéli, weathering has produced deep red tropical soils that are genuinely fertile when covered but which lose their thin organic surface layer within a few seasons of clearing on a steep slope.

Subsistence farming dominates and is largely a matter of intercropped tree and root crops: cassava, bananas and plantains, taro, sweet potato, coconut, breadfruit and maize, often grown together under a partial canopy in a system that resembles a managed forest garden more than a field. This arrangement is well adapted to steep ground because permanent tree cover holds the soil, and its erosion under population pressure, as farmers shift toward continuous open cultivation, is one of the country's central environmental problems. Livestock is limited: some cattle, goats and poultry, with little grazing land available. The country imports a large share of its food, especially rice, which is the staple.

The export economy rests on three aromatic crops, and their combined story is the economic geography of the archipelago in miniature. Ylang-ylang is a tree whose intensely fragrant yellow flowers are distilled into an essential oil used in fine perfumery, and the Comoros has long been among the world's leading producers, its oil a classic component of the great French perfumes. Cloves and vanilla make up most of the rest. Vanilla in particular is extraordinarily labour-intensive: outside its native Mexico the orchid has no effective natural pollinator, so every flower must be hand-pollinated during a few hours on the single day it opens, and the cured pods then require months of processing.

Two consequences are worth drawing out. First, all three crops are high-value, low-volume products sold into volatile world markets, so national export earnings swing violently with prices set elsewhere, and none of them feeds anyone. Second, and less obviously, ylang-ylang distillation is a direct driver of deforestation, because the traditional stills are fired with wood and the fuel demand is substantial. An export crop that appears benign is, through its processing, one of the pressures removing the forest that regulates the island's water. Improved stills that use far less fuel exist and their adoption is one of the more tractable interventions available.

Underlying all of this is the remittance economy. A large Comorian diaspora, concentrated in France and especially around Marseille, sends money home on a scale that has repeatedly been estimated at a fifth or more of national income, far exceeding the value of all agricultural exports combined. In economic terms the country's most important export is labour.

sections.heading: Settlement, borders and the crossing to Mayotte
sections.body:
People in the Comoros live around the edges. On Grande Comore the interior above the cultivation belt is essentially uninhabited, the road system is a coastal ring, and villages sit in an almost continuous chain along the shoreline. On Anjouan and Mohéli settlement follows the coast and the lower valleys, with cultivation climbing the slopes above. Moroni, the capital on the western coast of Grande Comore, is a small city by world standards, with a population in the low tens of thousands in the urban core. Mutsamudu on Anjouan holds the country's deepest-water port, which matters because Moroni's own harbour is shallow enough that larger vessels have often had to anchor offshore and transfer cargo by lighter.

Language and religion are archipelago-wide and reflect the islands' position in the Indian Ocean trading world. Comorian, or Shikomori, is a Bantu language closely related to Swahili, with a distinct variety on each island: Shingazidja, Shinzwani, Shimwali and Shimaore. French and Arabic have official status alongside it. The population is overwhelmingly Sunni Muslim, and Arabic script was historically used to write Comorian.

The political geography is unusual and consequential. A referendum in December 1974 asked the four islands whether they wished to leave France. Three voted overwhelmingly to go; Mayotte voted, by a margin usually given as around two-thirds, to stay. The Comoros declared independence for the whole archipelago on 6 July 1975; France retained Mayotte, which voted again in 2009 to become a full overseas department and did so in 2011. The Union of the Comoros has never recognised this and the United Nations General Assembly has passed resolutions supporting Comorian sovereignty over the island. The internal politics of the Union have been turbulent, with something on the order of twenty coups and attempted coups since independence, secession attempts by Anjouan and Mohéli in 1997, a settlement in 2001 creating the present federal Union with a presidency rotating among the islands, and an African Union-backed military operation in 2008 that restored Anjouan to Union control.

Out of this comes one of the most lethal short migrations in the world. Anjouan lies roughly seventy kilometres from Mayotte across open water. Until 1995 movement between them was free; a French visa requirement introduced that year made it illegal, and it continued anyway in small fibreglass outboard boats known locally as kwassa-kwassa. The gradient driving it is stark: Mayotte is by a wide margin the poorest part of France and by an equally wide margin the richest place in the archipelago, with a per-capita income many times that of the Union. Estimates of deaths on the crossing since the mid-1990s vary enormously and are frankly uncertain, but the commonly cited figures run into many thousands, and no serious observer disputes that the toll is very large. It is a border created by a referendum result and enforced across a channel that the sea, the currents and the eddies make dangerous.

sections.heading: Compound hazards, hard limits and what can actually be done
sections.body:
Put the strands together and the Comoros emerge as a place where several hazards overlap on a very small area, so that a shock in one system propagates immediately into the others. An eruption on Karthala contaminates the cisterns and produces a drinking-water emergency. A cyclone strips the roofs that fill those cisterns, and the rain that follows triggers landslides on slopes that were deforested to grow food and to fuel the stills that distil the export crop. Coral reefs weakened by warming dissipate less wave energy, and beaches mined for building sand no longer absorb what gets through. Off Mayotte, a deep magma reservoir emptying tens of kilometres below the seafloor is quietly lowering the island into the sea while global sea level rises to meet it.

Several things are genuinely tractable, and they are worth naming because they are not exotic. Rainwater harvesting can be made far more resilient with covered cisterns, first-flush diverters that discard the contaminated initial runoff, and household treatment; these directly address the ash and storm failure modes. Protecting and restoring highland forest on Anjouan is the single highest-value intervention on that island, because forest cover is what converts a flash flood into dry-season base flow, and the loss of perennial streams there is a demonstrated, reversible consequence of clearance rather than an act of climate. Terracing, agroforestry and tree-crop systems hold soil on gradients where open cultivation cannot. Crushed basalt aggregate can replace beach sand, and the island has an effectively unlimited supply of basalt. Fuel-efficient distillation stills cut the firewood demand of the perfume industry substantially. Community-managed marine protected areas, of which the Mohéli park is the regional model, have a real record of recovering reef fish stocks when local users control access.

Other limits are hard and should be stated without euphemism. Sea-level rise cannot be addressed locally by a country whose greenhouse gas emissions are negligible. The subsidence of Mayotte is a geological process no policy can stop. Karthala will erupt again, probably within decades, and the only question is warning time. And the economic gradient across the seventy kilometres between Anjouan and Mayotte is not something geography can close.

A final word on the uncertainty in all of this. Population figures rest on infrequent censuses in a country with large undocumented movement. Deforestation rates depend heavily on how forest is defined and vary widely between sources. The coelacanth population estimate is derived from a small number of individually identified animals. The origin of the archipelago itself remains a live scientific argument, reopened rather than settled by the discovery of a huge new volcano where nobody expected one. A reader should hold the physical geography of these islands with confidence and the numbers attached to it with a degree of caution.

guides.title: Geography of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
guides.summary: A full geographical account of the Democratic Republic of the Congo: its size and borders, the Congo River system, the central basin rainforest and peatlands, climate, the eastern rift highlands and volcanoes, the mineral-bearing southern plateaus, and how all of it shapes settlement and risk.

sections.heading: Orientation: Scale, Position, and Why This Geography Matters
sections.body:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo occupies about 2,345,000 square kilometres of central Africa, which makes it the second-largest country on the continent after Algeria and roughly the eleventh largest in the world. To give that number a shape a reader can hold: it is about the size of Western Europe, roughly a quarter the area of the United States, and about seventy-seven times the size of Belgium, the small European state that governed it as a colony and then a personal royal possession. It straddles the equator, extending from about five degrees north to about thirteen and a half degrees south, and from about twelve degrees east to thirty-one degrees east. That east–west span is wide enough that the country legitimately keeps two time zones, one hour apart, with the division running roughly through the middle of the territory.

Three facts about its position do most of the explanatory work for everything that follows. First, it sits astride the equator, so the sun's annual migration passes over it twice, and the rain belt that follows the sun therefore crosses the country twice a year. That single fact produces the double rainy season of the interior, the mirror-image seasons north and south of the line, and — indirectly — the extraordinary steadiness of the Congo River. Second, it occupies almost the whole of a single enormous structural basin, a saucer of ancient rock that collects the drainage of an area of about 3.7 million square kilometres, second in the world only to the Amazon. Almost the entire country drains to one river mouth. Third, it is very nearly landlocked despite that river: its Atlantic frontage is only about thirty-seven kilometres wide, a sliver at the river's mouth around the towns of Muanda and Banana. A country of this size with a coastline that short is a genuine geographical oddity, and it has consequences for trade, sovereignty and infrastructure that persist to this day.

Understanding this geography is not an academic exercise. The distribution of copper and cobalt in the far southeast, of coltan and gold in the eastern highlands, and of diamonds in the Kasai, has shaped conflict and migration for a century. The absence of usable roads across a rainforest the size of a subcontinent explains why river transport still matters more than highways. The volcanic and limnic hazards of the eastern lakes place millions of people in the path of rare but catastrophic events. This is a country where physical geography remains a first-order determinant of daily life.

It is also worth fixing the names early, because the region has produced an unusual amount of nomenclatural confusion. The country was the Congo Free State, then the Belgian Congo, then Congo-Léopoldville, then Zaire from 1971 to 1997, and has been the Democratic Republic of the Congo since. Its smaller northwestern neighbour, capital Brazzaville, is the Republic of the Congo, sometimes distinguished as Congo-Brazzaville. Both take their name from the same river, and older maps and books use whichever label was current when they were printed.

sections.heading: Borders, Coastline, and the Shape of the Territory
sections.body:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo shares land borders with nine countries, more than almost any other African state, and the character of those borders varies enormously. To the west and northwest lies the Republic of the Congo, a different country with a confusingly similar name, separated for much of its length by the Congo and Ubangi rivers. To the north lies the Central African Republic, with the Ubangi again forming much of the line. To the northeast is South Sudan, across remote savanna and gallery forest. The eastern frontier runs against Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania, and follows the chain of rift lakes so closely that the border through Lake Tanganyika is simply a line drawn down open water. To the southeast lies Zambia, across the mineral-bearing plateaus, and to the south and southwest Angola, including the separate Angolan exclave of Cabinda which sits between the DRC's coastal strip and the rest of Angola.

That coastal strip deserves attention because it is a deliberate historical artefact. At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 the territory was granted access to the Atlantic through a narrow corridor along the north bank of the Congo estuary, giving roughly thirty-seven kilometres of ocean frontage. For a country of 2.3 million square kilometres, that ratio of coast to area is among the most extreme in the world. The practical result is that the deep-water options are minimal, the main ocean port at Matadi lies about 150 kilometres upriver and is limited by the estuary's navigation constraints, and a great deal of Congolese trade has historically moved instead through foreign ports — Mombasa and Dar es Salaam to the east, Beira and Durban to the south, Lobito in Angola to the southwest.

The overall shape of the territory is that of a rough saucer with a spout.
