The terra firma rainforests of the north and the Chaillu and Mayombe uplands are tall, closed-canopy formations rich in commercial timbers, okoume, sapelli, sipo, limba, wenge among them, and in an immense diversity of lesser-known trees, lianas, and understory life. The inundated and swamp forests of the Cuvette, flooded for part or all of the year, are lower and more specialized, dominated by water-tolerant species and raffia palms. Gallery forests trace the rivers out into the grasslands, and the mosaic zones where forest and savanna interlock, as on the Bateke fringes and in the Niari, shift their boundaries over decades with fire and climate.

The savannas are the great counterpoint, covering the sandy plateaus, the Niari valley floors, and the coastal terraces. Most are anciently maintained by human burning as much as by soil and climate, and they carry their own flora of fire-hardened grasses and shrubs and a fauna adapted to open country; they are also where nearly all the republic's farming and grazing happens, since the forest soils, paradoxically, are mostly poor, their fertility locked in the living biomass rather than the ground. This inversion, rich-looking forest on poor soil, workable savanna on better soil, explains much of the country's settlement map and is a standard lesson in tropical geography.

The headline global issue is carbon. Congo Basin forests are a planetary carbon store and a net absorber of carbon dioxide, and within them the republic holds the jewel described earlier: its share of the Cuvette Centrale peatlands, the largest tropical peat complex known, whose thirty billion tonnes or so of stored carbon across the two Congos dwarf the annual emissions of entire continents. Peat is safe only while wet; drained, logged over, or dried by a shifting climate, it oxidizes or burns, and there is no practical way to put it back. This gives the republic an outsized role in climate diplomacy relative to its size, expressed in initiatives such as the Blue Fund for the Congo Basin and the 2018 Brazzaville peatland declaration, and in a growing, if uneven, flow of international conservation finance.

The pressures are real but, so far, more moderate than in many tropical countries. Deforestation rates in the republic have historically been low by global standards, a fraction of a percent a year, because population is small and concentrated in two cities; the main drivers are shifting agriculture around towns and roads, charcoal, and selective logging, which degrades rather than clears. Nearly all accessible forest outside parks is allocated to logging concessions, and the quality of their management varies, with some certified operations and others far looser. The long-term questions are infrastructural: proposed mines, new roads, oil interest near the peatlands, and the growth of Brazzaville's demand for land and fuel. The republic thus embodies, in one country, the central bargain of tropical conservation: a poor state holding assets of immense planetary value, and the unresolved matter of who pays to keep them standing.

sections.heading: Wildlife and National Parks: Gorillas, Elephants, and the Protected Estate
sections.body:
Few countries of any size hold wildlife riches comparable to the republic's, and its protected-area estate, covering more than a tenth of the national territory, guards some of the last great strongholds of Central African forest fauna. The flagship is Nouabale-Ndoki National Park in the far north, roughly 4,000 square kilometers of essentially pristine lowland rainforest between the Sangha and the Ndoki rivers, so untouched that early surveyors described chimpanzees showing no fear of humans. The park anchors the Congolese third of the Sangha Trinational, a transboundary World Heritage Site shared with Cameroon's Lobeke and the Central African Republic's Dzanga-Ndoki parks since 2012, and its research stations, above all the observation platform at Mbeli Bai, have produced decades of continuous study of western lowland gorillas, forest elephants, sitatunga, and bongo gathering in the sunlit clearing.

West of it, Odzala-Kokoua National Park is one of Africa's oldest, first designated under the French administration in 1935 and later expanded to over 13,500 square kilometers spanning forest, savanna mosaics, and a constellation of mineral-rich bais. Odzala is celebrated for gorilla densities among the highest recorded anywhere, alongside forest elephants, buffalo, bongos, and more than 440 bird species, and it has become the center of the republic's nascent high-end ecotourism, with lodge circuits built around gorilla tracking and bai viewing. The northern estate is completed by newer designations such as Ntokou-Pikounda National Park, created in 2013 toward the peatland margins, and the Lac Tele Community Reserve in Likouala, where conservation is run with, and by, the resident fishing communities of the swamp forests.

The south balances the ledger. Conkouati-Douli National Park on the Atlantic frontier is the country's most ecologically varied protected area, running from ocean waters, where humpback whales pass and sea turtles nest on the beaches, through lagoons and mangroves into forested hills with elephants, gorillas, and mandrills; a long-running sanctuary there rehabilitates chimpanzees. Near the capital, the Lefini Faunal Reserve and the adjoining Lesio-Louna sanctuary protect Bateke plateau savannas and gallery forests, and serve as the release landscape for orphaned gorillas rescued from the bushmeat and pet trades, while the Dimonika Biosphere Reserve holds a core of the Mayombe's mountain rainforest.

The species list behind these names is formidable: perhaps the world's most important populations of western lowland gorilla, tens of thousands strong; a large share of the surviving forest elephants, whose basin-wide numbers have been devastated by ivory poaching; central chimpanzees; leopards and golden cats; dwarf and slender-snouted crocodiles; hippos in the rivers; over 700 bird species nationally; and a fish fauna of the Congo system that ranks among the most diverse on Earth. The threats are the familiar ones, commercial bushmeat hunting feeding urban markets, ivory poaching, logging roads that open remote forest, and disease, for Ebola outbreaks around Odzala in the early 2000s killed thousands of gorillas, one of the worst wildlife epidemics ever recorded. Management increasingly runs through partnerships: international conservation organizations co-manage several parks with the state, notably in Nouabale-Ndoki and Odzala, funding rangers, research, and community programs. The result, imperfect but substantial, is that the republic remains one of the very few places where the full Central African forest fauna still exists at landscape scale.

sections.heading: Cities and Population: Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire, and an Urban Nation
sections.body:
For a country of forests, swamps, and empty plateaus, the republic has a startling human geography: it is one of the most urbanized nations in Africa, with roughly two-thirds of its approximately six million people living in cities, and well over half concentrated in just two of them. The pattern is extreme primacy on a double axis: nearly everything demographic and economic happens either at Brazzaville, the political capital on the Congo River, or at Pointe-Noire, the economic capital on the ocean, with the railway and highway between them stringing the principal secondary towns like beads, Dolisie and Nkayi chief among them. Vast departments of the north, Likouala and Sangha, count their populations in the low hundreds of thousands across areas the size of European states, and their density in single digits per square kilometer.

Brazzaville, with well over two million inhabitants, roughly a third of the entire nation, spreads along the north bank of Malebo Pool on sandy terraces below the Bateke escarpments. Founded in 1880 at the treaty between Brazza and the Makoko of the Teke, it served as the capital of French Equatorial Africa, and its history has continental resonance: during the Second World War it was for a time the symbolic capital of Free France, and the 1944 Brazzaville Conference held there set early terms for the postwar evolution of the French empire. The modern city is the seat of government, the university, and the river port where the inland waterway meets the railway; its districts range from the colonial-era core and the vibrant quarters of Poto-Poto and Bacongo to fast-growing sandy peripheries. Its face-to-face relationship with Kinshasa across the pool, the two capitals connected by a twenty-minute ferry and separated by an often-complicated border, is unique on Earth.

Pointe-Noire, with well over a million people, is the country's window on the world: the deep-water port, the terminus of the railway, and the headquarters of the oil industry, with a business skyline, an expatriate presence, and a franker commercial temper than the administrative capital. Its beaches, fishing quarters, and the nearby Diosso Gorge give it a coastal identity, and its port handles not only national trade but transit for the interior. Dolisie, the third city at perhaps a hundred and thirty thousand people, commands the western Niari and the routes into the Mayombe and toward Gabon; Nkayi anchors the sugar belt; Ouesso, Owando, and Impfondo are the modest metropolises of the forest north.

The human fabric is largely Bantu-speaking, with the Kongo group the largest nationally, concentrated in the south, the Teke on the plateaus, and the Mbochi and related peoples prominent in the north, alongside indigenous forest communities in the northern departments; French is official, while Lingala and Kituba serve as the great lingua francas of the river and the rail corridor respectively. Urbanization at this level, in a country whose farms cannot yet feed its cities, has decisive geographic consequences: the nation imports much of its food through Pointe-Noire, the corridor between the two cities carries the national life, and rural depopulation leaves the forests emptier of people even as urban demand for bushmeat, charcoal, and land radiates outward from the two poles. Understanding the republic demands holding this paradox: an equatorial forest state whose typical citizen is a city dweller.

sections.heading: Resources, Economy, and Transport: Oil, Timber, and the Congo-Ocean Railway
sections.body:
The republic's economy stands on a narrow geographic base: petroleum from beneath the Atlantic, timber from the forests, and the transport corridor that links river to ocean. Oil dominates everything. Discovered in the coastal basin in the late 1950s and developed offshore from the 1970s, production from fields off Pointe-Noire and toward the Angolan border made the country one of sub-Saharan Africa's principal producers, and hydrocarbons have long accounted for the great majority of export earnings and government revenue; the republic joined OPEC in 2018. The industry's geography is almost entirely marine, rigs and floating production vessels served from Pointe-Noire, with a refinery there supplying part of domestic demand, and its rents explain both the country's middle-income statistics and the classic distortions of an oil state, from debt cycles tied to crude prices to the underdevelopment of farming.

Timber is the second pillar and the most visibly geographic one. Nearly all accessible forest outside protected areas is organized into logging concessions, from the Mayombe and Chaillu in the south to the vast units of Sangha and Likouala in the north, producing okoume, sapelli, and other high-value species. Southern logs ride the railway to the port, northern ones move by river toward Brazzaville or by road through Cameroon; policy has pushed, with mixed success, for in-country processing rather than raw log export, and certification distinguishes the better-managed concessions. The mineral shelf behind these two pillars is long on promise: potash near the coast, iron ore at Zanaga and Mayoko, polymetallics in the Niari, gold and diamonds artisanally worked, but large-scale mining has repeatedly stalled on infrastructure costs and price cycles. Agriculture, cassava as the universal staple, plantains, peanuts, sugar at Nkayi, cocoa in the north, employs much of the rural population yet supplies well under half of national food needs, leaving the cities dependent on imports, a vulnerability every development plan promises to correct through the Niari's underused soils.

Transport is where geography rules most nakedly. Because the Livingstone Falls block the river below Malebo Pool, the country's economic spine is the overland link between Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire: the Congo-Ocean Railway, 510 kilometers through the Niari valley and the Mayombe, built between 1921 and 1934 at a human cost, tens of thousands of forced laborers dead, that remains a foundational national memory, and the parallel National Route 1, rebuilt in the 2010s as a modern paved highway with Chinese financing, which has taken much of the freight. From Brazzaville northward, the waterway takes over: barge convoys on the Congo and Ubangi serve the northern departments and landlocked Bangui, making the republic a transit state for its neighbors, while in the far north a road pushes through Ouesso toward Cameroon. Air links, Maya-Maya airport at Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire's airport chief among them, knit the roadless interior to the two poles.

The pattern, an extractive coast, a corridor, a river, and a vast, lightly touched green interior, is the republic's geography rendered as economics, and its future turns on familiar questions: whether farm and forest wealth can diversify an oil state, whether iron and potash projects will industrialize the corridor, whether a bridge will finally join Brazzaville to Kinshasa, and whether the standing forests and peatlands will earn more alive than cut. In each case the map, coast, mountains, valley, plateau, and basin, will have the deciding vote.

guides.title: Geography of Côte d'Ivoire
guides.summary: The physical and human geography of Côte d'Ivoire: its location, coast and lagoons, plateaus and western mountains, the four great rivers, climate and vegetation zones, national parks, the cocoa economy, cities from Abidjan to Yamoussoukro, resources, environmental pressures, and transport links.

sections.heading: Where Côte d'Ivoire Sits: Location, Size, and Borders
sections.body:
Côte d'Ivoire, known in English as Ivory Coast, occupies the central stretch of West Africa's Atlantic-facing coast, fronting the Gulf of Guinea between roughly 4 and 11 degrees north latitude and 2 and 9 degrees west longitude. With a land area of about 322,463 square kilometers, it is a medium-large African state, slightly larger than Poland or the American state of New Mexico, and it packs into that area an unusually complete cross-section of West African environments, from humid coastal lagoons through dense rainforest to open savanna approaching the Sahel. The country's compact, roughly squarish shape, spanning some 500 to 600 kilometers in each direction, means no point lies impossibly far from the coast, a fact with real economic consequences for a country whose life has long been organized around export agriculture flowing to Atlantic ports.

Five countries share its roughly 3,100 kilometers of land border. To the west lie Liberia, along about 780 kilometers of frontier largely defined by the Cavally River, and Guinea, along roughly 820 kilometers of upland border in the mountainous northwest. To the north are Mali, across about 600 kilometers of savanna frontier, and Burkina Faso, across roughly 550 kilometers, both borders drawn across the open Sudanian belt and both crossed for generations by labor migration toward the Ivorian plantations. To the east, Ghana adjoins along about 720 kilometers, a border that separates two of the world's dominant cocoa producers and cuts through culturally related Akan populations on both sides. The southern boundary is the Gulf of Guinea itself, a coastline conventionally measured at about 515 kilometers.

The borders, like most in West Africa, are colonial artifacts. France assembled the territory as a colony from 1893, fixing limits with British Gold Coast (Ghana), Liberia, and its own neighboring colonies of French Sudan (Mali), Upper Volta (Burkina Faso), and Guinea through treaties and administrative decisions between the 1890s and the 1940s; independence came on 7 August 1960, inheriting those lines. The consequence is a country that spans, deliberately from the colonizer's viewpoint, the full forest-to-savanna gradient, uniting a humid south suited to tree crops with a dry north oriented toward livestock and grains, a complementarity that has shaped internal migration, the national economy, and at times the country's politics.

In regional context, Côte d'Ivoire is the economic heavyweight of francophone West Africa and a founding member of the West African Economic and Monetary Union, using the CFA franc. Its position gives it a gateway role: the ports of Abidjan and San-Pédro serve not only the national territory but the landlocked economies of Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger, whose imports and exports move along Ivorian corridors. Geography, in other words, made Côte d'Ivoire a hinge between the Atlantic world and the West African interior, and most of the country's human story can be read as the working-out of that position.
steps: Locate the country on the Gulf of Guinea between Liberia and Ghana, with Guinea, Mali, and Burkina Faso inland to the north and west.
Fix the key magnitudes: about 322,463 square kilometers of territory, roughly 3,100 kilometers of land border with five neighbors, and about 515 kilometers of coast.
Read the borders historically: French colonial lines of 1893 to 1960 deliberately spanning the forest-savanna gradient that still structures the economy.

sections.heading: The Coastline and Lagoons of the South
sections.body:
The Ivorian coast runs about 515 kilometers along the Gulf of Guinea, and it divides into two contrasting halves at roughly the meridian of Fresco. The western coast, from the Liberian border to around Sassandra and Fresco, is a rocky, cliffed shore where the crystalline rocks of the interior plateau reach the sea, producing small bays, headlands, and pocket beaches, with the port town of San-Pédro occupying one of the few good natural sites. The eastern coast, from Fresco to the Ghanaian border, is entirely different: a low, straight sand barrier hundreds of kilometers long, built by the powerful west-to-east longshore drift of the Gulf of Guinea, which throws up beach ridges that seal off the river mouths behind them. The surf on this barrier coast is heavy and the shore almost harborless by nature, a fact that delayed European penetration for centuries and earned stretches of the Gulf their old reputation as a lee shore without refuge.

Behind the eastern sand barrier lies the coast's defining feature: a nearly continuous chain of lagoons stretching some 300 kilometers, the largest system of coastal lagoons in West Africa. The three principal complexes, from west to east, are the Grand-Lahou lagoon system at the mouth of the Bandama, the Ébrié Lagoon, and the Aby Lagoon shared with Ghana. The Ébrié Lagoon is the giant: roughly 130 kilometers long though rarely more than a few kilometers wide, covering on the order of 560 square kilometers, and it is on its northern shore that Abidjan grew. The lagoons receive the discharge of the great rivers, mix fresh and salt water in seasonal rhythm, and support fisheries, lagoon-side farming, and dense waterborne traffic; canoe and ferry transport across and along them remains part of daily life in Abidjan and the lagoon towns.

The decisive human intervention on this coast was the Vridi Canal. Because the sand barrier blocked all natural deep-water access, colonial engineers cut a channel through it directly south of Abidjan, completing the work in 1950 after earlier attempts had silted. The canal, roughly 2.7 kilometers long and dredged to ocean-going depth, connected the Ébrié Lagoon to the open sea and transformed Abidjan almost overnight into one of Africa's great ports, sheltered inside the lagoon yet open to the world. Nearly everything about modern Abidjan's primacy, its industry, its population of millions, follows from that single geographic surgery.

The coast is also where Côte d'Ivoire is most environmentally exposed. The same longshore drift that built the barrier now starves beaches interrupted by ports and the canal, and erosion eats several meters of shore per year in places; the historic first capital, Grand-Bassam, whose colonial quarter was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, and the town of Grand-Lahou have both lost ground to the advancing sea. Low elevation makes the lagoon rim sensitive to sea-level rise, and Abidjan's torrential June rains regularly flood low districts, making coastal management one of the country's permanent geographic problems.
steps: Divide the coast mentally at Fresco: rocky western shore with San-Pédro, and the long eastern sand-barrier shore backed by lagoons.
Learn the three lagoon systems west to east — Grand-Lahou, Ébrié (about 130 kilometers long, Abidjan's lagoon), and Aby on the Ghana border.
Remember 1950 and the Vridi Canal as the hinge event that made Abidjan a deep-water port, and note ongoing erosion at Grand-Bassam and Grand-Lahou.

sections.heading: Relief and Landforms: A Country of Plateaus Rising to Western Mountains
sections.body:
Most of Côte d'Ivoire is remarkably level. The national territory is essentially a vast, gently tilted tableland of ancient Precambrian basement rock, part of the West African craton, planed down by hundreds of millions of years of erosion into plains and low plateaus that rise gradually from the coastal zone toward the north. The southern third lies mostly below 200 meters; the center consists of plateaus between roughly 200 and 350 meters; and the northern savanna country runs generally between 300 and 400 meters, studded with isolated erosion-resistant hills. Travelers crossing the country therefore experience relief less as mountains than as a slow climb punctuated by inselbergs, the abrupt granite domes and knobs that rise from the plains, and by lateritic mesas capped with the iron-rich crusts characteristic of deeply weathered tropical shields.

The grand exception fills the west. Along and inland of the borders with Liberia and Guinea, the land rises into genuine highlands, the Ivorian share of the Guinea Highlands, locally called the region of the Dix-Huit Montagnes, the Eighteen Mountains, around the city of Man. Here summits regularly exceed 1,000 meters: Mont Tonkoui reaches about 1,189 meters and carries one of the country's few montane climates, and the ranges around Man, the Toura and Dan mountains, give the west its distinctive scenery of forested ridges, waterfalls, and cooler air. The country's culminating point stands on its very edge: Mont Richard-Molard in the Nimba Range, 1,752 meters, on the border with Guinea at the point where Liberia also approaches, the highest peak of both countries. The Nimba massif is geologically distinct, an itabirite ridge extraordinarily rich in iron ore, and ecologically famous enough that its slopes are protected as the Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site shared with Guinea.

Between mountain west and level east, a few secondary features organize the map. A belt of hills associated with ancient greenstone formations arcs through the center and north, including the Baoulé ridge country near Bouaké and ranges near Odienné in the northwest, and it is along these old volcanic-sedimentary belts that most of the country's gold occurs. The southeast contains the only notable sedimentary basin, a narrow coastal strip of younger rocks lying beneath the lagoons and supporting the offshore continental shelf where the country's oil and gas fields lie. River valleys are broad and shallow rather than gorge-like, though the larger rivers break over rapids and falls where they cross harder rock bands, a geography that frustrated navigation but eventually invited dams.

The practical readings of this relief are straightforward. Level terrain made road and rail building comparatively easy and agriculture expansive; the absence of internal mountain barriers helped a single national market form. The western highlands, wetter and cooler, grow distinct crops and shelter distinct cultures. And the deep tropical weathering that smoothed the land also created its soils: thick, leached, iron-rich mantles that are agriculturally workable but fragile, productive under forest and tree crops yet quick to harden and erode when stripped bare.
steps: Picture the country as a low tilted tableland: under 200 meters in the south, 300 to 400 meters in the north, spiked by granite inselbergs.
Reserve real mountains for the west: the Man region's Dix-Huit Montagnes with Mont Tonkoui (about 1,189 meters) and the border summit Mont Richard-Molard in the Nimba Range at 1,752 meters.
Connect geology to economy: gold along the old greenstone belts, iron in Nimba, oil and gas in the narrow coastal sedimentary basin offshore.

sections.heading: Rivers and Drainage: The Cavally, Sassandra, Bandama, and Comoé
sections.body:
Four principal rivers drain Côte d'Ivoire from north to south into the Gulf of Guinea, and their parallel courses, spaced across the country like the tines of a fork, organize its hydrology. From west to east they are the Cavally, the Sassandra, the Bandama, and the Comoé. All four share a family character set by the country's geology and climate: they rise in the northern savannas or the Guinea Highlands, flow across the plateau in broad valleys interrupted by rapids where resistant rock crosses their beds, swell dramatically in the rainy seasons and shrink in the dry, and reach the sea through barrier-blocked mouths and lagoons rather than open estuaries. None is navigable for modern commerce over any great distance, a fact that pushed the country's transport history onto roads and rails, but their waters power dams, irrigate crops, and water the cities.

The Cavally, roughly 700 kilometers long, rises in the Nimba country of Guinea and spends most of its course as the working border between Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia, reaching the sea near Tabou. It drains the wettest, most forested corner of the country and remains the least tamed of the four. The Sassandra, about 650 kilometers, gathers its headwaters, including the Tiemba and Férédougouba, from the Guinea highlands and the Odienné country, and flows south to enter the sea near the town of Sassandra; its middle course was dammed at Buyo, creating one of the country's great reservoirs, and its lower basin waters the booming southwestern cocoa lands. The Bandama is the national river, the longest lying wholly within the country at roughly 800 kilometers, formed of the White Bandama from the north and the Red Bandama, or Marahoué, from the northwest. Dammed at Kossou in the country's center, it reaches the Gulf at Grand-Lahou. The Comoé, easternmost, is the longest overall at around 1,000 kilometers or more counting its Burkinabè headwaters near Banfora; it enters Ivorian territory through the northeast, gives its name to the vast Comoé National Park through which it flows, and reaches the sea through the Ébrié Lagoon by Grand-Bassam.

Regime, the seasonal rhythm of flow, differs meaningfully between north and south. The northern rivers' headwaters respond to a single wet season, producing one great annual flood cresting around September; the southern tributaries answer the double rainy season of the forest zone, flattening and doubling the peaks downstream. Dry-season low flows can be severe, and the great reservoirs exist substantially to smooth this variability for power generation. Beyond the big four, a fringe of smaller coastal rivers, the Bia in the southeast, which was the site of the country's first dam at Ayamé, the Agnéby, the Boubo, and the San-Pédro river in the southwest, drain the immediate hinterland of the coast, and the far northern edge of the country sends a small share of its water away from the Atlantic entirely, into the Niger basin via tributaries such as the Bagoé, a reminder that the savanna north lies on the continental divide between Gulf and Sahel.
steps: Learn the four rivers west to east — Cavally, Sassandra, Bandama, Comoé — with the Cavally as the Liberian border and the Bandama as the longest wholly Ivorian river at about 800 kilometers.
Attach each to its landmark: Buyo dam on the Sassandra, Kossou dam on the Bandama, Comoé National Park on the Comoé, Tabou at the Cavally mouth.
Understand the regimes: single September flood from the savanna north, double peaks from the forested south, and dams built to smooth both.

sections.heading: Lakes and Dams: Kossou, Buyo, and the Hydropower System
sections.body:
Côte d'Ivoire has virtually no large natural lakes; its still waters are almost all the work of engineers, and the story of its reservoirs is the story of the national electricity system. The sequence began modestly on the small Bia River in the southeast, where the Ayamé I dam, completed in 1959 on the eve of independence, and Ayamé II shortly after, gave the young country its first hydroelectric capacity within reach of Abidjan. The decisive project came a decade later in the exact center of the country: the Kossou Dam on the Bandama, built between 1969 and 1972 with international financing as the flagship of president Félix Houphouët-Boigny's development program. Kossou's reservoir, Lake Kossou, is by far the country's largest water body, capable of flooding on the order of 1,500 to 1,800 square kilometers at maximum level and holding roughly 27 to 28 billion cubic meters, numbers that made it one of tropical Africa's major artificial lakes.

Kossou's human geography is as important as its hydrology. Filling the lake drowned scores of Baoulé villages in the Bandama valley and required the planned resettlement of a population usually estimated between 75,000 and 100,000 people, an operation, the Kossou resettlement, that remains one of West Africa's largest development displacements and left lasting marks on the region's settlement pattern, including the new towns built for the displaced. The lake never consistently reached its design levels, because the decades after construction proved drier than the hydrological record used to plan it, a cautionary tale in African water planning; even so, it reshaped the center of the country, creating fishing economies, waterside farming, and the landmark around which the capital region of Yamoussoukro sits.

Downstream and on the other rivers the system grew. Taabo, commissioned in 1979 on the Bandama below Kossou, added a second stage on the same water. Buyo, completed in 1980 on the Sassandra, created the country's second great lake, on the order of 600 to 900 square kilometers, and powers the southwest. The newest major step is Soubré, downstream of Buyo on the Sassandra, a 275-megawatt plant inaugurated in 2017 with Chinese financing and construction, the largest single power station in the country, with further plants planned or building on the same river staircase. Alongside the large dams, several hundred small agro-pastoral reservoirs dot the northern savannas, watering cattle and dry-season gardens around towns like Korhogo, a quieter but regionally vital hydraulic landscape.

Hydropower today supplies a substantial minority of Ivorian electricity, commonly a quarter to a third depending on rainfall, with gas-fired plants burning offshore gas providing most of the rest, and the country exports power to its neighbors in good years. The reservoirs also carry costs: displaced histories, drowned forests, bilharzia and other waterborne diseases around new shorelines, and vulnerability to the drying trends that already humbled Kossou. The lakes are, in every sense, the signature of a state that chose to re-plumb its geography.
steps: Sequence the system: Ayamé on the Bia (1959), Kossou on the Bandama (1972), Taabo (1979), Buyo on the Sassandra (1980), Soubré (2017, 275 megawatts).
Attach Kossou's two defining facts: the country's largest lake by far, and the resettlement of roughly 75,000 to 100,000 people to create it.
Balance the ledger: a quarter to a third of national electricity and power exports, against displacement, disease shorelines, and rainfall risk.

sections.heading: Climate: Equatorial South, Savanna North, and the Harmattan
sections.body:
Côte d'Ivoire's climate is a north-south gradient driven by the annual migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, the band where the moist Atlantic monsoon air from the southwest meets the dry Saharan air from the northeast. As that boundary swings north in the boreal summer and south in winter, it drags the rains across the country, and the number of times and length of time it passes over a given latitude determines that place's seasons. The result is three broad climate belts. The southern coastal and forest zone, below roughly 8 degrees north, has an equatorial regime with four seasons: a long rainy season from about April or May to July, a short drier break in August and September, a short rainy season in October and November, and a long dry season from December to March. The center has a transitional tropical regime with the two wet seasons merging, and the north, above roughly 9 degrees, has a pure Sudanian regime: one rainy season from about May or June to October and a single long dry season the rest of the year.

Rainfall totals follow the same gradient. The wettest places are the southwest corner around Tabou and the western mountains, where annual totals reach 2,000 millimeters and locally more; Abidjan receives on the order of 1,800 to 2,000 millimeters, with June alone often delivering 500 millimeters or more in spectacular daily downpours that flood the city's low quarters. Totals decline northward through 1,200 to 1,400 millimeters in the center to roughly 900 to 1,200 millimeters at the northern border towns such as Odienné and Ferkessédougou, and, as everywhere along the Sahel margin, the northern rains vary sharply from year to year, with the drier decades since the 1970s having measurably shifted vegetation and river flows.

Temperatures are warm and remarkably even in the south, where the ocean moderates the air: Abidjan's monthly means sit between about 24 and 28 degrees Celsius year-round, with high humidity doing more to define comfort than the thermometer. Seasonal and daily ranges widen northward; Korhogo and the savanna towns see hot late-dry-season afternoons approaching 40 degrees in March and April, and surprisingly cool dry-season nights. The western highlands around Man are the cool exception, with montane freshness on the ridges of Tonkoui.

The characteristic wind of the dry season is the harmattan, the dusty northeasterly flowing off the Sahara, which reaches the north every year between roughly December and February, dropping humidity, hazing the sky with fine dust, parching skin and vegetation, and occasionally pushing all the way to the coast for a few days. Its arrival and retreat bracket the burning season in the savannas, when farmers and herders fire the grasslands. For agriculture, the whole calendar hangs on these rhythms: cocoa and the tree crops of the south depend on the double rains and dread long dry spells, while the cotton, maize, and cattle economy of the north lives inside the single wet season's window.
steps: Divide the country into three climate belts: four-season equatorial south, transitional center, and single-wet-season Sudanian north.
Anchor the numbers: about 1,800 to 2,000 millimeters of rain at Abidjan and the wet southwest, tapering to 900 to 1,200 millimeters in the far north.
Track the two great seasonal actors: the ITCZ migration that delivers the rains, and the December-to-February harmattan dust wind off the Sahara.

sections.heading: Vegetation Zones: Rainforest, Mosaic, and Savanna
sections.body:
Vegetation in Côte d'Ivoire mirrors the climate gradient in three great bands, and learning them is learning the country's ecological map. The southern band is, or was, Guinean moist forest, the Ivorian share of the Upper Guinean forest block that once ran nearly continuously from Sierra Leone to Ghana. In its natural state this is closed-canopy tropical rainforest and moist semi-deciduous forest: emergent trees rising past 40 meters, commercial timbers like iroko, sapele, and African mahogany, and an understory dense with lianas. The Upper Guinean forests are recognized as a global biodiversity hotspot, home to forest elephants, pygmy hippopotamus, twelve or more primate species including chimpanzees, and an exceptional roll of endemic plants; the western wet forests around Taï preserve the largest surviving fragment. It must be said plainly, and a later section details it, that most of this band is forest zone today only in the climatic sense: outside protected areas the canopy has largely been converted to cocoa farms, plantations, and secondary regrowth.

The central band is the forest-savanna mosaic, the tension zone where climate could support either cover and fire, soils, and human history decide locally between them. Its most famous feature is the Baoulé V, a wedge of savanna that plunges far south into the forest zone between the Bandama and Comoé basins, its point reaching almost to Toumodi and Dimbokro. Within the V and across the mosaic belt, open grasslands with fire-hardy trees interfinger with gallery forests that follow every watercourse, and island patches of dense forest survive on favorable soils. The mosaic is old cultural country, the Baoulé heartland, and its landscapes have been shaped for centuries by farming and the annual dry-season fires that hold the savanna open against forest regrowth.

The northern band is Sudanian savanna: open woodlands and tall-grass plains under a single wet season. Characteristic trees are the fire-resistant and human-valued species of the West African parklands, shea butter trees, néré locust beans, kapok, baobab, and the karité parkland pattern, in which farmers clear grain fields but deliberately spare the useful trees, gives the north its distinctive look of cultivated savanna orchard. Gallery forests line the rivers even here, and the far northeast around Comoé National Park preserves the largest intact sweep of this ecosystem in West Africa, a mosaic of savanna, woodland, and gallery forest vast enough to carry lions historically, and still elephants, buffalo, and hundreds of bird species.

Two transitional details complete the picture. Along the coast itself, distinct littoral vegetation, mangroves in the lagoon mouths, coastal thicket and savanna on the sand barrier, forms a narrow fourth zone of its own, ecologically small but economically busy. And in the western mountains, altitude creates montane grasslands and cloud-moistened forests on the high ridges of Nimba and Tonkoui, holding relict species far from their nearest kin. For any reader of Ivorian landscapes, the essential skill is reading each band twice: once as the potential vegetation the climate writes, and once as the actual cover that fire, farms, and chainsaws have negotiated with it.
steps: Learn the three bands south to north: Guinean rainforest, forest-savanna mosaic with the Baoulé V wedge, and Sudanian savanna parkland.
Attach each band's signature species: mahoganies and primates in the forest, gallery forests threading the mosaic, shea and néré parklands in the north.
Always distinguish potential from actual cover: outside parks, most of the forest band is now cocoa farms and secondary growth.

sections.heading: National Parks and Protected Areas: Taï, Comoé, and Nimba
sections.body:
Côte d'Ivoire's protected-area system contains some of West Africa's most important wild land, anchored by three UNESCO World Heritage properties. The crown jewel of the forest zone is Taï National Park in the far southwest, between the Sassandra and Cavally rivers: on the order of 3,300 square kilometers of core park plus buffer, protecting the largest remaining block of primary Upper Guinean rainforest anywhere. Created a national park in 1972 from earlier colonial reserves and inscribed by UNESCO in 1982, Taï shelters pygmy hippopotamus, forest elephant, eleven primate species, and, most famously, the chimpanzees whose stone and wooden nut-cracking tool culture has been documented by researchers for decades, one of the classic long-term primate study sites on earth. Its integrity is constantly pressed by poaching, gold panning, and the cocoa frontier that has consumed the forests around it, but the core has held.

The savanna counterpart is Comoé National Park in the northeast, one of West Africa's largest protected areas at about 11,500 square kilometers, larger than some countries in the region. Straddling the Comoé River, whose gallery forests thread its grasslands, the park spans an exceptional gradient from Sudanian savanna to forest islands, and carries elephants, buffalo, several antelope species, chimpanzees in its southern galleries, and a great raptor and waterbird fauna. It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1983, spent the years of the Ivorian crises on the List of World Heritage in Danger, from 2003 until 2017, as poaching and grazing surged while ranger control lapsed, and its removal from the danger list stands as one of African conservation's quiet good-news stories. The third World Heritage property is shared: the Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve, protecting the Ivorian slice of the Nimba massif's montane grasslands and forests along the Guinea border, a reserve of extraordinary endemism, including the viviparous Nimba toad, that remains listed in danger largely because of iron-mining pressure on the massif's Guinean side.

Beneath the big three spreads a national network of parks and reserves. Banco National Park is a rarity, a block of true rainforest of roughly 30 square kilometers enclosed within Abidjan itself, the city's green lung and a textbook case of urban conservation. Azagny National Park guards mangroves and coastal savannas near the Bandama mouth; the Îles Ehotilé park protects lagoon islands in the Aby system; Marahoué, Mont Péko, and Mont Sângbé parks hold mosaic and mountain country in the center and west, though Marahoué and Mont Péko suffered heavy farming invasion during the conflict years; and the N'Zo and other reserves buffer Taï. In the north, classified forests and hunting zones extend the protected estate around Comoé.

The geography lesson of the system is double. First, the parks now function as the reference archive of what each vegetation band actually is, since so much unprotected land has been transformed. Second, conservation here is inseparable from the agrarian story: the same cocoa and land hunger that felled the wider forest tests every park boundary, and the fate of Taï and its peers will be decided as much in commodity markets and rural policy as inside the park limits.
steps: Memorize the three World Heritage anchors: Taï (rainforest, chimpanzee tool culture, 1982), Comoé (11,500 square kilometers of savanna, 1983, off the danger list in 2017), and shared Mount Nimba.
Note Banco National Park as the rainforest inside Abidjan, and Azagny, Ehotilé, Marahoué, Mont Péko, and Mont Sângbé as the supporting network.
Read every park's prospects through the cocoa frontier: protected areas survive here only where the agrarian pressure around them is managed.

sections.heading: Agriculture and Land Use: Cocoa, Cashew, and the Working Landscape
sections.body:
No fact of Ivorian geography matters more to the world economy than this: Côte d'Ivoire is the planet's leading producer of cocoa, harvesting roughly two million tonnes of beans in a typical recent year, around 40 percent or more of global supply. The cocoa tree, an understory species of American origin, thrives in the humid forest zone's climate and deep soils, and its Ivorian career has been a moving frontier: beginning in the southeast under colonial rule, sweeping through the center-west after independence, and concentrating today in the southwest around Soubré, Méagui, and the San-Pédro hinterland, each stage advancing by clearing forest for young farms. Several million smallholders and farm workers, including large communities with roots in Burkina Faso and Mali drawn south over generations, live directly from the crop, and the state's finances have risen and fallen with its price since the boom decades that Ivorians call the miracle years.

Cocoa headlines a much broader tree-crop economy. Coffee, robusta almost entirely, was the miracle's co-star and remains widespread though diminished. Rubber has boomed spectacularly, making Côte d'Ivoire Africa's largest natural-rubber producer, with plantations spreading through the south; oil palm plantations feed domestic and regional vegetable-oil demand; and bananas and pineapples from the southeast ship to European markets. The north has its own export champion: cashew, whose drought-tolerant orchards have spread across the savannas so fast that Côte d'Ivoire has become the world's largest producer of raw cashew nuts, commonly cited above a million tonnes a year, transforming incomes around Korhogo and Bondoukou. Cotton anchors the north's older cash economy, feeding gins in Korhogo and the textile trade, while mangoes from the same parklands ride refrigerated ships to Europe.

Food farming underpins everything. Yams are the great staple of the center and the cultural crop of the Baoulé and Akan worlds, with harvest festivals to match; cassava, plantain, and maize feed the forest zone, with the plantain-based dishes of the south a national cuisine; rice, grown in lowlands and increasingly in irrigated schemes, is the urban staple whose imports remain a strategic worry; and the north grows millet, sorghum, and maize within its parkland agroforestry of shea and néré. Livestock is northern by geography, cattle herding tied to the savannas and to seasonal movements interlinked with Mali and Burkina Faso, while the humid south's tsetse flies historically excluded cattle and still shape the livestock map. Lagoon and coastal fisheries, plus the tuna port and canneries of Abidjan, complete the food geography.

The land-use ledger has two famous costs. The first is deforestation, treated later, since the tree-crop frontier consumed most of the natural forest. The second is dependence: a national economy geared to a handful of soft commodities lives exposed to their prices and to the climate that grows them, which is why every Ivorian development plan since the 1980s has preached processing at home, grinding cocoa, spinning cotton, shelling cashew, to capture value beyond the farm gate, with slow but real progress, notably in cocoa grinding, where the country now ranks among the world leaders.
steps: Fix the headline facts: about 40 percent of world cocoa, world's largest raw cashew producer, Africa's largest rubber producer.
Map crops to zones: cocoa, rubber, oil palm, coffee, banana in the forested south; cotton, cashew, mango, shea, and cattle in the savanna north; yams and plantain as the great staples between.
Read the landscape historically as a moving cocoa frontier — southeast, then center-west, now southwest — and note the policy push toward domestic processing.

sections.heading: Cities and Population: Abidjan, Yamoussoukro, and the Urban Network
sections.body:
Côte d'Ivoire counted about 29.4 million people at its 2021 census, and its population geography is dominated by one metropolis. Abidjan, spread around the Ébrié Lagoon in the southeast, holds roughly 6.3 million people in its autonomous district, more than a fifth of the nation, and functions as the economic capital in every practical sense: the main port, the industrial zones, the banks and headquarters, the international airport, and the cultural weight of West African francophone media and music. Its site is a geography lesson in itself, a city of peninsulas and islands, Plateau's high-rise core facing the popular quarters of Treichville and Marcory across the lagoon, the island commune of Petit-Bassam carrying the port, and bridges, including the Henri Konan Bédié toll bridge opened in 2014, stitching the halves together while lagoon ferries carry commuters between them. Abidjan's growth from a village to one of Africa's largest French-speaking cities in under a century followed the rail terminus and, above all, the Vridi Canal of 1950 that made it a deep-water port.

The political capital is elsewhere, and deliberately so. In 1983 president Félix Houphouët-Boigny transferred the capital to Yamoussoukro, his home town in the Baoulé country of the center, and endowed it with monumental infrastructure: broad boulevards, an international-class airport, the presidential complex with its famous crocodile lake, and the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, consecrated by Pope John Paul II in 1990 and recorded by Guinness as the largest church building in the world, its dome rising about 158 meters above the savanna. Yamoussoukro itself remains a modest city of a few hundred thousand, and most ministries and embassies still operate from Abidjan, making Côte d'Ivoire a classic case of the split between constitutional and functional capitals.

The secondary urban network is well developed by regional standards. Bouaké, in the center on the rail line, is the second city with on the order of 800,000 people, the market hub of the Baoulé region and the former headquarters of the northern rebellion during the 2002 to 2011 crises, a history that still marks it. Daloa and Gagnoa anchor the center-west cocoa country; San-Pédro, purpose-built with its port in the late 1960s and opened in 1971, commands the southwest and ships more cocoa than any port on earth; Man is the western mountain capital; Korhogo, the great town of the Sénoufo north, leads the savanna economy; and Abengourou, Bondoukou, Divo, and Odienné round out the regional centers. The east-west contrast matters: the forest south is densely settled and heavily urban, the north more thinly peopled, a gradient reinforced by decades of southward labor migration.

Two further facts shape the human map. First, migration: Côte d'Ivoire hosts one of Africa's largest immigrant populations, with roughly a quarter of residents having foreign origins, above all Burkinabè and Malian families drawn to the plantation economy, a demographic reality entangled with the citizenship politics of the crisis years. Second, youth and growth: with fertility still high and the census showing growth near 2.9 percent a year, the urban system, Abidjan above all, must absorb hundreds of thousands of new residents annually, which is why housing, lagoon flooding, and the new Abidjan metro under construction are permanent headlines.
steps: Anchor the hierarchy: Abidjan (about 6.3 million, economic capital and port) versus Yamoussoukro (political capital since 1983, home of the 158-meter basilica consecrated in 1990).
Place the regional capitals: Bouaké in the center, San-Pédro's cocoa port in the southwest, Daloa in the west, Korhogo in the north, Man in the mountains.
Remember the demographic drivers: 29.4 million people (2021), dense urban south versus thinner north, and a large immigrant population tied to the plantation economy.

sections.heading: Administrative Geography: Districts, Regions, and the Two Capitals
sections.body:
The administrative map of Côte d'Ivoire has been redrawn repeatedly since independence, and knowing its current logic helps in reading Ivorian news, statistics, and road signs alike. The framework in force since a 2011 reorganization is a four-tier pyramid: the country is divided into twelve districts plus two autonomous districts, the districts into thirty-one regions, the regions into departments, and the departments into sub-prefectures, with communes as the municipal layer inside them. The two autonomous districts are exactly the places a student of the country would guess: Abidjan, whose metropolitan sprawl and national weight demanded a government of its own, and Yamoussoukro, the political capital district. The twelve ordinary districts, with names drawn from geography and history such as Vallée du Bandama, Savanes, Montagnes, Lacs, Comoé, and Bas-Sassandra, mostly bundle two or three regions each and exist chiefly as planning and deconcentration frames; the region, each with its own capital and council, is the everyday unit of administration and identity below the national level.

The departments, numbering over a hundred, descend from the colonial cercles and have multiplied steadily as governments subdivided them to bring administration closer to citizens, and, critics add, to distribute prefectures as political rewards. Each department is run by a prefect representing the state, in the French tradition the country inherited and kept; sub-prefects administer the rural sub-prefectures, and elected mayors run the roughly two hundred communes. This dual system, appointed prefectoral authority alongside elected local councils, is the standard francophone West African pattern, and Côte d'Ivoire is among its most thoroughgoing practitioners.

The map's history explains some of its quirks. At independence in 1960 the country had a handful of departments; waves of reform in 1974, 1980, the 1990s, and the 2000s subdivided the territory into ever more departments and, from 1991, grouped them into regions whose number itself kept changing, sixteen, then nineteen, before the 2011 settlement at thirty-one regions within fourteen districts. The 2011 reform also formalized the autonomous status of Abidjan and Yamoussoukro, acknowledging in law the split-capital reality created in 1983 when Yamoussoukro became the official capital while Abidjan retained the ministries, embassies, and economy. Decentralization has moved in the same period from promise toward practice, with regional councils elected since 2013 and given budgets for schools, health posts, and rural roads, though the state's prefectoral spine remains the stronger vertebra.

For practical geography, a few district-level associations are worth carrying. Savanes district around Korhogo is the Sénoufo north; Montagnes around Man is the western highlands; Bas-Sassandra around San-Pédro is the cocoa southwest; Comoé and Sud-Comoé face Ghana in the southeast; Vallée du Bandama around Bouaké is the Baoulé center; Zanzan around Bondoukou is the northeast toward the Comoé park; and Lagunes is Abidjan's hinterland along the lagoon coast. These names, more than the frequently redrawn lower units, are the stable vocabulary in which Ivorians locate events in their country.
steps: Learn the 2011 pyramid: 12 districts plus the autonomous districts of Abidjan and Yamoussoukro, subdivided into 31 regions, then departments and sub-prefectures.
Distinguish the two authority lines: appointed prefects representing the state, and elected regional councils and mayors handling local affairs.
Carry the district vocabulary as mental geography: Savanes for the north, Montagnes for the west, Bas-Sassandra for the cocoa southwest, Vallée du Bandama for the center.

sections.heading: Natural Resources and Mining: Gold, Manganese, Oil, and Gas
sections.body:
For most of its modern history Côte d'Ivoire was the West African economy that prospered without mining, its wealth grown on farms while neighbors dug; the last two decades have changed that picture substantially. Gold leads the change. The same Birimian greenstone belts that make Ghana and Mali gold giants run through Ivorian territory, and since the 2000s their systematic development has lifted national output from a few tonnes to roughly 50 tonnes a year, with industrial mines such as Tongon in the north near the Malian border, Ity in the west, one of the country's oldest gold districts, Agbaou and Bonikro in the center-south, and Sissingué and newer projects filling the map. Alongside the industrial sector runs a vast informal one: artisanal gold digging, orpaillage, employs great numbers in the north and west, with the familiar costs of mercury use, pit deaths, school leakage, and, in places, smuggling networks, and periodic government campaigns attempt to formalize or clear the camps.

The hydrocarbon story is offshore. The narrow coastal sedimentary basin widens beneath the Gulf of Guinea into a producing province where fields such as Espoir and Baobab, developed from the 1990s and 2000s in deep water off Jacqueville and Grand-Lahou, made the country a modest oil producer, on the order of tens of thousands of barrels per day, and a more consequential gas producer, since the associated and non-associated gas, from fields like Foxtrot, fuels the thermal power stations that dominate the electricity mix. The game changed in 2021 when the Italian major Eni announced the Baleine discovery in the deep offshore, the country's largest find ever, with resources announced in the billions of barrels of oil equivalent; production began in 2023 and is planned to rise in phases, with the operator marketing it as a low-emissions development. The national refinery, SIR in Abidjan, one of West Africa's larger refineries, processes domestic and imported crude for the national and regional market.

Beyond gold and hydrocarbons the inventory is respectable if less developed. Manganese is mined in the east and northeast, notably around Bondoukou and at Lauzoua near the coast; nickel and cobalt laterites near Biankouma-Touba in the west and bauxite occurrences at Bénéné in the center-east have drawn projects; diamonds, historically dug around Séguéla and Tortiya and once embargoed by the UN during the crisis years for financing rebellion, flow again in modest legal volumes; and the Nimba region's iron ore, so consequential on the Guinean and Liberian sides of the massif, remains an Ivorian prospect constrained by conservation and infrastructure. Construction materials, granite, sand, and clinker inputs, feed the building boom, and the lagoons yield sand controversially.

The geographic summary is a country diversifying from an agricultural base rather than replacing it: minerals and hydrocarbons now supply a meaningful share of exports and state revenue and most of the electricity, but cocoa, cashew, rubber, and the working landscape remain the economy's floor, and the policy problem is the classic one of using extractive windfalls, Baleine above all, without letting them unbalance the farm-grown economy that employs the nation.
steps: Track gold as the headline mineral: Birimian belts, industrial mines like Tongon and Ity, output around 50 tonnes a year, plus a large artisanal sector.
Note the offshore sequence: Espoir and Baobab from the 1990s-2000s, gas fueling the power grid, and Eni's 2021 Baleine discovery producing since 2023.
Fill in the supporting cast — manganese, nickel laterites, diamonds at Séguéla and Tortiya, Nimba iron prospects — and remember agriculture remains the economy's base.

sections.heading: Environmental Pressures: Deforestation, Coastal Erosion, and Climate Change
sections.body:
The defining environmental fact of modern Côte d'Ivoire is the loss of its forest. At independence in 1960 the country held roughly 16 million hectares of forest; by the 2020s the commonly cited figure for remaining natural forest is under 3 million hectares, much of it degraded, a decline of more than 80 percent that gave Côte d'Ivoire, during several stretches, one of the highest deforestation rates on earth. The driver is no mystery: the cocoa frontier, joined by logging, rubber and palm expansion, and farm clearance generally, converted the Upper Guinean forest into the world's cocoa pantry. The loss reaches even the protected estate, where classified forests exist in name while carrying farms and villages, and parks like Marahoué and Mont Péko were extensively planted during the conflict years when enforcement collapsed. The consequences run from biodiversity, with forest elephants and primates squeezed into fragments, to climate itself, since the forest recycled moisture into the rains on which the same cocoa depends, and researchers link parts of the region's drying to the deforestation. Policy has responded with forest-code reform, promises of zero-deforestation cocoa negotiated with the chocolate industry and the European Union's due-diligence rules, agroforestry programs to put shade trees back into farms, and replanting campaigns, against the hard arithmetic of land hunger.

The coast contributes the second pressure. The sand-barrier shore is a dynamic system fed by river sediment and longshore drift, and dams that trap sediment, the Vridi Canal, and port works have starved segments of it, while sea-level rise pushes from offshore; erosion rates of one to several meters a year are recorded along stretches of the eastern coast, and the losses are not abstract: colonial-era Grand-Bassam, a World Heritage Site, and Grand-Lahou, whose old town has largely surrendered to the sea, are the emblematic cases. Lagoon pollution parallels the erosion, with Abidjan's domestic and industrial effluent, plastic, and the 2006 Probo Koala toxic-waste dumping scandal marking the Ébrié Lagoon's troubled recent history.

Climate change overlays everything. Observed trends include warming near 1 degree Celsius since the mid-twentieth century, more erratic rains with the northern belt drying in the Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and 1980s and partially recovering since, and heavier extreme downpours in the south, where Abidjan's June floods and deadly landslides on its slopes have become near-annual events. Projections point to hotter dry seasons, more variable planting rains, and stress on the cocoa belt's climatic envelope, with suitability shifting toward the cooler west, exactly where the last forests stand, a collision the zero-deforestation agenda must manage. Northern agriculture faces the classic Sahel-margin gamble of shorter, sharper wet seasons.

The remaining pressures are the familiar ones of a fast-growing middle-income country: water quality around mining and orpaillage, mercury in rivers, overfished lagoons and inshore waters worked by industrial fleets, charcoal demand gnawing the savanna woodlands, and air quality in a metropolis of six million. The national environmental story is thus not simple decline but a race: between degradation with deep economic roots and a state and society that have begun, unevenly, to reinvest in the geography that carries them.
steps: Anchor the headline numbers: forest down from about 16 million hectares in 1960 to under 3 million today, driven chiefly by the cocoa frontier.
Pair the coast's two emblems of erosion — Grand-Bassam and Grand-Lahou — with its causes: sediment starvation from dams and ports plus rising seas.
Frame climate change as the multiplier: hotter dry seasons, erratic rains, Abidjan's flood Junes, and a cocoa belt shifting toward the last forested west.

sections.heading: Transport Geography: Ports, the Railway, and the Corridors North
sections.body:
Côte d'Ivoire's transport map is built around a simple geographic proposition: connect the productive forest zone and the wider West African interior to two Atlantic ports. The first and greater is the Port of Abidjan, made possible by the Vridi Canal of 1950 and today one of sub-Saharan Africa's leading harbors, handling containers, the tuna fleet and canneries, oil products from the SIR refinery, and the cocoa, cashew, and timber trades; a second container terminal opened in 2022 with expanded draft for larger vessels, part of a sustained program of widening the canal and deepening berths. The second port is San-Pédro in the far southwest, opened in 1971 precisely to unlock the then-remote southwestern forests; it grew with the cocoa frontier it helped cause and now claims the title of the world's largest cocoa-exporting port, with ambitions in containers and minerals. Between them the two ports give the country a resilience most single-port West African economies lack.

The historic spine inland is the railway. The Abidjan-Niger line, begun by the colonial administration in 1904, crept north through Bouaké and Ferkessédougou and reached Ouagadougou in Upper Volta, today's Burkina Faso, in 1954, a meter-gauge single track of roughly 1,150 to 1,260 kilometers depending on the measuring points, of which around 630 kilometers lie on Ivorian soil. Operated since 1995 under concession by Sitarail, it carries freight, fuel and containers north, cotton and livestock south, and a storied passenger service, and it remains landlocked Burkina Faso's principal maritime outlet, which is why every Ivorian crisis reverberated instantly in Ouagadougou. Rehabilitation programs aim to restore speeds and capacity on aging track, and long-discussed extensions toward Niger and new mineral lines belong to the country's perennial project list, joined now by the Abidjan metro, an urban rail line under construction along the lagoon city's north-south axis.

Roads carry most of the traffic. The national network radiates from Abidjan: the coastal corridor east to Ghana and west toward San-Pédro and Liberia, the great northern axis through Yamoussoukro, Bouaké, and Korhogo to the Burkinabè and Malian borders, and the western roads to Man and Guinea. A motorway links Abidjan to Yamoussoukro and continues toward Bouaké, among the better expressways in the region, and the country participates in the Abidjan-Lagos coastal corridor project that would bind the Gulf of Guinea megacity chain from Côte d'Ivoire to Nigeria. Trucking dominates the interior corridors, complete with the region's classic frictions of checkpoints and fees, and the northern corridors to Bamako and Ouagadougou are among West Africa's busiest freight arteries.

Air and water complete the system. Félix-Houphouët-Boigny International Airport at Port-Bouët, Abidjan, is the national gateway and a regional hub for Air Côte d'Ivoire, with secondary airports at Yamoussoukro, Bouaké, San-Pédro, Korhogo, and Man. On the water, lagoon ferries and pinasses move Abidjan commuters and coastal villagers, and the lagoons' historical role as the coast's east-west highway survives in modest freight and growing water-bus services. The sum is the classic gateway geography: a country whose infrastructure funnels a subcontinent's interior toward its own two ocean doors, and prospers by keeping those doors wide.
steps: Fix the two ocean doors: Abidjan (via the 1950 Vridi Canal, second container terminal 2022) and San-Pédro (opened 1971, the world's top cocoa port).
Follow the spine inland: the 1904-1954 Abidjan-Ouagadougou meter-gauge railway run by Sitarail, Burkina Faso's main outlet to the sea.
Trace the road corridors — coastal Ghana-to-Liberia, the northern axis to Mali and Burkina Faso, the Abidjan-Yamoussoukro motorway — plus the Abidjan airport hub and lagoon ferries.
